The Plan · §7

7. Editorial Integrity & Canon Rules

The project must remain imaginative without confusing fiction, theory, evidence and live mechanisms.

The production system must protect the integrity of the source library while allowing creative expansion. This is the section that defines the boundaries.

7.1 The four-tier canon

Tier 1 — Core Source Canon (Locked)

The 29 foundational source files and verified technical records. These establish what the original corpus says. Immutable reference floor. The 29 HTML texts and the verified on-chain contracts (LIVE).

Tier 2 — Verified Expansion & Consistency-Checked Canon

Scripts, diagrams, adaptations and production material checked against Tier 1. Scripts, cutdowns, and guild productions verified against Tier 1 rules (four operators remain four; no living person named in fiction; every claim tagged).

Tier 3 — Community Variations & Dialects

Independent creative work that honours the core framework but may have its own artistic interpretation. Animation, comics, music, regional nodes like LondonX or BeastX that honour the Egg's core laws and pass the Bond Test.

Tier 4 — Heresies & Experimental Branches

Alternative, divergent, or deliberately speculative work. Allowed to exist openly as labelled alternatives, never silently merged into Tier 1. It may be explored, but it must not be silently merged into the source canon.

The tiers are not a hierarchy of quality. They are a hierarchy of authority. A Tier 4 work can be better than a Tier 2 work and still not be part of the canon.

7.2 The epistemic labels

Every important factual or conceptual claim must be classified. Use explicit labels consistently:

Label Meaning
OBSERVED A measurement, record or event that can be independently checked. Directly documented or independently verified.
MODEL A conceptual or structural model stated by the books. An explanatory framework or interpretation.
HYPOTHESIS A proposed explanation that remains unproven. A proposition that remains to be tested.
PATTERN A proposed relationship or recurring structure, not proof by itself. A comparative interpretation.
OBJECTION A serious challenge or alternative explanation. A substantive challenge.
FALSIFIER What evidence would weaken or disprove the claim. A condition or observation that would weaken or disprove a claim.
STORY Fictional narrative, dramatic device or invented character/event. Fiction, mythology or dramatised narrative.

Use the label that fits the statement. Do not promote a model or story into an observed fact through confident narration. The labels should be visible in the production where they matter. In documentary-style shows, they can be displayed as small on-screen icons. In fiction, they are handled by the fiction contract.

7.3 The mechanism labels

For token and system mechanisms, use a separate system:

Badge Meaning
LIVE Verified as currently deployed and functioning, supported by current on-chain or primary technical evidence. Deployed and verifiable on a PulseChain block explorer today.
DESIGN Specified or designed, but not necessarily deployed. An arrangement of already-live pieces requiring no new smart contract (such as the EROS Liquidity Tree).
PROPOSED An idea or future option, not yet implemented. A design discussion or threshold-gated future specification.

Verification rule. Any claim about contract ownership, total supply, transfer split, burn address, pools, liquidity or deployed token mechanics must be freshly verified before publication. Historical statements in a draft are not sufficient evidence of current state. A mechanism's status must be checked before publication.

7.4 The two-rail separation

Keep two editorial rails distinct:

Rail A — Documented history and investigation

The Illumination Strategy and Show 08. Primary sources, statutes, public records, dates, citations, verifiable claims, competing explanations and explicit uncertainty. Strictly primary-source, statute-driven, and falsifiable (DOCUMENTED, INFERRED, HYPOTHESIS).

Rail B — Mythic and speculative archive

Men of Renown, Masks, and the fictional material. Mythology, cosmology, symbolic readings, fiction and speculative interpretation. Held explicitly inside a Fiction Contract (ARCHIVE 7, STORY). It must carry an explicit fiction or speculation contract.

The rails may illuminate one another creatively, but Rail B cannot be used as evidence for Rail A. The two rails may be compared at clearly identified structural points, but fictional events must never be presented as documented history.

7.5 Known fiction and narrative devices

The following are fictional and must be presented as such:

  • Dr. Elara Vance and the 3:47 AM Atacama event in The Living Egg are fictional framing. Do not present them as a real scientific discovery or event.
  • The 422-name ledger and 11 active practitioners in The First Resonance are narrative devices, not empirical research.
  • The First Resonance, Sixteen Doors and The Continuity File are fiction projects and should be presented as such.
  • The Four operators are part of the EROS mythic/philosophical framework, not established historical or scientific entities.
  • The Visitor, the Room above the bakery, the stone, the ledger — all fiction.
  • Dr. Maya Okonkwo and the kitchen scene in the Continuity File — fiction.
  • The Strategic Continuity Office, Ines Calloway, the Commander, NEXUS-8 — fiction.
  • Cmdr. Helen Park, Dr. Rafael Mendez, Asha Varga, Nyra, Private Cole, President Elena Voss, Marcus Hale, Gina Ortiz, Jae Park — fiction (Sixteen Doors anthology cast).

7.6 The fiction contract

Fictional characters, organisations, events, and dramatic devices must remain identifiable as fictional. This includes:

  • The Dr. Elara Vance Atacama scene
  • The Visitor
  • The First Resonance ledger
  • The Continuity File's fictional institutional events
  • Cal, Hana, Owen, Ilse
  • The Ray, the Stone, the Room
  • The 422/11 ledger
  • The masked cast of the Continuity File
  • The courtroom, the chair, and the envoy

The story can ask powerful questions without pretending that its invented events happened. The fiction contract is what allows the project to be both dramatic and credible. The Continuity File's own contract says that the first thirty seconds of any adaptation must carry a spoken line: "The Continuity File. A dramatised archive. Fiction, built on a real instrument."

7.7 The Illumination special rule

The Illumination Strategy covers financial history, government instruments, national security, monetary policy, public statements, and other contentious subjects. Its programmes must show the difference between:

  1. What a primary document actually says.
  2. What a source or commentator claims it means.
  3. What the EROS analysis infers.
  4. What remains unverified or speculative.

Sensational questions are welcome. Unsupported conclusions presented as facts are not.

The Illumination Strategy's source is explicit: sensationalise the question, not the evidence. Do not imply institutional concealment, wrongdoing or scientific proof without robust evidence.

7.8 The on-screen display

In the documentary and investigative shows, the evidence classification should be displayed subtly but visibly. A small icon in the corner of the frame can indicate whether the claim currently being presented is OBSERVED, MODEL, STORY, HYPOTHESIS, PATTERN, OBJECTION, or FALSIFIER. In the fiction shows, the contract is handled by the framing — the audience knows they are watching fiction, and the fiction does not pretend otherwise.

The evidence system is not bureaucracy. It is the thing that lets the project be bold without being dishonest. It is the reason a viewer can trust the cosmology episode even when it is presenting a model, because the model is clearly labelled as a model. It is the reason a viewer can trust the tokenomics episode even when it is describing a proposed mechanism, because the mechanism is clearly labelled as proposed.

7.9 The Empty Column device

The Atlas 8F finding (documented in Section 13 of the Series Bible) handed the production an original device that the rest of the slate can use. Whenever an episode touches a primary record, a three-column card appears:

What the document says Filled in on screen.
What the retelling says Filled in on screen.
What you find This column is yours.

The third column is always blank and always lit. The narrator ends the beat on it: "This column is yours." It turns every verification gap into an invitation, which is what a participation loop needs, and it means no episode ever claims more than the record supports.

The Footprint Hunt is the standing weekly community event. Viewers find a primary document that bears on any claim in any show and fill in the empty column. The best find becomes the cold open of the next Open Call. It rewards exactly the behaviour the library says it values and creates a reason to come back every week.

7.10 The Bond Test

Every scene is tested against the bond before it is posted. Does it hold two things in relation without collapsing them into one? If a scene merely extracts, it fails. If it merely preaches, it fails. If it holds, it passes.

The Creator Contract (from Men of Renown, Section 18). On-screen text, in the book's own wording:

  • Four operators remain four.
  • Archive figures are actors or masks.
  • Density movement is a mask skill, not a fifth office.
  • No racial hierarchy. No atrocity tourism.
  • Illumination and Archive stay separate; connect by hinges only.
  • Functions are archetypes for drama, not saints.
  • Public bond and kit, not secret-order recruitment.
  • Meta-worldview is literacy, not a license to sneer.
  • Bond test every scene before you post it.

Rail rule (from the book's closing posts). Rail A is documented and falsifiable. Rail B is held inside a fiction contract. Connect only at money, recovery events, mythology homework and disclosure weather. Do not merge.

The Plan · §8

8. Technical & Economic Explanation Rules

The audience should be able to understand the instrument and its architecture without being pushed into hype.

This section is the rulebook for every token-related beat in Shows 05, 06, 07 and 13. It is what separates a documentary from a sales pitch. It is also what protects the project legally and reputationally. Every claim about a mechanism must be checkable before it is spoken aloud.

8.1 The core rules

Explain what is documented

Start with the primary record. If a mechanism is live, show the explorer. If it is designed, show the design. If it is proposed, say so.

Explain what is a design choice

Not every decision is a natural law. Say when a choice was made, by whom, and what alternatives existed.

Explain what remains proposed

A proposed mechanism is a proposal. It is not a product. It may not deploy. It may not be adopted. It is a design discussion, and the discussion is the point.

Explain ownership and participation in plain language

What does holding actually mean? What can a holder do? What can a holder not do? What is the difference between a holder and a builder? Say it plainly.

Explain liquidity as a structure with risks

Not as a guaranteed outcome. Liquidity is a design with dependencies. The dependencies can fail. Say so.

Keep fee and cost discussion brief

Unless a specific technical choice makes a fee material, do not foreground it. Focus on architecture, ownership, liquidity structure, human behaviour and practical design.

8.2 The AMM explanation rule

For automated market makers, the constant-product relationship (x × y = k) can be explained as a model of pool balances. It is a seesaw with two weights. Drop a coin on one side, the other side rises. The larger the coin drop, the more the seesaw tilts.

Shallow liquidity can amplify price movement and slippage. A small trade in a shallow pool produces a large price change. The same trade in a deep pool produces a small price change. This is not a design flaw. It is a feature of the mechanism, and it cuts both ways: shallow pools can amplify selling as easily as buying.

The number of pools alone does not prove depth or usable liquidity. Ten pools of ten dollars each are not the same as one pool of a hundred dollars. The count is not the depth. Depth is what happens when someone tries to trade size through the pool, and the slippage is small.

Do not present the number of liquidity pools as proof of liquidity depth. Do not treat a revoked administrative key as proof that liquidity or market value is protected. Do not present a price increase as guaranteed attention or demand.

8.3 The hybrid NFT and vault rule

Any hybrid NFT, vault, or withdrawal concept needs precise definitions of rights, unlocks, claims, and withdrawal mechanics. Do not imply guaranteed value or liquidity. Locked tokens do not automatically guarantee an NFT's market value or liquidity.

The cultural vault concept refers to the accumulated books, lore, mythology, community archive, art and education. It is distinct from an on-chain vault. Do not merge the two. The cultural vault is a library. The on-chain vault is code and control. The lock is the connection between the market cycle and the cultural cycle, but they are not the same thing.

Do not describe proposed hybrid NFTs, internal economies, or holographic environments as completed products. Keep fictional economic systems distinct from actual financial rights and deployed mechanisms.

8.4 The flywheel rule

The flywheel — attention and price discovery → visibility → discovery of the vault → participation → creation → renewed attention — is a strategic hypothesis, not an automatic mechanism.

The cycle can fail at every step. Attention can fail if the work is not interesting. Discovery can fail if the front door is not clear. Understanding can fail if the explanation is not good. Participation can fail if the ask is too large. Creation can fail if the brief is too vague. Renewed attention can fail if the work does not travel.

The episode should show both sides: the shape of the loop and the place where it can break. Show 06 does this explicitly with the four-frame loop and the red marker that blinks "can fail here" at each frame.

8.5 The verification rule

Any claim about contract ownership, total supply, transfer split, burn address, pools, liquidity or deployed token mechanics must be freshly verified before publication.

Historical statements in a draft are not sufficient evidence of current state. A mechanism's status must be checked against current on-chain data at the time of recording. The date-stamp goes on screen. The check happens again on the day of publication.

The production rule is: if you are going to say "live," show the explorer. If you are going to say "designed," show the design document. If you are going to say "proposed," say "proposed" and mean it.

8.6 What the show must never do

Never Why
Present a price increase as guaranteed attention or demand. Price is an observation, not a mechanism. It can go down as easily as up.
Present the number of liquidity pools as proof of liquidity depth. Count is not depth. Depth is slippage resistance at trade size.
Treat a revoked administrative key as proof that liquidity or market value is protected. Renunciation removes one lever. It does not protect the pool from a large sell.
Describe proposed hybrid NFTs, internal economies, or holographic environments as completed products. Proposed means not deployed. Saying otherwise is dishonest.
Keep fictional economic systems indistinct from actual financial rights and deployed mechanisms. The fiction contract exists for a reason. The audience must be able to tell the difference.
Imply institutional concealment, wrongdoing or scientific proof without robust evidence. Sensationalise the question, not the evidence.

8.7 The Cold-Viewer Trust Test

Every tokenomics episode should pass a simple test: would a sceptical newcomer trust this more after watching it than before?

If the episode is honest about what is live and what is proposed, if it shows its sources on screen, if it names the risk register as a feature rather than hiding it, if it teaches the viewer to check for themselves — then the answer is yes, and the viewer leaves with something they can use.

If the episode hedges, overclaims, hides the risks, or asks for trust without evidence, then the answer is no, and the viewer leaves thinking they have been sold something. That is the failure mode.

The three questions every viewer should be able to ask after watching.

  1. Who can change the rules?
  2. Where is the supply?
  3. Who stays when nothing is pumping?

These are the three questions Show 05 teaches. Ask them of anything. Then see what is left.

The Plan · §9

9. Distribution Strategy

Use a hub-and-spoke model. Do not try to make every platform the primary home.

The principle is simple: publish everywhere appropriate. Keep the library organised in one place.

9.1 One permanent home, many discovery channels

The EROS website should be the canonical, durable library and navigation system. It is not a marketing site. It is the library. YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, audio, and Telegram should distribute and connect people to it.

The website is the home. The platforms are the roads that lead to it. If a platform disappears, the library does not. If a platform changes its algorithm, the library does not. The website is the place that never disappears.

9.2 The EROS website — the permanent library

The website should become the central EROS Media experience. Each show receives a dedicated page with:

  • Title and short description
  • Trailer
  • Full episode
  • Short clips
  • Original source books
  • Transcript
  • Relevant diagrams and illustrations
  • Interactive material where useful
  • Evidence and source references
  • A simple viewer challenge
  • A contribution pathway

The existing EROS Corpus and Media pages provide the starting point. We should improve and connect those pages rather than create a disconnected website.

The website should be mobile-first, fast, searchable, and easy to navigate. The 3D Universe should be an optional deeper experience, not a requirement for understanding the material.

Infrastructure rule. The website should be simple, fast and maintainable. Do not delay the first release for a complete bespoke platform. A clean set of well-structured pages is enough to start.

9.3 YouTube — the primary screen destination

YouTube should be the main public video channel. Use it for:

  • Flagship episodes
  • Series playlists
  • Three-to-five-minute explainers
  • Shorts
  • Production diaries
  • Community discussions
  • Occasional live Open Calls

The 20-minute programme remains the flagship format, but not every subject needs 20 minutes. The length should serve the subject. Use audience-retention data and recurring format performance to decide what to produce more of. Group content by format and topic, review performance over time, and build repeatable formats rather than relying on one-off trends.

Make the first seconds understandable. Give each video one central promise. Provide a route to the relevant source page.

Platform rule. Video platforms frequently restrict or demonetise token-focused content. Plan for Shows 05, 06 and 07 to live primarily on the EROS web hub, Telegram (t.me/Eros_Revival), and X, while using Shows 00, 01–04, 08–13 as broad-reach discovery engines on YouTube and general platforms.

9.4 Short-form platforms — TikTok, Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts

These channels are the front doors. Produce original vertical versions of the strongest moments in the books and episodes.

A short should normally have:

  1. A strong opening question, statement, or visual.
  2. One idea.
  3. A clear demonstration or explanation.
  4. A memorable closing thought.
  5. A route to the full episode or source.

Use captions, readable text, and mobile-safe framing. Do not simply crop a landscape episode and expect it to work as a vertical video.

Create vertical, captioned clips from the same master production assets. Do not merely cut random moments out of long episodes. Write and edit each short as a self-contained discovery unit. Test different hooks and lengths. Platform guidance is a design signal, not a guarantee of reach.

Short-form examples from the source material.

  • The Mouth — 30 seconds. "Say SPREAD. Now say SPRAY." A visual demonstration, then an invitation to see the full episode.
  • Inward Is Forwards — 45 seconds. "What if the boundary is part of the explanation?" A question, an animated diagram, and a link to the cosmology.
  • The Web — 45 seconds. "Why might a network of smaller liquidity pools behave differently from one giant pool?" An analogy that leads into the technical explanation.

9.5 Audio and podcast

The books should also become an audio library. Possible formats:

  • Narrated book chapters
  • Full audio episodes
  • Short audio explainers
  • Interviews and discussions
  • Production diaries
  • Weekly community reviews

This is a relatively accessible contribution pathway for people who do not have animation or video skills. A single recorded passage is a complete contribution.

Where a show works as a conversation or narrated explanation, release an audio version. Keep the audio master and transcript connected to the episode page. Do not create an audio feed for every visual-heavy piece if it adds work without value.

9.6 Telegram and X — community coordination and distribution

Telegram remains the community coordination and distribution environment. Use it for:

  • New releases
  • Production briefs
  • Contributor recruitment
  • Feedback
  • Work-in-progress previews
  • Open Call submissions
  • Community discussion
  • Watch/listen sessions
  • Recognising contributors and linking to published work

X can be used for public announcements, short extracts, discussion, and directing new audiences to the library.

Archive rule. Telegram is a community coordination and conversation channel, not the only permanent archive. Important outputs must also be stored on the website or in the canonical project repository so they are not lost in chat history. Platform policies and content restrictions should be checked before publishing token-specific material. The website should always retain the complete, properly contextualised source package.

9.7 The distribution map

Platform Role Content type Token-adjacent?
EROS website Permanent home Everything — full library, transcripts, evidence, source books Yes — complete context
YouTube Primary video destination Flagship episodes, playlists, explainers, Shorts Selective — cosmology and story broad reach
TikTok / Reels / Shorts Discovery front doors Original vertical clips, one idea each Selective — strongest moments only
Audio platforms Audio library Narrated chapters, full audio episodes, explainers Yes — full context on the website
Telegram Coordination and community Releases, briefs, WIP, feedback, Open Call Yes — community direct
X Public announcements Short extracts, discussion, directing to library Selective

9.8 One master package, controlled derivatives

The production rule is: one master asset package, then controlled derivatives. Do not create separate research for every platform. Create one properly researched source package, and cut multiple outputs from it.

A standard episode package:

Output Typical format
Flagship episode8–20 minutes
Trailer30–90 seconds
Short clips3–6 clips
Explainer3–5 minutes
Vertical video3–5 versions
Illustrated articleWebsite
AudioNarrated episode or chapter
Interactive elementDiagram, map or HTML experience
Community taskOne achievable contribution

These are production targets, not rigid quotas. The subject and available resources determine the final package.

9.9 The release sequence

The first public release package should be:

Release 1 — The EROS Trailer

A short, visually strong introduction to the world and the library. Deliverables: 90-second trailer, 30-second cut, 15-second cut, vertical versions, website introduction.

Release 2 — The Map

The first complete flagship episode. It explains the four volumes, the four doors, the shows, and the production invitation. Deliverables: full episode, three-to-five-minute overview, short clips, illustrated map, website page, transcript and audio.

Release 3 — Receipts

The first instrument-focused episode. It demonstrates how a viewer can inspect the architecture and distinguish verifiable mechanisms from claims or proposals. Technical data must be checked at recording time.

Release 4 — Inward Is Forwards

The first major cosmology episode. It introduces the EROS world model through strong storytelling and visual explanation, while clearly identifying what is model, hypothesis, evidence, and fiction.

Release 5 — The Open Call

The first public demonstration of the Guild. Show people what they can make, how to contribute, and how the work will be reviewed and published.

This release sequence gives the project both a public face and a working community structure. It follows the cold-viewer sequence: Trailer → Show 00 → Show 05 → viewer choice of world.

Why the sequence is this order. The trailer establishes the whole project. The Map makes the library legible. Receipts honours "crypto first" — it proves the instrument is checkable before asking anyone to explore philosophy. Inward Is Forwards is where the curious viewer is rewarded with the strangest and most distinctive material. The Open Call is where the viewer who wants to build finds a way in. The sequence is a recommended release order, not a claim that the episodes are already produced or fact-checked.

The Plan · §10

10. The Book-to-Media Production Engine

Every source should enter one repeatable pipeline. This is the core operating system of the project.

The pipeline has twelve stages. Every source book, every episode, every short should move through the same sequence. The sequence is what makes the production repeatable. It is what makes each production easier than the last.

10.1 The twelve-stage pipeline

Stage 1 · Ingest

Identify the authoritative file and version. Confirm the canonical filename and source ID. Mark duplicates, overlaps and superseded versions.

Stage 2 · Extract

Capture structure, passages, concepts, claims, characters, visuals and cross-links. The extraction must preserve the author's actual meaning and wording where needed. For every source, capture: canonical title and filename; purpose and subject; main thesis; major sections; key terminology; verbatim passages; characters and narrative material; diagrams and visual concepts; technical mechanisms; evidence and citations; questions and objections; links to other books.

Stage 3 · Classify

Assign evidence labels (OBSERVED, MODEL, HYPOTHESIS, PATTERN, OBJECTION, FALSIFIER, STORY) and mechanism labels (LIVE, DESIGN, PROPOSED). Every substantive claim gets a label. Every mechanism gets a badge.

Stage 4 · Pattern-match

Identify repeated concepts, dependencies, contradictions, missing bridges and unique contributions across books. The production team should compare: repeated concepts; shared terminology; common mechanisms; contradictions; complementary explanations; repeated characters and symbols; similar visual structures; ideas that build upon one another. Each relationship should be recorded as one of: same idea repeated; same idea expanded; complementary idea; dependent idea; contradiction; alternative interpretation; new proposal.

Stage 5 · Editorial synthesis

Decide what the audience needs to understand and what the source can support. Each production receives: one central theme; one intended audience; one learning objective; one opening question; one narrative or explanatory structure; one conclusion; one next step for the viewer.

Stage 6 · Adapt

Produce the episode/short/page/audio brief and script. A book does not automatically become one episode. Several books may combine into one episode, and one book may support an entire serial. The aim is not to compress the books until their technical detail disappears. It is to find the clearest way to communicate the whole idea.

Stage 7 · Research and fact-check

Verify factual, historical, scientific and live technical claims. Every claim that touches the real world goes through a primary source pass. Every mechanism claim goes through a fresh on-chain check at the time of recording.

Stage 8 · Storyboard and asset plan

Specify scenes, diagrams, characters, visual references, sound and required new assets. Separate existing assets from new assets. Mark each asset as READY, REVIEW, EDIT, MISSING or NEW.

Stage 9 · Produce

Record, animate, edit, caption and master. Lock the script before recording. Record the narration as a scratch track and cut an animatic from still boards first to lock pacing before rendering motion.

Stage 10 · Publish

Release the master and derivatives to the right channels. Keep the master on the website. Distribute to YouTube, short-form platforms, audio and Telegram according to the distribution strategy.

Stage 11 · Connect back

Link the published item to its source passages, related shows and next step. Every published piece ends with a door. Every door leads somewhere. The journey is the point.

Stage 12 · Learn and iterate

Use audience questions, retention and community feedback to improve the next release. Review viewer retention, repeat viewers, website visits, book engagement, audience questions, contributor responses, production effort and reusable assets created. Use the results to improve the next production.

10.2 The master production package

Every episode should have fourteen deliverables. This is the checklist that separates a finished production from a draft. If a deliverable is missing, the episode is not finished.

# Deliverable Purpose
1Episode briefOne page: theme, audience, learning objective, opening question, conclusion, next step.
2Source mapWhich source passages feed which beats. The traceability record.
3Claim and evidence ledgerEvery factual assertion, tagged by grade and by episode.
4ScriptThe locked narration and scene directions.
5StoryboardEvery beat, one board per beat, written as a single prompt unit.
6Shot listThe storyboard as a numbered shot sequence.
7Character and location referencesLocked visual sheets for every recurring character and set.
8Visual asset requirementsWhat exists, what is required, what is new. Status per asset.
9Sound and narration requirementsVoice, music, SFX, silence map.
10Production instructionsFor the editor, animator, sound designer.
11Short-form cutdown planWhich 3–6 clips, which vertical versions, which hooks.
12Transcript and website copyFor the show page and the search engine.
13Community contribution tasksThe Guild tasks this episode generates.
14Editorial approval recordWho approved, when, and what was changed.

10.3 The standard derivative package

Each flagship episode should produce several related outputs. A standard package:

Output Typical format
Flagship episode8–20 minutes
Trailer30–90 seconds
Short clips3–6 clips
Explainer3–5 minutes
Vertical videos3–5 versions
Illustrated articleWebsite
AudioNarrated episode or chapter
Interactive elementDiagram, map or HTML experience
Community taskOne achievable contribution

These are production targets, not rigid quotas. The subject and available resources determine the final package.

10.4 What not to extract

Equally important — leave these in the books:

Dense argumentation and repeated justifications

The show demonstrates; it does not argue.

Internal caveats and hedging

The written text has its own protections. On screen, the evidence ladder replaces them.

Full parameter tables

Visualise the mechanism. Do not narrate the spreadsheet.

Redundant cross-references

Consolidate once in the glossary rather than repeating per episode.

Anything that requires reading to understand

If it cannot be shown or spoken, it does not belong in the extraction.

10.5 The cross-cutting registers

Some assets are more valuable gathered in one place than per book. Build these six registers:

1 · Master glossary

Every coined term (Eros Enclosure, Iteration Codex, resonance, affinity, operator, etc.) with definition, first appearance, variant spellings, and the visual metaphor attached. This becomes the writers' style guide and the on-screen lower-third source.

2 · Visual language inventory

Every recurring symbol — the Egg, the Torus, the Tree, the Bridge, the instruments (EROS, ErosX, 33EROS) — with all descriptions from all books collated in one entry. You need a single canonical description per symbol, because AI-generated assets will drift otherwise.

3 · Character bible

Every named entity (NaUn, Ra-Shen, Thoth, EROS, and any human characters from First Resonance / Eros Stories) with role, attributes, relationships, visual reference, and which strand(s) they appear in. This is what stops Thoth looking different in Episode 5 and Episode 6.

4 · Claim / evidence ledger

One row per factual assertion, tagged by evidence grade and by episode. This is the fact-checker's bible and the source of the on-screen credibility icons. It also protects you legally and reputationally on Men of Renown and Illumination Strategy.

5 · Cosmology / timeline map

A single diagram showing how the books relate conceptually and chronologically: which is foundational, which is a perspective, which is supporting material.

6 · Contradiction log

Where two books disagree, or where a term is used differently. You will find these across 29 files. Log them now so continuity does not break mid-season.

10.6 Strand-specific extraction

Each strand needs one extra layer beyond the universal sheet.

Strand Extra extraction layer
Cosmology (S1) Extract the sequence of unfoldings — the exact order in which the model reveals itself (point → torus → lobes → crossover → enclosure → observer). This sequence is the season arc. Also extract the observer's position in each book, because that is your recurring human anchor.
Mythology (S1) Extract operator functions — what each god does in the system, not just what they symbolise. The Episode 5 insight ("gods as operators") depends on having each role stated functionally. Also extract the most cinematic scenes already written.
Tokenomics (S2) Extract mechanisms as processes — every flow, loop, gate, and condition described as a thing that moves. Then extract parameters (numbers, ratios, thresholds) separately, because they will be visualised, not narrated. Crucially, tag every mechanism Live / Designed / Proposed — this is your Episode 4 credibility safeguard.
Human story (S3) Extract real voices — community contributions, testimonials, the emotional "why" passages from We Are With You Eros, Front Door, Open Call. Also extract fictional characters and situations from Eros Stories / Continuity File and keep them clearly separated from documentary material.
Financial documentary (S4) Extract primary sources and citations from Illumination Strategy — every chart, date, institution, and source. This strand lives or dies on source transparency. Extract the repricing thesis chain as a step-by-step argument so each episode can advance it one link.

10.7 Extract the four pilots first

Do not extract all 29 books to full depth before piloting. Do these four completely, because they test four different pipelines:

Pilot 01 — The Crack in the Sky

Files to extract fully: SRC-012 Living Egg, SRC-019 Eros Enclosure.

What you are testing: Cinematic CGI + narration; the "model vs data" hook; the Egg visual.

Pilot 02 — The Gods Were Operators

Files to extract fully: SRC-010 Gods of EROS.

What you are testing: Character animation; operator functions as drama.

Pilot 03 — The EROS Flywheel

Files to extract fully: SRC-021 The Flywheel, SRC-001 Architecture of Participation.

What you are testing: 3D educational animation; mechanism-as-motion; Live / Designed / Proposed tagging.

Pilot 04 — The First Resonance

Files to extract fully: SRC-020 First Resonance.

What you are testing: Cinematic animated drama; human emotional payoff.

Extract these four at full field depth, build the pilots, then extract the remaining 25 using the lessons learned.

10.8 The single deliverable

Everything above should produce one structured database — one row per concept, claim, character, and visual — tagged by source file, strand, episode, and evidence grade. That database, not the 29 HTML files, becomes what writers, storyboard artists, and fact-checkers work from.

Build the per-book sheets first (29 rows), then the six cross-cutting registers, then the four pilot extractions. By the time you write the Television Bible, you will be assembling it from structured records rather than re-reading source material — which is exactly how a repeatable production system stays repeatable.

The Plan · §11

11. The Creative Guild

The Guild is the community's production structure. It should allow people with different skills, experience and available time to contribute without needing to understand every book.

The Guild is a distributed production network. People should be able to contribute at different skill levels, with small, clearly bounded tasks and visible standards. Seven studios provide the working structure. These are functional groups, not status levels. A contributor should be able to join one studio, complete one task, and see the result become part of the larger project.

11.1 The seven studios

Writers & Story

Responsibility: Scripts, treatments, dialogue, narrative continuity and short-form copy.

Typical contribution: One scene or explanation.

Visual Design

Responsibility: Identity, title cards, diagrams, thumbnails, character sheets and visual references.

Typical contribution: One image or character sheet.

Animation & Motion

Responsibility: 2D/3D animation, explainers, transitions and scene assembly.

Typical contribution: One short sequence.

Sound & Voice

Responsibility: Narration, voice performance, music direction, sound design and audio cleanup.

Typical contribution: One recorded passage.

Research & Verification

Responsibility: Source checking, claim ledger, citations, technical verification and objections.

Typical contribution: One verified reference.

Web & Interactive

Responsibility: Website pages, navigation, interactive diagrams, archive and accessibility.

Typical contribution: One web component.

Publishing & Community

Responsibility: Scheduling, descriptions, captions, translations, release notes, feedback and contributor credits.

Typical contribution: One finished cutdown or upload.

People may work across studios. These are functional work areas, not rigid departments.

11.2 The Guild task format

Every task brief must contain twelve fields. This is the smallest practical production unit. A contributor should be able to open a brief and know exactly what to make, in what format, and to what standard, without needing to read the rest of the project documentation.

Field What it contains
Task ID and titleA unique identifier and a short descriptive name.
Show / episode / sourceWhich show, episode or source book the task belongs to.
Studio or skill areaWhich of the seven studios the task sits in.
Why the task mattersOne sentence: why this contribution is needed.
Exact deliverableThe precise item required. Not a category. A thing.
Source material and referencesThe book, episode, script or production brief the task draws from.
Constraints and editorial labelsEvidence chips, mechanism badges, canon tier, fiction contract.
Acceptance criteriaWhat makes the work suitable for publication.
Suggested format / specificationFile type, aspect ratio, length, resolution.
Person responsible and reviewerWho owns the task, who reviews it.
Status and due dateWhere the task is, when it is expected.
Credit and attributionHow the contributor will be acknowledged. Where the finished work is stored.

11.3 Contribution principles

Make the first task small enough to complete.

Provide examples and templates.

Define "done" before work starts.

Keep source files and editable project files where possible.

Credit contributors consistently.

Review work constructively and promptly.

Do not let volunteers guess at factual claims or token mechanics.

Give contributors a clear path from beginner tasks to more advanced responsibility.

11.4 The first Guild task package

Start with bounded tasks that can be completed independently. These are the kind of tasks that can be picked up by a contributor on day one:

TASK-0001 · Review and tag one source chapter

Studio: Research · Format: Structured extraction sheet · Credit: Named in the source register.

TASK-0002 · Check one factual claim against a primary source

Studio: Research · Format: Citation + page reference + one-paragraph finding · Credit: Named in the claim ledger.

TASK-0003 · Create one diagram from an approved storyboard

Studio: Visual · Format: SVG or PNG, 16:9, matching the palette · Credit: Asset register entry.

TASK-0004 · Produce one 15–30 second vertical short

Studio: Animation / Publishing · Format: 9:16, captioned, with the mouth sting · Credit: Named in the release notes.

TASK-0005 · Record a short narration sample

Studio: Sound · Format: 60–90 seconds, 48 kHz WAV · Credit: Voice credit on the episode page.

TASK-0006 · Build one episode page from a template

Studio: Web · Format: HTML page with transcript, sources, evidence chips, and a contribution pathway · Credit: Build credit in the page footer.

TASK-0007 · Review captions and transcript for clarity

Studio: Publishing · Format: Cleaned SRT + plain-text transcript · Credit: Transcript credit.

TASK-0008 · Create a character or visual reference sheet

Studio: Visual · Format: Four-view sheet, colour-coded per the palette · Credit: Asset register entry, named in the character bible.

TASK-0009 · Design the Cosmic Egg master reference

Studio: Visual · Format: 4K still, multi-angle · Credit: Named in the visual inventory and the asset register.

TASK-0010 · Animate a 10-second toroidal sequence

Studio: Animation · Format: MP4, 4K, 10 seconds, loop-ready · Credit: Sequence credit in Show 01.

No contributor should need to build an entire show to make a meaningful contribution. The smallest contribution should be small enough to be completed, and meaningful enough to matter.

11.5 The contribution process

1 · Propose

A contributor proposes an idea, character, scene, or asset. Or picks up an existing Guild task.

2 · Check

The submission is checked against the World Bible and the relevant source.

3 · Classify

It is classified as canon, compatible expansion, alternate interpretation, or experimental.

4 · Approve

Approved material receives a version and an attribution.

5 · Reuse

Production teams can reuse it without rebuilding it from scratch.

This is particularly important if the EROS universe is eventually built by many independent contributors. The process is not designed to slow people down. It is designed to keep the world coherent as it grows.

11.6 AI production rules

AI can help with: drafting scripts and dialogue, storyboard concepts, visual and video generation, animation assistance, voice and narration drafts, research organisation.

Human approval remains necessary for: canonical story decisions, final character designs, continuity and quality control, technical accuracy, approved voices and performance, evidence and source verification, world-building suggestions, and acceptance into canon.

AI should accelerate production, not become the authority on what EROS means. The project's voice, canon, and editorial standards come from the people, not from the tools.

11.7 The Guild starter kit

The immediate deliverables are the Guild starter kit and the first task board. The starter kit must contain:

Guild charter and operating principles

Studio descriptions and responsibilities

Contributor onboarding page

Task brief template

Acceptance and review checklist

Asset naming and handover rules

Credits and attribution policy

First 10–20 starter tasks

Weekly editorial and production rhythm

A clear way to submit work and receive feedback

11.8 The Guild's three operating registers

These are the immediate next deliverables. They turn the blueprint into an operating system. All three should share the same source IDs, show IDs and task IDs.

A · Master Source Extraction Register

One record per source, with section-level extraction underneath. It must reconcile the six fully extracted texts against the 29-file source register and distinguish: registered; ingested; structurally mapped; extracted; editorially reviewed; claim-checked; production-ready. It should also capture exact source passages, definitions, claims, diagrams, story elements, cross-links and intended media use.

B · 14-Show Completion Tracker

One record per show, plus episode-level records for the serials. Track: source package; editorial brief; script; research/fact-check; storyboard; asset list; voice/sound; production/edit; captions/transcript; website page; publication; derivative shorts; feedback and revision. The tracker must distinguish writing completion from production and publication completion.

C · Guild Task Board and Starter Kit

Create: Guild charter and operating principles; studio descriptions; contributor onboarding page; task brief template; acceptance/review checklist; asset naming and handover rules; credits and attribution policy; first 10–20 starter tasks; weekly editorial/production rhythm; a clear way to submit work and receive feedback.

11.9 Stable IDs

Use stable IDs across every register. Do not rename original source files merely to fit the repository. Keep canonical filenames and map them to stable IDs.

Entity ID format Example
SourcesSRC-001 to SRC-029SRC-012 Living Egg
ShowsSHOW-00 to SHOW-13SHOW-01 Inward Is Forwards
ClaimsCLM-0001 onwardCLM-0042
MechanismsMECH-0001 onwardMECH-0007
AssetsAST-0001 onwardAST-0113 Cosmic Egg master model
Guild tasksTASK-0001 onwardTASK-0003 One diagram from storyboard

11.10 What the Guild proves

The Guild is not just a structure. It is a proof. It is the proof that the EROS universe can grow beyond what any central team could produce. It is the proof that the community can make things that matter. It is the proof that a contributor can start from zero and end up in a published piece.

The success measure is not the number of contributors. It is the number of contributors who return for a second task. The Guild should gradually become capable of operating without constant central intervention.

The Plan · §12

12. Parallel Creation & Fractal Branching

The community does not have to wait for the central team to finish a show. They can take a source, concept, character, visual, or task and begin developing something in parallel, while keeping the relationship to the larger EROS project clear.

This is the central community invitation of the project. It is what makes the Guild a production network rather than a fan club. It is what makes the EROS universe expand beyond what any central team could produce. We create. We expect the community to parallel work with us or fractally branch off from our inspiration.

12.1 How it works

1 · Identify

A contributor identifies a piece of the EROS world that interests them — a character, a concept, a source passage, a visual, a question the books leave open.

2 · Check the source

They check the source material. They check the canon tiers. They decide what tier their work will be in.

3 · Propose

They propose a contribution. The proposal is reviewed against the World Bible and the relevant source.

4 · Classify

If accepted, the work enters the production pipeline. If experimental, the work is published as a branch and clearly labelled as such.

5 · Build and submit

The contributor can work alone, or form an independent studio cell with other contributors. The work is produced under the Guild structure and submitted for review.

6 · Publish and credit

The work is published under the EROS banner with the contributor credited. The work enters the archive. It becomes something the next contributor can build on.

12.2 The independent studio cell

A studio cell is a small group — two to five people — who take on a larger contribution together. The cell operates under the same contribution brief format as an individual contributor, but the brief can be larger.

A studio cell can be formed around any part of the EROS universe. A cell might focus on the Gift of Thoth, or on the operators, or on the First Resonance characters, or on the liquidity architecture, or on the 3D Universe, or on a community-created corner of the world that does not yet exist.

The cell does not need central permission to form. It needs to register with the Guild, adopt the contribution brief format, and agree to the canon tiers and the evidence rules. Once registered, the cell can produce work and submit it for review.

The cell's work is published under the EROS banner with the cell credited. The cell can grow, split, or dissolve as its members choose. The point is not to create a permanent organisation. The point is to let people make things together.

Fractal branching. A studio cell can spawn another studio cell. A branch can be forked. A community corner of the universe can become its own sub-universe, still connected to the core, still speaking the same visual language, still honouring the four operators and the Egg's laws. The universe grows by division, not by central expansion. Every branch that passes the Bond Test strengthens the whole.

12.3 The relationship to canon

Parallel work does not automatically become canon. It is classified by tier.

Tier 1 — Core Source Canon

The 29 source files. Locked. A parallel studio cell cannot change Tier 1.

Tier 2 — Verified Expansion

A parallel studio cell's work can be Tier 2 if it is checked against the source and approved.

Tier 3 — Community Variation

It can be Tier 3 if it is a creative interpretation that honours the framework.

Tier 4 — Experimental Branch

It can be Tier 4 if it is deliberately divergent. All three are legitimate. The tier determines how the work relates to the rest of the universe, not whether it is good.

The tiers are not a hierarchy of quality. They are a hierarchy of authority. A Tier 4 work can be better than a Tier 2 work and still not be part of the canon. The question is not "is this good?" The question is "what does this work claim to be, and is that claim accurate?"

12.4 The five contribution pathways

There are several pathways a parallel contributor can take. The pathways are not mutually exclusive. A contributor can start with a single task, move to a personal project, form a studio cell, and eventually produce a branch. The system is designed to let contribution grow.

Pathway What it is Typical commitment
The single task Pick up a Guild brief, complete it, submit it, see it published. The smallest unit of contribution. 1–4 hours
The personal project Take on a larger piece of work — a comic, an audio episode, a visual novel chapter — and produce it under the Guild structure. 1–4 weeks
The studio cell Form a small group to produce a larger work together. Two to five people. Shared brief, shared credit, shared deadline. 1–3 months
The experimental branch Produce work that deliberately diverges from the canon, and publish it as a Tier 4 branch. Labelled clearly. Allowed to exist openly. Variable
The research contribution Verify sources, build evidence registers, check claims. Research is a contribution pathway equal to production. 1–8 hours per claim

12.5 The fractal principle

The EROS universe is designed to grow fractally. Every branch is a complete thing, and every branch contains the seed of the whole. A single door from Sixteen Doors carries the Egg's laws, the four operators, and the bond test in miniature. A single episode of The First Resonance carries the practice, the ledger, and the visitor. A single short from The Web carries the mechanics, the risk, and the philosophy.

This is what makes fractal branching possible. A contributor does not need to understand the whole universe to make something that belongs in it. They need to understand the small piece they are making, and to let that piece carry the shape of the whole.

The fractal test. If you make a door, does the door contain the universe? If you make a scene, does the scene contain the practice? If you make a diagram, does the diagram contain the mechanism? If the answer is yes, the branch is sound. If the answer is no, the branch is decoration.

12.6 What the community gets

Credit

Every contributor is named. Every task has a credit line. Every branch has an author. The work is not anonymous.

Reusable assets

Contributors can reuse the assets they and others have made. The asset register is open. The visual library is shared.

A path to more

A single task can lead to a personal project. A personal project can lead to a studio cell. A studio cell can lead to a branch. There is a visible ladder.

Ownership that means something

The work is real. The credit is real. The contribution is visible. The contributor can point at something and say "I made that."

A share in the growth

Every finished piece increases demand for EROS and TitanX. Every burn increases scarcity. The community that builds the universe shares in its success.

A universe they helped make

The value stays because the community built it. The universe is not extracted from them. It is made by them.

The Plan · §13

13. The First Release Sequence

The recommended first public sequence is:

Trailer → Show 00: The Map → Show 05: Receipts → viewer choice of world.

This sequence establishes the whole project, explains the instrument, and then allows the viewer to choose the subject that interests them. It follows the cold-viewer sequence recommended in the Unified Bible. It balances orientation, practical understanding, distinctive EROS philosophy and community activation. It is a recommended release order, not a claim that the episodes are already produced or fact-checked.

13.1 Release 1 — The EROS Trailer

Release 1

The EROS Trailer

A short, visually strong introduction to the world and the library.

Purpose: Stop the scroll. Establish the visual identity. Make the promise. End on the mouth sting and a choice.

Deliverables

  • 90-second trailer
  • 30-second cut
  • 15-second cut
  • Vertical versions
  • Website introduction

Source material: The trailer script in Part 5 (Section 16.4 of the Series Bible), with 16 shots drawn from Shows 01, 12, 03, 04, 05, 06, 07, 02, 08, 10, 11, and 13.

Narration: "Every few centuries a civilisation changes its picture of what is real. The people who live through it call it chaos. The people who come after call it normal. Here is a library with a different picture… One library. Fourteen shows. Sixteen doors. Inward is forwards. Pick a door."

13.2 Release 2 — The Map

Release 2

The Map

The first complete flagship episode.

Purpose: Explain the four volumes, the four doors, the shows, and the production invitation. Make the whole system legible in 20 minutes without overwhelming the viewer. Leave the viewer with a choice: which door do they walk through next?

Deliverables

  • Full episode (20:00)
  • Three-to-five-minute overview
  • Short clips (3–6)
  • Illustrated map
  • Website page
  • Transcript and audio

Source material: The full script in Part 5 (Section 4.1 of the Series Bible). The script has nine timed beats: cold open, sting, District I (Instrument), District II (Demand), District III (Cosmology), District IV (Production), the scoreboard, Pin the Door, and the tag.

Failure mode to avoid: The Map becomes a corporate explainer. It should feel like the opening of a great documentary — awe, curiosity, invitation — not like a pitch deck.

13.3 Release 3 — Receipts

Release 3

Receipts

The first instrument-focused episode.

Purpose: Demonstrate how a viewer can inspect the architecture and distinguish verifiable mechanisms from claims or proposals. Be the trust-building episode. Show that the project is not asking for blind faith.

Deliverables

  • Full episode (20:00)
  • Technical verification package (all on-chain data checked at recording time)
  • Short clips (3–6)
  • Website page with the claim ledger and the evidence chips
  • Transcript and audio

Source material: The full script in Part 5 (Section 4.2 of the Series Bible). The script has eight timed beats: cold open (the founders who walked), sting, the Confession, one transfer four destinations, ownership, the Risk Register as a feature, three questions, and the tag.

Technical data must be checked at recording time. Every mechanism claim in Receipts is checked against current on-chain data on the day of recording, and checked again on the day of publication. The date-stamp goes on screen.

13.4 Release 4 — Inward Is Forwards

Release 4

Inward Is Forwards

The first major cosmology episode.

Purpose: Introduce the EROS world model through strong storytelling and visual explanation, while clearly identifying what is model, hypothesis, evidence, and fiction. Leave the viewer with a shape in their mind: the Egg, the Torus, the observer inside the enclosure.

Deliverables

  • Full episode (20:00)
  • Three-to-five-minute overview
  • Short clips (3–6), including "The Lid" (Act 1 as a 3-minute short) and "Zero Apples" (Act 2 as a 90-second short)
  • Website page with the model/hypothesis/evidence/fiction labels visible on every claim
  • Transcript and audio

Source material: The full script in Part 5 (Section 2 of the Series Bible), with the corrections applied in Section 14.1: the "85% of the matter" fix, the 1917 Einstein model, the post-1945 defense funding context, and the four independent dark-matter evidence lines.

The corrected hook: "A scientist deletes 85% of the matter in the universe and the math still works."

Failure mode to avoid: The episode becomes a lecture on a scientific theory with no emotional or visual hook. The model must be experienced, not explained.

13.5 Release 5 — The Open Call

Release 5

The Open Call

The first public demonstration of the Guild.

Purpose: Show people what they can make, how to contribute, and how the work will be reviewed and published. Convert a viewer into a maker in nine minutes. This is the flywheel in practice.

Deliverables

  • Episode 1 (9:30): "One paper. One camera."
  • The Guild starter kit (charter, studios, task template, first 10–20 tasks)
  • The first task board, live
  • Website page with the submission form
  • Transcript and audio

Source material: The Episode 1 skeleton in Part 5 (Section 16.3 of the Series Bible). The run sheet has six segments: Sting and Open, Paper of the Week, The Honest Questions, The Scoreboard, Ask the Studio, and The Ask.

Why this show matters most: It is the only show that does not need a studio. It converts a viewer into a maker in nine minutes. Every other show is fed by it.

13.6 Why this order

The trailer establishes the whole project. The Map makes the library legible. Receipts honours "crypto first" — it proves the instrument is checkable before asking anyone to explore philosophy. Inward Is Forwards is where the curious viewer is rewarded with the strangest and most distinctive material. The Open Call is where the viewer who wants to build finds a way in.

This sequence gives the project both a public face and a working community structure.

13.7 The cold-viewer funnel

Step What the viewer sees What they should feel What they should do next
1 The 90-second trailer "This is something. I want to see more." Watch The Map
2 Show 00: The Map "I understand the whole thing now. There are four doors." Pick a door, or watch Receipts first
3 Show 05: Receipts "The instrument is checkable. This is not a pitch." Explore the world they chose
4 Show 01, 02, 03, 04 (Cosmology) or 08, 09 (Archive) or 10–12 (Fiction) "This is strange and specific and worth my time." Check a source, join a discussion, or open the Guild page
5 Show 13: The Open Call "I can actually help build this." Pick up a task, submit a branch, join a studio cell

The funnel is a recommendation, not a gate. A viewer can arrive at any step and move in any direction. The point is that every step is a good step, and every step points to the next one.

The Plan · §14

14. The First 90 Days

The schedule is a practical starting plan. It assumes a small coordinating team and volunteer or part-time contributors, with production pace adjusted to actual capacity.

The 90-day plan is a sequencing framework. Dates and output volume should be adjusted to real volunteer capacity and production quality. The milestones are what matter. The dates are a starting estimate.

Phase 1 · Days 1–14

Foundation

The team knows what exists, what is missing, what is authoritative and what work can start.

Tasks

  • Confirm the 29-file source register and authoritative versions.
  • Reconcile the extraction-status discrepancy.
  • Establish the canonical folder/repository structure and naming/version rules.
  • Create the 14-show completion tracker.
  • Create the claim/mechanism verification workflow.
  • Confirm the first release sequence and the minimum website structure.
  • Publish the Guild's first contribution guide and task template.

Exit condition

The team knows what exists, what is missing, what is authoritative and what work can start.

Phase 2 · Days 15–30

First production package

The community has something tangible to make.

Tasks

  • Complete or review the source packages for Show 00 and Show 05.
  • Lock the editorial promise and audience for each.
  • Review scripts for clarity, length, evidence labels and source traceability.
  • Build approved storyboards and asset lists.
  • Produce the title sting and core visual templates.
  • Create the website episode-page template.
  • Prepare a small batch of short-form scripts.

Exit condition

The first episode can enter production without unresolved core editorial questions.

Phase 3 · Days 31–60

Produce and test

At least one polished public release package is ready or published, with a repeatable workflow demonstrated.

Tasks

  • Produce the trailer/sting.
  • Produce Show 00 or a deliberately scoped pilot cut.
  • Produce Show 05 as the next practical explainer.
  • Create vertical derivatives from approved material.
  • Prepare captions, transcripts, source links and thumbnails.
  • Test the website-to-YouTube-to-Guild journey with a small group.
  • Collect feedback and fix friction before scaling.

Exit condition

At least one polished public release package is ready or published, with a repeatable workflow demonstrated.

Phase 4 · Days 61–90

Launch the Guild and expand

The Guild has real tasks, completed contributions and a visible route into future production.

Tasks

  • Open the Guild with the starter kit and first task board.
  • Publish the first release sequence as production capacity permits.
  • Assign small tasks to contributors and review them.
  • Build the next show packages from the source register.
  • Establish a sustainable publishing cadence based on actual capacity.
  • Review performance and audience questions; improve the format.

Exit condition

The Guild has real tasks, completed contributions and a visible route into future production.

14.1 The 90-day map at a glance

Phase Days Focus Milestone
1 Days 1–14 Foundation One coherent production system
2 Days 15–30 First production package The community has something tangible to make
3 Days 31–60 Produce and test One polished public release package and a repeatable workflow
4 Days 61–90 Launch the Guild and expand Real tasks, completed contributions, a visible route into future production

14.2 The four operational registers to build next

The immediate next deliverables are the three operational registers described in Section 11.8, plus the master source extraction register as the fourth. These turn the blueprint into an operating system.

A · Master Source Extraction Register

One record per source, with section-level extraction underneath. Reconciles the six fully extracted texts against the 29-file source register.

B · 14-Show Completion Tracker

One record per show, plus episode-level records for the serials. Distinguishes writing completion from production and publication completion.

C · Guild Task Board and Starter Kit

The charter, the studios, the onboarding page, the task brief template, the acceptance checklist, the first 10–20 starter tasks, the weekly rhythm.

D · Claim and Mechanism Registers

One row per factual assertion, tagged by evidence grade and by episode. One row per mechanism, tagged LIVE, DESIGN or PROPOSED. The fact-checker's bible.

All four should share the same source IDs, show IDs and task IDs. They are the working spine of the production system.

The Plan · §15

15. Measures of Progress

Measure the production system, not just views.

The project should not be judged by views alone. We need to know whether the books are being expressed, understood and extended. The measures are grouped into four families: audience, Guild health, library readiness and publishing.

15.1 Audience measures

Video retention

Returning viewers

Website visits

Episode completion

Book and source-page engagement

Viewer questions

Movement between related shows

Short-form reach and click-through to deeper material

Website visits from video and community channels

Audio listens where relevant

15.2 Guild health measures

Contributors participating

Tasks accepted

Tasks completed

Time taken to complete tasks

Number of reusable assets created

Number of community productions published

Contributors returning for another task

Time from submission to review

Distribution of work across studios

Contributor retention and satisfaction

15.3 Library readiness measures

Source files registered

Source files extracted

Source files reviewed

Source files production-ready

Percentage of episode claims with a source and verification status

Number of unresolved contradictions and questions

Claims classified

Contradictions identified and resolved

Episodes completed

Assets catalogued

Books connected to published media

15.4 Publishing measures

Releases completed on schedule

Long-form viewing and completion patterns

Short-form reach and click-through to deeper material

Website visits from video and community channels

Audio listens where relevant

Time from approved brief to first cut

Number of reusable assets and templates

Number of shows with approved source packages, scripts, boards and assets

15.5 The most important measure

The most important measure is whether each production makes the next production easier.

If the asset library is growing, if the templates are reusable, if the character sheets are locked, if the visual grammar is documented, if the source extraction is deepening — then the system is working. If every production starts from zero, the system is not working, no matter how good any individual episode is.

15.6 Avoid vanity metrics as the only measure

A smaller audience that understands, verifies and participates may be more valuable than a large audience that only sees a clip. Views matter. Retention matters. But the deepest measure is whether a person who has never read an EROS book watches a 20-minute episode, understands one idea from the books, and wants to read more.

Everything else — views, engagement, token price, community size — is downstream of that. If the expression system produces that outcome, it is doing its job. If it does not, no amount of production polish will compensate.

15.7 The twelve operating principles

The Guild should work according to these principles. They are the standards that every production decision should be measured against.

1. The books remain the source material.

2. The master project provides the production direction.

3. Every episode has a clear purpose.

4. Every contributor receives a manageable brief.

5. Creative freedom is encouraged within clearly stated boundaries.

6. Evidence and fiction are never silently mixed.

7. Reusable assets are preferred over unnecessary reinvention.

8. The website remains the permanent home.

9. Social platforms are distribution channels, not the source of truth.

10. Contributors receive clear credit and recognition.

11. The project should be understandable to newcomers.

12. The Guild should gradually become capable of operating without constant central intervention.

15.8 The risks and controls

Risk Control
Adding more books instead of expressing existing work Prioritise extraction, adaptation and publication before expanding the canon.
Source material is misrepresented in adaptation Maintain passage-level traceability and editorial review.
Speculation is presented as fact Apply evidence labels and keep the two rails distinct.
Token mechanics are described as live without current proof Verify against current primary/on-chain evidence before publication.
Too many platforms create workload One master asset package, then controlled derivatives.
Guild contributors receive vague tasks Use bounded briefs and acceptance criteria.
Production becomes over-ambitious Release a small polished pilot and scale to demonstrated capacity.
Chat channels become the only archive Store canonical outputs in the website/repository.
"Complete" is used ambiguously Track source, script, research, storyboard, production and publication separately.
The project becomes inaccessible to newcomers Keep four public doors and a simple Start Here journey.

15.9 Decisions already made

Treat these as current working decisions unless later evidence or an explicit project decision changes them:

  1. The books are made; the priority is expression and distribution.
  2. The 14-show slate in Unified Bible v1.0 is the current production architecture.
  3. The four public doors remain Instrument, World Model, Stories and Applications.
  4. The website is the permanent home; YouTube is the primary video destination.
  5. TikTok, Reels and Shorts are discovery channels, not separate editorial universes.
  6. Telegram/community channels support coordination and participation, but are not the sole archive.
  7. The EROS community is to be organised as a Creative Guild with clear studios, tasks and standards.
  8. Source extraction and verification must precede adaptation where source detail or factual claims matter.
  9. Fiction, myth, models, hypotheses and observed facts must remain distinguishable.
  10. The first release sequence is Trailer/Sting → Show 00 → Show 05 → Show 01 → Show 13, subject to production readiness.
  11. Start with the lowest-resistance, repeatable production path; do not wait for a full studio.
  12. The next operational work is the three registers: Source Extraction, Show Completion and Guild Task Board.

15.10 Open questions that must be resolved through source review

Do not guess at these:

Which 23 sources beyond the six extracted texts have been structurally or substantively reviewed?

Does the 12-field register in Master Series Bible R contain real source-level extraction records for all 29, or only a high-level register?

Which version of each source file is canonical?

Which existing scripts and storyboards have been approved, and by whom?

Which claims in the show bible still require primary-source verification?

Which visual/media assets exist as accessible original files, and which are only mentioned in an export or index?

What is the actual available contributor capacity and skill mix?

What website/platform infrastructure is already active and maintainable?

Which first episode can be completed to release quality with the least unresolved work?

15.11 The final direction

The books are the foundation. The series is the expression. The website is the home. The platforms are the distribution. The Guild is the engine. The audience becomes a participant, and participants become creators.

One library. Many doors. One Guild. Inward is forwards. If you do not own it, you're not in it.

The Plan · §16

16. The Asset Register

Every asset should have one record. The register distinguishes an existing file from an asset merely mentioned in a script. Without it, production reinvents what already exists, and continuity drifts.

16.1 The record structure

Field What it contains
Asset IDPermanent reference, e.g. EROS-VID-001, AST-0113.
Asset nameOriginal filename or descriptive title.
Media typeImage, video, audio, animation, 3D, document.
SourceBook, website, Telegram, or newly created.
Source referenceFile, chapter, page, or Telegram message ID.
SubjectWhat the asset depicts or explains.
ProgrammeInstrument, World Model, Mythology, Illumination.
EpisodeIntended episode or possible reuse.
Production roleOpening, explanation, transition, character, background, ending.
StatusAvailable, Needs review, Needs editing, Missing, New creation.
RightsOwnership or permission confirmed / pending.
VerificationFactual review required / passed / not applicable.
NotesContinuity, technical requirements, reuse limits.

16.2 The five production statuses

READY

File exists, reviewed, rights checked, suitable for use.

REVIEW

Asset located but still needs visual, factual, or editorial review.

EDIT

Exists but needs editing, updating, compositing, or re-rendering.

MISSING

Referenced in the library, but actual media file is not available.

NEW

Needs to be created from scratch.
