The Plan · §17

17. The Extraction Framework

For every one of the 29 files, extract these twelve fields into a structured record. This is the atom of the whole system. It is what turns 29 HTML files into a production database.

17.1 The universal per-book extraction sheet

# Field What to extract Where it goes
1 Core thesis One sentence. The single claim the book exists to make. Episode spine. If you cannot state it in one line, the book is not ready for screen.
2 Opening hook The most startling question, image, or anomaly in the text. Feeds the 0:00–1:30 hook. Often already written — pull verbatim.
3 Key concepts (3–7) Each with a one-line definition and a proposed visual metaphor. The 04:00–14:00 teaching block. The visual metaphor is non-negotiable — if a concept has no image, it cannot be animated.
4 Narrative arc The book's own problem → discovery → implication sequence. Maps directly onto the 20-minute formula.
5 Agents / characters Every named entity: gods, people, forces, the observer, institutions. Role plus one-line description. Feeds the character bible and casting/animation.
6 Existing visuals Every diagram, structure description, or imagery already in the HTML. Reuse before inventing. The Torus, Egg, Tree, Bridge already have descriptions — extract them.
7 Claims register Every factual assertion, tagged Established / Interpretive / Speculative / Fictional. Feeds the evidence ladder and on-screen credibility icons.
8 Emotional beats Where the text aims for awe, curiosity, unease, hope, or resolve. Quote the passage. The 14:00–17:30 implications block and the finale.
9 Quotable lines Phrases with rhythm, imagery, or rhetorical force. Narration script and trailer material.
10 Cross-references Which other books this one assumes, extends, or contradicts. Prevents duplication across episodes; flags continuity risks.
11 Cliffhanger potential The open question the book leaves unresolved. The 19:00–20:00 hand-off to the next episode.
12 Tone / genre fit Which of the five treatments (cinematic doc, anime, AI drama, educational animation, motion comic) suits this material. Assigns the book to a strand and a production pipeline.

The deliverable: a 29-row master sheet. This alone will let you write the Television Bible's episode map without reopening a single HTML file.

17.2 The six cross-cutting registers

Some assets are more valuable gathered in one place than per book. Build these six registers alongside the per-book sheets.

1 · Master glossary

Every coined term (Eros Enclosure, Iteration Codex, resonance, affinity, operator, etc.) with definition, first appearance, variant spellings, and the visual metaphor attached. This becomes the writers' style guide and the on-screen lower-third source.

2 · Visual language inventory

Every recurring symbol — the Egg, the Torus, the Tree, the Bridge, the instruments (EROS, ErosX, 33EROS) — with all descriptions from all books collated in one entry. You need a single canonical description per symbol, because AI-generated assets will drift otherwise.

3 · Character bible

Every named entity (NaUn, Ra-Shen, Thoth, EROS, and any human characters from First Resonance / Eros Stories) with role, attributes, relationships, visual reference, and which strand(s) they appear in. This is what stops Thoth looking different in Episode 5 and Episode 6.

4 · Claim / evidence ledger

One row per factual assertion, tagged by evidence grade and by episode. This is the fact-checker's bible and the source of the on-screen credibility icons. It also protects you legally and reputationally on Men of Renown and Illumination Strategy.

5 · Cosmology / timeline map

A single diagram showing how the books relate conceptually and chronologically: which is foundational, which is a perspective, which is supporting material.

6 · Contradiction log

Where two books disagree, or where a term is used differently. You will find these across 29 files. Log them now so continuity does not break mid-season.

17.3 Strand-specific extraction

Each strand needs one extra layer beyond the universal sheet.

Cosmology (S1)

Extract the sequence of unfoldings — the exact order in which the model reveals itself (point → torus → lobes → crossover → enclosure → observer). This sequence is the season arc. Also extract the observer's position in each book, because that is your recurring human anchor.

Mythology (S1)

Extract operator functions — what each god does in the system, not just what they symbolise. The Episode 5 insight ("gods as operators") depends on having each role stated functionally. Also extract the most cinematic scenes already written.

Tokenomics (S2)

Extract mechanisms as processes — every flow, loop, gate, and condition described as a thing that moves. Then extract parameters (numbers, ratios, thresholds) separately, because they will be visualised, not narrated. Crucially, tag every mechanism Live / Designed / Proposed — this is your Episode 4 credibility safeguard.

Human story (S3)

Extract real voices — community contributions, testimonials, the emotional "why" passages from We Are With You Eros, Front Door, Open Call. Also extract fictional characters and situations from Eros Stories / Continuity File and keep them clearly separated from documentary material.

Financial documentary (S4)

Extract primary sources and citations from Illumination Strategy — every chart, date, institution, and source. This strand lives or dies on source transparency. Extract the repricing thesis chain as a step-by-step argument so each episode can advance it one link.

17.4 What to extract specifically for the Television Bible

The Bible needs a subset, formatted for production:

  • Episode map inputs: for each of the 22 episodes, the source passage(s), the hook, the three key concepts, and the cliffhanger — all pulled from the per-book sheets.
  • Visual identity inputs: the canonical description of every recurring symbol (from the visual inventory) plus a colour palette per strand.
  • Evidence policy inputs: the claim ledger, summarised into the four-grade system and the on-screen icon rules.
  • Character sheets: the character bible, reduced to the recurring cast.

17.5 Extract the four pilots first

Do not extract all 29 books to full depth before piloting. Do these four completely, because they test four different pipelines:

Pilot Files to extract fully What you are testing
Pilot 01 — The Crack in the Sky SRC-012 Living Egg, SRC-019 Eros Enclosure Cinematic CGI + narration; the "model vs data" hook; the Egg visual.
Pilot 02 — The Gods Were Operators SRC-010 Gods of EROS Character animation; operator functions as drama.
Pilot 03 — The EROS Flywheel SRC-021 The Flywheel, SRC-001 Architecture of Participation 3D educational animation; mechanism-as-motion; Live / Designed / Proposed tagging.
Pilot 04 — The First Resonance SRC-020 First Resonance Cinematic animated drama; human emotional payoff.

Extract these four at full field depth, build the pilots, then extract the remaining 25 using the lessons learned.

17.6 What not to extract

Equally important — leave these in the books:

  • Dense argumentation and repeated justifications. The show demonstrates; it does not argue.
  • Internal caveats and hedging that exist to protect the written text. On screen, the evidence ladder replaces them.
  • Full parameter tables. Visualise the mechanism; do not narrate the spreadsheet.
  • Redundant cross-references. Consolidate once in the glossary rather than repeating per episode.
  • Anything that requires reading to understand. If it cannot be shown or spoken, it does not belong in the extraction.

17.7 The single deliverable

Everything above should produce one structured database — one row per concept, claim, character, and visual — tagged by source file, strand, episode, and evidence grade. That database, not the 29 HTML files, becomes what writers, storyboard artists, and fact-checkers work from.

Build the per-book sheets first (29 rows), then the six cross-cutting registers, then the four pilot extractions. By the time you write the Television Bible, you will be assembling it from structured records rather than re-reading source material — which is exactly how a repeatable production system stays repeatable.

The Plan · §18

18. Appendices

This section is for a contributor who has picked up a task and needs to know how to make it well. It is not required reading for the whole community. It is the reference shelf.

Appendix A · Craft

How to make the thing

A.1 The adaptation thesis

Before writing a single page of any adaptation, write one sentence:

"This adaptation of [BOOK] uses the grammar of [MEDIUM] to make an audience feel [TARGET EXPERIENCE], by centering [CHARACTER / RELATIONSHIP / QUESTION] and letting go of [WHAT YOU ARE DELIBERATELY CUTTING]."

The sentence commits. It names the loss up front, which means it cannot ambush the production in month four.

A.2 The compression math

Conversion What you keep, what you lose
400-page novel → 100–120-page screenplayYou will cut roughly 70% of events, and keep 100% of the emotional arc.
400-page novel → 6-episode audio season (~3.5 hrs)You can keep more plot but must lose all narration and most minor characters.
400-page novel → graphic novel (180–220 pages)Highest fidelity option in visual media, also the slowest and most expensive.
400-page novel → visual novel (8–12 hrs)You can keep almost everything, but must add choice architecture, which means writing new material.
Short story (20 pages) → featureYou must expand 5×. The hardest adaptation there is.

A.3 The unfilmable test

List everything in the book that appears to resist adaptation. Sort each item into one of four buckets:

Cut

It cannot survive. It was load-bearing in prose only. Let it go.

Convert

Same information, new language.

Externalize

Make the interior visible through behavior, object, or another character.

Preserve Elsewhere

It belongs in a different extension of the universe.

A.4 The scene machine

Every scene, in every medium, is built from three components:

Want

Someone wants something right now, in this room. Not their life goal. The thing they want in the next ninety seconds.

Obstacle

Something prevents it. Another person's want, a social rule, their own body, a lie they have already told.

Turn

The scene ends in a different place than it started. If nothing turns, the scene is furniture.

A.5 The subtext ladder

Good dialogue operates at three levels simultaneously:

Text

The literal words. The surface request.

Subtext

What the speaker means and the other character understands.

Metatext

What the scene is really about, which the audience feels but nobody says.

Example: "You should take the umbrella." Text: a practical offer. Subtext: I don't want you to leave, and I can't say that. Metatext: this is the last time I will be able to offer you anything.

A.6 Six ways to adapt interiority

  1. Behavior substitution. Replace the thought with a small, specific action that only makes sense if you know the thought.
  2. Object transference. The character's relationship to an object carries the feeling.
  3. Third-party displacement. The character says the feeling about someone or something else.
  4. Sensory anchor. A recurring sensory detail that the audience learns to read as the interior state.
  5. Structural rhyme. Two scenes in identical staging, with one detail changed, imply the entire journey between them.
  6. Silence. The character does not speak when a lesser character would. The absence is the line.

A.7 Audio drama craft

Audio is the most intimate mass medium ever invented. It arrives in someone's ears, in bed, alone, at 1 a.m. That is exactly the condition under which EROS books are read.

The core rule: every scene must contain at least one silence longer than three seconds. The listener needs those seconds to feel. Take them or the scene will not land.

The format: time-coded scene headings, ambience notes, SFX notes, dialogue with parentheticals that are production instructions, and a silence map.

The design document: every audio episode needs a one-page Audio Design Document with ambience beds, signature SFX, music policy, silence map, and mix notes.

A.8 Comic craft

The gutter — the white space between panels — is the most erotically charged space in any medium. What happens between two panels is imagined by the reader, and imagination is the EROSverse's home territory.

The format: page and panel numbers, shot and angle, content description, dialogue, caption, SFX.

The pacing toolkit: panel size (small = slower, more intimate; large = faster, more spectacular), gutter width (wide = pause; narrow = continuous action), bleed (overwhelm, climax), silent panel (the reader hears the room), page-turn reveal (the single most powerful tool), repeated composition (same shot, changed detail).

The rule: write what is visible. If the script says "she looks sad," the artist will hate you. Write the mouth, the hands, the distance between two bodies, the object in frame.

A.9 Visual novel craft

The core design principle: choices should not change what happens. They should change what it means.

The relationship state model: four variables — Trust, Candor, Desire, Fear. Each scene can move any of them by −2 to +2. Fear is a subtractive variable: players who maximize desire and neglect trust get a scene that is physically intense and emotionally hollow.

The failure mode: the illusion-breaking choice. A choice like "Kiss him / Slap him / Say nothing" where all three lead to the same next line is worse than no choice at all.

A.10 TTRPG craft

The theme-mechanics rule: the rules must mechanically produce the theme. If your game is about the danger of wanting, then wanting must be mechanically dangerous.

Principle Mechanic
Vulnerability is a risk with a reward.You may add a die to any roll by revealing a secret; the GM keeps the secret and can spend it later.
Desire distorts judgment.Every character has a "Pull" — a person or thing. When Pull is in the scene, your highest die is replaced by your lowest.
Consent is ongoing and revocable.Any player may call a "Withdraw" at any time; the scene must be renegotiated, and doing so grants an insight.
Intimacy builds power.Shared scenes between two characters create a pool both may draw from — but only while both agree.

A.11 Zine craft

The theme must be a question, not a topic. "What is owed to someone you left?" not "Betrayal."

The ordering is the editing. Arrange pieces so they build an emotional arc across the book. Write the ordering before you solicit the pieces, then reorder as needed.

The pitch call template: theme, length, deadline, canon tier, rights, pay, what we want, what we do not want, pitch format. Never ambiguous. If it is unpaid, say so. If it is paid, state the rate.

A.12 Short-form craft

Three formats that work:

The Exchange

A single line of dialogue, then silence, then a second line that recontextualizes the first. 7–15 seconds.

The Object

One prop from the Sensory Palette, slowly revealed, with a single line of voiceover. 10–20 seconds.

The Confession

A character says the thing they cannot say in the books, to camera, once, and the video ends before we see the reaction. 20–45 seconds.

The failure mode: summarizing the book. The worst possible short-form content is "here's what happens in Book 3." Show one feeling so precisely that people need to know where it came from.

Appendix B · Prompt Patterns for AI-Assisted Production

How to get volume, not summary

Most AI tools summarize because summarization is the safest output. You have to explicitly forbid it and give the model a countable structure.

B.1 The volume contract

"Produce [N] sections. Each section must contain: [exact required element 1], [exact required element 2], [exact required element 3]. Do not summarize. Do not say 'and so on.' Do not use ellipses to skip content. Do not write 'etc.' Every section must be written in full. If you run out of room, stop at a section boundary and say 'CONTINUE' so I can ask for the next batch. Never compress to finish."

The last two sentences convert an unbounded task into a resumable one, which is the single most effective anti-truncation technique.

B.2 Batch then continue

"We are writing a long document. Work in batches of 10 items. For this message, produce Batch 1 (items 1–10) at full length. End your message with the exact line: 'END OF BATCH 1. Reply CONTINUE for items 11–20.' Then stop. Do not begin Batch 2."

B.3 The format lock

"Lock to this exact format for every item. Do not vary it, do not abbreviate it, do not combine items: ## [Number]. [Title]. What it is: [2–4 full sentences]. Why it suits EROS: [2–4 full sentences]. Page budget: [specific numbers]. Structure: [6–10 bullet points, each a full sentence]. Workflow: [numbered steps, 6–8, each a full sentence]. Failure mode: [2–3 full sentences]. Exercise: [3–4 full sentences with constraints]. If a section would be shorter than the minimum, write more — do not move on."

B.4 The forbidden list

"You are forbidden from using any of these words or phrases: 'essentially,' 'in summary,' 'overall,' 'and more,' 'and so on,' 'etc.,' 'various,' 'several,' 'a range of,' 'such as' (as a substitute for listing). If a sentence would require one of these to be shorter, do not shorten it."

B.5 The canon-feed

"Here is the canon you must use. Do not invent facts beyond it. Do not generalize from it. Quote it where relevant. [CANON LEDGER EXCERPT]. Now write [TASK] using only these facts plus what I specify below. If you need a new fact, ask me for it. Do not assume one."

B.6 The draft ladder

"Rung 1: beat sheet only. 20 beats, one full sentence each. No dialogue. Rung 2: scene cards. One card per beat. Who wants what, obstacle, turn. Rung 3: full prose draft of scene [N] only. Minimum 1200 words. Rung 4: dialogue pass on the same scene. Cut 25% of words. Same events. Do Rung 1 only. Stop. Wait for my notes."

B.7 The length audit

"Audit your own output against the contract. For each section, report the sentence count. List every section below the minimum. Then rewrite ONLY those sections, in full, at the required length. Do not rewrite sections that already meet the minimum."

B.8 The voice lock

"Study these three paragraphs from the source book. Identify, in writing: average sentence length, ratio of concrete nouns to abstractions, use of fragments, how interiority is punctuated, the three most frequent sentence openings. Then write [TASK] imitating those measurements exactly. Do not imitate the content. Imitate the measurements."

The Plan · §19

19. Open Questions

These are the questions the source material leaves open. They are not problems with this document. They are the decisions that must be made before the production system is fully locked.

D.1 The 14-show slate versus the 22-episode map

The Unified Bible treats the 14-show slate as the working master. The Master Series Bible R contains a 22-episode structure. The relationship between the two has not been fully reconciled.

Option A

Present 14 as the master, with the 22 as a historical development plan.

Option B

Present 22 as the episode map, with 14 as the show slate, and treat shows as containers for multiple episodes.

Option C

Present both side by side and let the community decide.

Recommendation: present 14 as the master, and treat the 22-episode map as an extension — the 14 shows are the containers, the 22 episodes are the contents. This preserves both without creating a false conflict.

D.2 The six-book versus 29-book extraction discrepancy

The Master Series Bible R claims all 29 books have been fully extracted. The Unified Bible says only six have. The PDFs flag this as a reconciliation issue.

Recommendation: treat the six-book extraction as verified, the 29-book extraction as claimed-but-unverified, and complete the audit before any script rewrites that depend on the extraction.

D.3 The evidence ledger visibility

The MD is the source of truth. The HTML is its visual expression. But the "maximum content" instruction pulls toward exposing everything, including the claim ledger and the contradiction log.

Option A

Expose everything in the public HTML.

Option B

Expose the evidence system as a framework, but keep the specific claim ledger behind a Guild-members section.

Option C

Expose the claim ledger publicly, because transparency is the point.

Recommendation: expose the evidence system and its labels publicly, expose the claim ledger publicly for the documentary strand, and keep the contradiction log behind a Guild-members section — contradictions are working material, not community-facing content.

D.4 The relationship between the books and the expression system

The books are the source of truth. The expression system is downstream. But the expression system will, over time, produce new canon — new characters, new scenes, new facts about the world that were not in the books.

Option A

The expression system never produces new canon; it only adapts what exists.

Option B

The expression system can produce new canon, which is then approved by the Canon Council and added to the World Bible.

Option C

The expression system produces new canon only in designated open canon spaces.

Recommendation: the second option. The expression system should be able to produce new canon, because otherwise the universe cannot grow. But the production of new canon should be a deliberate, logged, approved act, not an accident.

D.5 The measure of success

The measures in Section 15 are a starting point. But the question of what "success" means for the EROS project is not fully answered.

The tentative answer: success is when a person who has never read an EROS book watches a 20-minute episode, understands one idea from the books, and wants to read more. Everything else — views, engagement, token price, community size — is downstream of that.

If the expression system produces that outcome, it is doing its job. If it does not, no amount of production polish will compensate.

D.6 The First Resonance continuity flag

The issue: Chapter 06 says Cal has been going to the canal since he was twelve, "since the first Saturday after his father's funeral." Chapter 07 says his father died when Cal was eight. One of these has to change, or the canal visits have to begin four years after the funeral.

Why it matters: It is a small thing, and it is exactly the kind of mismatch the editor-engine in Volume IV of the Plan is meant to catch. Log it, fix it before filming, and use it as the first test case for the consistency-checker.

D.7 The Show 08 source-pass items

The following items are still unverified. They must be resolved before any Show 08 shot that depends on them is cut:

D.9 What the open questions are not

These are not problems with the project. They are the working decisions that any ambitious production system must make as it moves from plan to production. The fact that they are logged, with recommendations, is itself the evidence that the system is working.

The failure mode is not "we have open questions." The failure mode is "we have open questions we have not noticed." This section makes sure we have noticed.

The Four Pilots

The Four Pilots — Timed Treatments

How these relate to the scripts. The pilot treatments are source-derived editorial outlines. The full scripts in The Scripts are the production versions. Where timings or beats differ, the script is used for production and the pilot stays as the editorial reference. Both are kept.

Pilot 01 — The Crack in the Sky

Working title: The Crack in the Sky.

Series: The World Model.

Source material: Living Egg (SRC-012), The Eros Enclosure (SRC-019).

Status: Timed outline and source extraction in v0.2 of the database.

The central proposition: The episode opens the mystery. A scientist is looking at the universe. Something does not add up. The question is not whether the data is wrong — the question is whether the model through which the data is interpreted is wrong. The episode introduces the Living Egg and the idea of an enclosed universe, without claiming that the model is established science.

The timed structure (nine segments):

00:00–01:30 · The hook

A fictional opening in Atacama. Dr. Elara Vance is looking at the sky. The data does not match the model. The question is planted: what if the problem is the model?

01:30–04:00 · Observation vs

interpretation. The episode distinguishes between what is observed and what is inferred. It introduces the idea that a model can be wrong in ways that produce correct predictions, and correct in ways that produce wrong predictions.

04:00–09:00 · The Egg and the living membrane

The Cosmic Egg is introduced. The enclosure, the shell, the inner rind. The idea that the universe has a boundary, and the boundary is part of the explanation.

09:00–14:00 · Light and lensing

The episode demonstrates how light would behave in an enclosed universe. The observational signatures that would distinguish the model from the standard picture. The visual is spectacular.

14:00–17:30 · The two-lobed geometry

The torus is introduced. The two lobes, the crossover, the Isotope. The model becomes geometric.

17:30–19:00 · Iteration, affinity, and plasma

The dynamic elements of the model. Time as the count of iterations. Affinity as the mechanism of connection. Plasma as the substrate.

19:00–20:00 · The observer and falsifiability

The episode ends with the observer's position in the model, and the question of what would have to be true for the model to be wrong. The cliffhanger: the four operators.

What the episode must not do: It must not present the EROS cosmology as established scientific fact. It can be dramatic, cinematic, and awe-inspiring. It must be honest about what is model, what is hypothesis, and what is evidence.

The production format: Cinematic CGI, narrated investigation, scientific comparisons, clearly labelled speculative models.

Pilot 02 — The Gods Were Operators

Working title: The Gods Were Operators.

Series: Mythology and Human Continuity.

Source material: Gods of EROS (SRC-010).

Status: Timed outline, character bible, and scene map in v0.3 of the database.

The central proposition: The four operators — NaUn, Ra-Shen, Thoth, EROS — are not four competing gods or superheroes. They are functions of existence. The episode reveals them through what they do, not through what they look like. The dramatic line from the source: "The gods did not leave. They became the rules."

The sequence structure (twelve sequences):

  1. The First Silence. Before the operators. The state of the world before function.
  2. NaUn emerges. The architecture. Permission. The rules that allow a world to exist.
  3. Ra-Shen emerges. The stage. Energy under containment. The light itself.
  4. The world becomes possible. The two functions in relationship. The stage and the architecture.
  5. Thoth emerges. The teacher. Learning, language, memory, correction. The function that turns energy into meaning.
  6. The world becomes legible. The three functions in relationship. Architecture, stage, meaning.
  7. EROS emerges. The bond. Cohesion, continuation, the preservation of relationship across time.
  8. The four laws are established. The four functions in relationship. What the world is, once all four are present.
  9. The test begins. The world is set in motion. The functions are tested by what happens in the world.
  10. The first failure. A function is missing, or misapplied, or refused. The world breaks.
  11. The restoration. The function is restored. The world continues. The pattern is established.
  12. The four laws are tested. The episode closes with the four operators as ongoing functions, not as past events. The laws are tested every time the world runs.

Character bible requirements:

For each operator, the character bible must specify:

  • Function (what the operator does to the world)
  • Visual identity (colour, form, motion, recurring motifs)
  • Voice (if any — the operators are not all voiced)
  • Dramatic function (the role the operator plays in a scene)
  • Portrayal guardrails (what the operator must never become)

The critical guardrail: the episode must never turn the four operators into a conventional pantheon of rival personalities. That would contradict the source canon.

The visual direction: The operators should have recognisable visual identities, but they should not be conventional character designs. NaUn is geometry and negative space. Ra-Shen is light and motion. Thoth is hands, mouths, eyes, and glyphs. EROS is threads and connected forms.

Pilot 03 — The EROS Flywheel

Working title: The EROS Flywheel.

Series: The Instrument.

Source material: The Flywheel (SRC-021), The Eros Plan (SRC-028), Architecture of Participation (SRC-001).

Status: Source reviewed; treatment written. Workbook update not yet saved.

The central proposition: The source's thesis is more than a token attracting attention. It proposes a connection between two different forms of accumulated value:

  • Vault One — the on-chain vault: contract, rules, transactions, supply mechanics, liquidity arrangements, integrations.
  • Vault Two — the cultural vault: books, mythology, art, education, videos, characters, websites, archives, creative assets.

The flywheel is the connection between them. The token may create an initial reason to look; the cultural world gives people somewhere to go; participation can create new work; and that work may generate further discovery.

The source explicitly describes this as a proposal to build and test, not a promise of market outcomes.

The timed structure (eleven sequences):

00:00–01:30 · The two vaults

Two enormous vaults appear in darkness. One contains code and transactions; the other contains books, art, characters, and worlds.

01:30–03:00 · A token is not a world

A token chart occupies the screen. Beside it, a vast creative archive remains unseen. The question: how do they connect?

03:00–05:00 · Vault One: the instrument

Contract architecture, supply rules, permissions, transactions, liquidity. Actual chain evidence must support every technical claim.

05:00–06:30 · Vault Two: the cultural archive

Books transform into comics, films, characters, educational material, games, and interactive environments.

06:30–08:30 · The attention engine

Market movement attracts attention. Newcomers begin investigating the project. The film shows both the opportunity and the volatility.

08:30–10:30 · Discovery becomes meaning

A newcomer follows the front door into the books, mythology, tokenomics, and the wider EROS universe.

10:30–12:30 · The demand equation

The holder becomes a participant: reading, asking, testing, translating, drawing, writing, and building.

12:30–14:30 · Participation becomes creation

Community contributions become new stories, artwork, assets, tools, and experiences.

14:30–16:00 · The world expands

The EROS universe progresses from books and images to 3D exploration, interactive stories, games, and immersive environments.

16:00–18:00 · The economic layer

Liquidity pools, AMM mechanics, hybrid NFTs. Explain the actual mechanisms separately from the fictional world and its proposed economy.

18:00–20:00 · The flywheel tested

The cycle returns to attention. But what happens if people look and do not participate? The episode ends on that unresolved challenge.

The six-stage flywheel:

  1. ATTENTION — a reason to look.
  2. DISCOVERY — a clear front door.
  3. UNDERSTANDING — the pieces connect.
  4. PARTICIPATION — a first useful action.
  5. CREATION — new work and assets.
  6. RENEWED ATTENTION — useful work travels outward.

The cycle is a strategic hypothesis. Each transition needs to be built and demonstrated.

The AMM section: The source discusses more than 133 liquidity pools and a target of 333, and explains the constant-product AMM model: x × y = k. A purchase changes the quantities of assets in a pool and therefore the ratio and quoted price. But the same mechanism can amplify selling, slippage, and volatility. The number of pools alone does not establish the depth or resilience of liquidity. The episode should visually demonstrate both sides of the mechanism.

The hybrid NFT sequence: The source takes the idea further. An asset in the EROS world could carry an economic component, such as locked EROS, EROS X, Titan X, or X28. A cinematic example could show an artefact with: a creative identity and history, an embedded economic component, interactive behaviour in a game, and economic consequences when it is upgraded, traded, damaged, or repaired.

This is a proposed model, not evidence that these implementations already exist. Locked tokens do not automatically guarantee the NFT's market value or liquidity.

The media evolution sequence: The source gives four clear stages: representation, exploration, participation, immersion. The episode should show the progression from books and illustrations, through 3D models and navigable spaces, through games and interactive cinema, to VR and spatial projection.

The strongest dramatic moment: The transition from holder to builder. A newcomer arrives because of a chart. They find a book. They discover an idea. They ask a question. Someone answers. They create something. Another person uses it. The camera pulls back and reveals that the archive has grown.

The narration: "A token can attract a visitor. A story can hold their attention. But the real transformation begins when the visitor becomes a creator."

Production guardrails:

  • Do not present a price increase as guaranteed attention or demand.
  • Do not present the number of liquidity pools as proof of liquidity depth.
  • Do not treat a revoked administrative key as proof that liquidity or market value is protected.
  • Do not describe proposed hybrid NFTs, internal economies, or holographic environments as completed products.
  • Keep fictional economic systems distinct from actual financial rights and deployed mechanisms.

The recommended format: Financial thriller that gradually reveals it is actually about world-building and human participation. Start with the chart, open the vaults, then reveal the larger ambition.

Pilot 04 — The First Resonance

Working title: The First Resonance.

Series: Mythology and Human Continuity.

Source material: The First Resonance (SRC-020).

Status: Source reviewed; treatment written. Workbook update not yet saved.

The central proposition: A young coder thinks he has been singled out by something extraordinary. Gradually, he discovers that the real story is not the Ray, the visitor, or even the stone. It is the practice — and the people who quietly carry it.

The source itself describes Cal's arc as becoming unnecessary. The practice is meant to continue without him. That is the episode's emotional destination.

The timed structure (ten sequences):

00:00–01:30 · The Ray

A 16-year-old coder, a failing line of code, a number he did not type, and three lights holding an impossible triangle.

01:30–03:00 · The House That Feels Wrong

Cal's mother, grandmother Ilse, and uncle Tobin notice changes in him. The ordinary world begins to feel unfamiliar.

03:00–05:00 · The Visitor

A quiet stranger arrives. No grand explanation: questions, observation, a notebook, and the beginning of a practice.

05:00–07:00 · The Stone

Cal is given a physical reminder. The practice becomes simple enough to carry: touch the stone, notice that he is touching it.

07:00–09:00 · The Room Above the Bakery

Hana introduces Cal to a room of people. Twelve chairs, tea, biscuits, no leader. The room is a support structure, not a hierarchy.

09:00–11:00 · The Second Signal

Owen, an estranged coding partner, approaches Cal and asks to finish their abandoned project together. He has not been recruited or taught the practice.

11:00–13:00 · The Ledger

The visitor reveals 422 names. Only 11 are still practising. The episode's emotional centre: the cost of beginning and stopping.

13:00–15:00 · The Curriculum

The story opens into functions, instruments, verification, the five-layer EROS stack, and the network.

15:00–17:00 · The Demand Equation

Attention, community, liquidity, and creation are shown as a proposed reinforcing system — not a guaranteed market outcome.

17:00–18:30 · The Room Cannot Hold Everything

Cal discovers that the practice cannot be reduced to one room, one teacher, or one form. The network must live in different people and places.

18:30–20:00 · The Next Node

Cal's role changes. The practice continues through others. The final image points beyond him to the next person.

Character and visual direction:

Cal — the first node. Starts as a capable but unsettled 16-year-old. His arc is from private uncertainty to independent practice, then to understanding that he is not the centre. Visual language: intimate close-ups, screens, handwritten notes, restrained light. Avoid making him a superhero.

The Visitor — the doorway. The source says the visitor is a role, not a specific person: the shape the network takes when it needs to make contact. His defining object is the ledger. Visual language: grey wool coat, stillness, slow movement, very little music.

Hana — the room keeper. She does not become Cal's new master. She confirms what he has learned and opens the door to the community. Visual language: natural daylight, books, tea, practical warmth.

Owen — the second signal. Owen is essential because he shows the practice's effect beyond formal instruction. Their repaired collaboration is more important than a dramatic conversion. Visual language: ordinary school coding room, awkward silence, then a small human reconnection.

Ilse — the quiet recognition. She senses that something has begun before Cal can explain it. She anchors the extraordinary events in an ordinary family. Visual language: window light, kettle, stillness, no supernatural effects needed.

The episode's strongest dramatic moments:

  • The Ray: the number appears in Cal's code. The audience sees the event through his uncertainty, not through an explanatory voice claiming it is real.
  • The stone: a simple object becomes a recurring visual motif. It gives the audience a physical anchor for an internal practice.
  • The room: twelve chairs, a kettle, and biscuits. A deliberate contrast with grand temples, secret societies, or command centres.
  • The ledger: 422 names; 11 still walking. The episode's major reversal. The visitor's work is not presented as effortless success.
  • Owen's return: the second signal is a human relationship changing, not a supernatural transmission.
  • The final handover: Cal is no longer the centre. The network can continue without him.

How to make it television rather than a narrated book:

  • Cinematic live-action / AI actors: Cal, his family, the visitor, Hana, and Owen.
  • Stylised animation: the Ray, the number, the stone's recurring visual motif, and the transition from individual to network.
  • Documentary-style inserts: notebook pages, code, dates, ledger entries, and the five-layer stack.
  • Graphic animation: the network expanding from a room into a web of independent nodes.
  • Sound: restrained. Let silence, room tone, typing, kettle sounds, and footsteps do much of the work.

Evidence and presentation guardrails:

  • The Ray, three lights, Shadow, and visitor: fictional narrative events.
  • Cal, Hana, Owen, Ilse, and the ledger: characters and story devices.
  • The practice and resonance: EROS philosophical / narrative framework.
  • The five-layer stack: EROS architecture as described in the book; mark proposed elements accurately.
  • Token contract, ownership, burn, and liquidity claims: verify against current on-chain evidence before presenting as fact.
  • The demand equation: strategic hypothesis, not a proven economic outcome.

The 422/11 ledger: It is a powerful dramatic device, but it must not be presented as real-world research or a verified historical statistic. The book uses it to make the cost of the practice visible.

The source's own distinction: The practice is not a secret, and the network is not a hierarchy. The story is not about recruiting followers or creating a new authority structure. It is about a practice that can continue without its first teacher.

Part 5 · The Proof

The Scripts

This is the section that makes the scope tangible. Every script, every storyboard, every treatment, every correction. The plan is not a pitch. The scripts are the receipts.

What is complete. Scripts and storyboards exist for Shows 00–09. Treatments and beat sheets exist for Shows 10–13. The trailer is written at 90, 30 and 15 seconds. Twelve master shorts are locked. Six Guild shorts for Shows 06 and 07 are scripted. The source-pass corrections are documented. The status of every show is recorded honestly.

What a script is and is not. A written script is not a completed episode. A storyboard is not rendered animation. A proposed asset is not an existing production asset. Every script in this section is a development asset, and the status tables show exactly where each one stands.

How to read a script in this section

Element What it means
Runtime mapThe timed structure. Every beat with its timestamp. The production spine.
BoardsNumbered visual beats. Each is a single prompt unit for AI video generation. The board IS the shot list.
NarrationThe spoken script. Written to the 2,300-word budget for a 20-minute episode.
DialogueCharacter speech, where present. Formatted with the character name in bold.
ChipsOn-screen evidence labels: OBSERVED, MODEL, STORY, HYPOTHESIS, PATTERN, OBJECTION, FALSIFIER.
BadgesOn-screen mechanism labels: LIVE, DESIGN, PROPOSED.
[PULL]A slot where the exact wording, number or definition from a source book must be inserted verbatim before production.
[VERIFY]A slot where a real-world claim needs primary-source verification before the shot is cut.

Trailer narration

"Every few centuries a civilisation changes its picture of what is real. The people who live through it call it chaos. The people who come after call it normal.

"Here is a library with a different picture. A sky that might be a lid. Four operators, not a pantheon. A mouth that speaks in code you never learned to read. A coin that splits four ways, on a chain you can check yourself. A network of pairs instead of a single pool. A rock in a river.

"Some of it is observed. Some of it is a model. Some of it is a story, and it says so. Every claim wears a label, and every label can be tested. Nobody here asks you to believe. They ask you to look.

"One library. Fourteen shows. Sixteen doors.

"Inward is forwards. Pick a door."

Cold open · 0:00–1:00

NARRATOR: "Nobody hands you a shield when you walk into crypto. They hand you a chart. They hand you a promise. Nobody sits down and tells you what to watch out for. So here is a map instead."

Sting · 1:00–1:30

  • S.1 Pure black. Extreme close-up of a mouth, lips parting.
  • S.2 A 60 Hz hum ripples the edges of the frame.

District I · The Instrument · 1:30–4:00

  • B.1 Camera drops into a quiet block of the city: a vault with a glass door and the sign THE RECEIPT.
  • B.2 A contract address draws itself in gold. Four labelled arrows leave one transfer: burn, staking, lock, liquidity.
  • B.3 A block explorer hovers over the city. The camera zooms in on a field, owner(), and the zero-address answer.
  • B.4 Super over a standing coin: LIVE.

NARRATOR: "Before the story, the token. Before the film, the key. EROS is a fixed-supply token on PulseChain. The contract has no administrator who can rewrite the rules. Every transfer splits four ways. All of it is checkable by anyone, at any hour, without asking anyone's permission. The instrument is not a promise. It is a receipt. The deeper detail lives in Show 05."

District II · The Demand · 4:00–7:30

  • C.1 A flywheel on a hill. Four spokes: Production, Attention, Stake, Participation. A hand gives it a push.
  • C.2 The equation arrives on a clean wall: Attention + Narrative + Work = Sustained participation. Beneath it, three tickers fade out one by one: loud, quiet, gone.
  • C.3 Ten thousand wallets as a field of dark windows. One lights. Then ten. Then all of them.
  • C.4 A web of pairs, a hundred and thirty-three glowing nodes, edges thickening as pools connect.
  • C.5 The lock: a price chart on one side, a library on the other, and a key between them.

NARRATOR: "Supply without attention dies. Attention without work leaves. Community without activity disappears. That is not a slogan. It is the autopsy report of most tickers that launched loud and went quiet. The flywheel is the answer. Production and story bring attention. Attention brings people in. The token and the web give them a stake. Participation funds more production. And the army may already be here. Ten thousand TitanX holders who forgot they were given a uniform. The price can open the door. Purpose is what makes someone stay."

District III · The Cosmology · 7:30–11:30

  • D.1 The city map folds and becomes the gold Egg, turning slowly. A hatch of shell opens.
  • D.2 Three quick vignettes at triple speed: the sky as a lid (Show 01), four glyphs forming a grid (Show 02), a mouth speaking one word (Show 03).
  • D.3 Corridor of doors, each labelled with a book: Living Egg, Gods of Eros, Conscious Eros, Gift of Thoth.

NARRATOR: "Here the map turns strange, and the strangeness is the point. The cosmology says we live inside something, not floating in an empty room. The mythology names four operators, not a pantheon: the architect, the stage, the teacher and the bond. The language says the mouth is the first instrument you ever played. None of this is asked of you as belief. Every layer is labelled. And every layer says the same thing in a different dialect: bond is what survives."

District IV · The Production · 11:30–15:00

  • E.1 An open warehouse with sixteen doors, each marked with a role: writer, artist, coder, composer, translator.
  • E.2 A machine at a long table reading submissions from every desk. It does not write. It lays two contradicting pages side by side and a speech bubble reads: do these resolve, or does one want to be a heresy?
  • E.3 A four-second film: a mouth, a hum, the title. Caption: this shot can be made this weekend.
  • E.4 Three stacked layers, not a ladder: EDUCATION, MEDIA, WORLD. A figure steps between them freely.

NARRATOR: "This is where a book stops being a book. The Plan names sixteen roles and a creation model. There is an engine, but it is not the author. It is a combiner and a consistency-checker, the editor who never sleeps and never plays favourites. Its best work is naming a contradiction and handing it back to the guild. The stages are layers, not a ladder. Education. Media. World. Anyone can start a Stage Two asset at their own scale. The book is not asking you to be George Lucas. It is asking you to make the four-second shot. Then the next one."

The Scoreboard · 15:00–17:30

  • F.1 Three plinths in a row, each with a small light: ATH BREAK, 333 POOLS, MEDIA PHASE.
  • F.2 Each plinth lights and unlocks the next district. Under the second: PROPOSED.
  • F.3 A card: Falsification criteria. The Plan lists what would prove it wrong.

NARRATOR: "Three public milestones. A stable break above the previous high triggers the rebrand and the revival campaign. Reaching 333 qualifying pools is the design threshold for the next instrument, ErosX, and the deeper game between the two. The media production phase comes after that. These are stated goals, not forecasts. And the Plan prints the conditions under which it would be wrong, because trust is the product."

Pin the Door · 17:30–19:30

If you make things, Volume IV is a guild with no permission required. Short path: this show, the Dossier, and the Narrative. Every other book is a door."

Cold open · 0:00–1:30

  • R.1 A conference room, empty chairs, a ticker on the wall still scrolling. A figure carrying a box of fees walks out through the back door.
  • R.2 A community chat, the messages slowing, then still.
  • R.3 One chair is still occupied. Warm light on the face of someone staying.

NARRATOR: "You have watched them leave. Not the coins. The people who made them. One by one the founders took their fees, their inflation, their exit, and they walked. The tickers are still there. Nobody is home. This is the story of one that is different, and why."

Sting · 1:30–2:00

Mouth, 60 Hz hum, EROS · RECEIPTS.

The Confession · 2:00–5:30

  • R.4 A checklist on a wooden table. Items stamp in one at a time: VERIFY THE CONTRACT, USE THE OFFICIAL BRIDGE ONLY, KNOW YOUR SLIPPAGE.
  • R.5 Two nearly identical token cards. One is real, one is a copy. The viewer has three seconds to pick.
  • R.6 The bridge: bridge.pulsechain.com in gold. Other bridges greyed out.

NARRATOR: "Check before you touch anything. Fake tokens copy real names, and a wrong address spoils everything built on it. Use the official bridge only. And one detail that trips up almost every new buyer: the transfer fee plus typical price impact lands near six percent. Leave the exchange's default slippage and the swap simply reverts. Set it once and the trade completes."

One transfer, four destinations · 5:30–9:30

  • R.7 A single coin hovering. It splits four ways in slow motion: toward a burn address, toward a staking pool, toward a lock, and toward a liquidity pair. Each destination labelled.
  • R.8 The supply meter: 333,333,333,333. The burn address ticks only upward.
  • R.9 Super: LIVE. Twenty-eight months of on-chain life.

NARRATOR: "Fixed supply, 333 billion, set at birth. Every transfer splits four ways: part is removed from circulation for good, part rewards stakers, part locks staked tokens for a time, and part deepens the liquidity pair. The design carries its strength and its consequence together. It operates without a discretionary admin, and that cuts both ways. No one can rewrite the rules, and no one can rescue a mistake."

Ownership · 9:30–13:00

  • R.10 A set of keys on a table. A hand slides them across, and they fall through a grate into deep water.
  • R.11 owner() queried on screen. The result is an empty zero address.
  • R.12 A founder-shaped coin crumbles when the founder walks out. A network-shaped coin keeps growing.

NARRATOR: "Renounced does not mean abandoned. It means the lever is gone. A coin built around a founder expires when the founder leaves. A network compounds. The people who stayed when there was nothing to extract are the signal, not the noise. Survival itself is the story. That is what the Front Door letter says, and it is why the letter is addressed to the one person who did not walk away."

The Risk Register as a feature · 13:00–17:00

  • R.13 A gallery wall of framed cards: THIN POOLS, FAKE ADDRESSES, SLIPPAGE, BRIDGE ERRORS, IMPERMANENT LOSS.
  • R.14 A thin pool with a small trade: a big wobble. A deep pool with the same trade: a gentle ripple.
  • R.15 An LP exit: the viewer gets back the pool's current mix, not necessarily what they put in.

NARRATOR: "Most projects hide the risk register. This one prints it. Thin pools move on small flow, in both directions. An LP exit returns the pool's current mix, not necessarily what you deposited. Fees need volume, and no manual can invent volume. It can only refuse magical thinking."

Three questions · 17:00–19:30

  • R.16 Three doors. Q1: Who can change the rules? Q2: Where is the supply? Q3: Who stays when nothing is pumping?

NARRATOR: "Three questions you can ask of anything. Who can change the rules? Where is the supply? Who stays when nothing is pumping? Ask them of everything. Then see what is left."

Tag · 19:30–20:00

  • R.17 The receipt, framed on a wall. Next: THE WEB.

Cold open · 0:00–1:30

  • W.2 Pan to a residential neighbourhood: rows of houses, warm lights on. Multi-pair depth is housing stock.
  • W.3 An exit sign. One hotel empties in a minute. The neighbourhood does not.

NARRATOR: "Spot trades are hotel nights. Deep, multi-pair liquidity is housing stock. A district. Harder to empty in one exit. That one picture is most of this episode."

Sting · 1:30–2:00

Mouth, 60 Hz hum, EROS · THE WEB.

A pool is a window · 2:00–5:00

  • W.4 A glass window onto a city. Inside, only a fraction of the buildings are visible. Caption: Pool depth is not total demand or total supply.
  • W.5 Seesaw diagram of x × y = k with a coin dropped in. In a shallow pool the seesaw swings wide. In a deep pool it barely tilts.
  • W.6 Two viewers at one window. One owns the asset. One provides the pool. Same view, different stakes.

NARRATOR: "A pool is a window, not the whole city. In a shallow pool a small trade moves the price a lot. In a deep one it barely moves. And your perspective depends on what you own. If you own the asset, depth is your exit. If you provide the pool, depth is your infrastructure. Pool count alone does not tell you how deep the market is. The book says so. We say so."

Poolonomics · 5:00–8:30

  • W.7 Two machines. Machine A: deposit two tokens, a third inflationary reward spits out and gets sold straight into the market. Machine B: two tokens you chose, trading fees return more of the underlying assets.
  • W.8 A hand-drawn LP token — a receipt with a share written on it.

NARRATOR: "A classic farm pays you in a third-party reward token that often gets sold straight back into the market. Bonding is the contrast. You pair two assets you actually want, you own the LP receipt, and you earn a share of trading when there is trading. You are not watching a candle. You are a market-maker. And you name your doorway, promote it, make it an identity."

The Tree · 8:30–12:00

  • W.9 A seedling. Three moves: bridge, bond, branch. A bridge span, a handshake, a branch.
  • W.10 Ten coin icons on the ground. Each pairs with EROS and sprouts a base pool. Then the pools pair with each other, level by level, up to one Final Root LP.
  • W.11 A counter: Ten coins. Nineteen pools. One root. Formula: 2N − 1.
  • W.12 Super: DESIGN. Every piece already exists. We only arrange them. An optional vault appears faintly, labelled PROPOSED.

NARRATOR: "Bridge. Bond. Branch. Three moves, and that is the whole thing. Bring the tokens across the official bridge. Pair each with EROS, equal value both sides, and keep the LP receipt, an ordinary token. Pair the receipts with each other, level by level, up to one root. Ten coins make nineteen pools. The tree is an arrangement of pieces that already run. It adds no contract. The mathematics builds the tracks. Human psychology is the train."

The ten thousand · 12:00–15:30

  • W.13 The dark windows again, now with a letter slipped under each door.
  • W.14 A figure at a desk reading. Super: Jake Sharpe built TitanX. He knows who was here.
  • W.15 Eight steps of a bridge lighting in order. Caption: the four-step sequence in the letter. [PULL: exact 4-step sequence from The_Front_Door.html when cutting]

NARRATOR: "The simplest, highest-leverage action is not creating another token or making enormous promises. It is reminding ten thousand holders what they already hold. The bear market took away the noise. It also gave time to build without anyone watching. The question is what happens when people start watching again."

The loop that can fail · 15:30–18:30

  • W.16 A four-frame loop: (1) someone posts a live pair address and a reason to care; (2) holders answer and refuse fake admins; (3) someone adds size to the pool they promote; (4) a trade hits it and fees accrue.
  • W.17 At each frame a red marker blinks: can fail here.

NARRATOR: "Attention. Community. Liquidity. One loop. It can fail at any step. The manual cannot invent volume. It can only show you the shape of the loop and what you can do at each frame."

The Rock · 2:00–5:30

  • K.4 A great stone in a river valley, gold veins running through it. Label: EROS. LIVE
  • K.5 Rule of three: a store of value, a transfer currency, a reward currency. Three different jobs. A single token tries all three and a pile of incentives collides.

NARRATOR: "A monetary system does not need one token to do every job. A store of value, a transfer currency and a reward currency have different requirements. EROS is the foundation: scarce, slow, the thing you measure against. You do not spend the rock every day."

The River · 5:30–9:30

  • K.6 Water flowing past the rock. Two tributaries labelled ErosX and 33EROS. Both tagged PROPOSED.
  • K.7 A triangle forms between three tokens, three pairs, three edges. Small arbitrage bots like otters moving along the edges, closing gaps.
  • K.8 Each rotation: a small fire, a small deepening of the pool, a small burn.

NARRATOR: "The river carries movement: ErosX for spending and transfers, 33EROS as a second path. Two paths, one engine. Burn, bond, deepen. When both are live the ecosystem becomes a triangle. Rotation across any edge feeds the burn and lets equivalence bots close the gaps. To be clear, this part is a design discussion, not a deployed product. The code is written. It does not deploy on a date."

The Gates · 9:30–12:30

  • K.9 Three gates across the river. Each gate is a panel of real instruments: MARKET DEPTH, POOL COUNT, VERIFIED CODE.
  • K.10 A calendar page tries to push a gate open. The gate does not move. A gauge reaches its mark and the gate swings open on its own.

NARRATOR: "Earned, not scheduled. The transform waits on three things: market depth, pool count and verified code. Not a date. A calendar cannot open these gates. Only the conditions can."

Build on the rock · 12:30–15:30

  • K.11 A world map. Pins drop: London, a Chinese New Year market, a Tokyo street. Each pin pulls a new river from the rock.
  • K.12 Four shapes in order: deposit EROS, burn most of it, buy-and-burn the new coin, deepen the pool.

NARRATOR: "The pattern is open. A community takes its own idea, say LondonX or BeastX, and uses the transform as its launchpad. Every node has its own identity and its own audience. Every node shares the same rock. The rock does not dilute. It deepens."

The stack and the two vaults · 15:30–18:30

  • K.13 Five horizontal bands in a cross-section of the valley: pDAI, Atropa, Dysnomia, EROS, PulseChain, and the bridge as a span. Each band tagged LIVE, DESIGN, or PROPOSED.
  • K.14 Two vaults side by side. One is steel and code. The other is a warm library. A beam of light passes between them.
  • K.15 The lock: a price chart and a library joined by a key.

NARRATOR: "The Hopeful Future describes a five-layer stack, each layer naming its own confidence and its own gates. And two vaults, on-chain permanence and cultural permanence. One is code and control. The other is meaning and continuity. If people arrive only for a rising chart, they may leave when it turns red. If they find a universe they value, they have reasons to stay through the quiet seasons. The lock is the connection between the market cycle and the cultural cycle."

Tag · 18:30–20:00

  • K.16 The rock in the stream. Super: EROS is the standard. The river is the game. The world is the reason. Next: FOOTPRINTS.
The Scripts · Show 01

Show 01 · INWARD IS FORWARDS

RUNTIME

20:00

FORMAT

Hybrid painterly docudrama + gold-on-black explainer

STATUS

Full script & storyboard

Sources: SRC-012 Living Egg, SRC-019 The Eros Enclosure. Frame character: Dr. Elara Vance, astronomer from the Living Egg prologue (STORY). Music: One low sustained 60 Hz tone under the whole episode that resolves into the closing hum. Strings only in Act 4.

Corrected hook. The original said "a scientist deletes 85% of the universe." The figure that holds up is that dark matter is about 85% of the matter and roughly a quarter of the universe's total energy budget. The corrected line loses nothing and passes the first test a knowledgeable viewer will apply.

The hook used throughout: "A scientist deletes 85% of the matter in the universe and the math still works."

Three visual registers

The Atacama frame

Painterly night-blue, long lenses, a control room lit by monitors. Elara lives here.

The explainer

Luminous diagrams on black, gold linework, one idea per shot.

The myth

Ink wash and violet geometry, slower cuts, no text on screen except the operator names.

Cold open · 0:00–1:30 · The Crack in the Lens

  • 1.1 Black. A single sound: wind. Slow push over the Atacama at night, the dish arrays small against a vast sky. Super: Atacama Desert, Chile. 3:47 AM.
  • 1.2 Interior control room, wide. One woman, Elara, alone, coffee gone cold. Monitors wash her face blue. Insert: a clock, 3:47.
  • 1.3 Close on the screen: a gravitational lensing plot, arcs of distant quasars bent around a galaxy. One line of the equation glows gold: the dark matter term.
  • 1.4 Elara's hand hovers over the keyboard. She hesitates. Holds.
  • 1.5 Extreme close: the delete key. Press.
  • 1.6 The gold term dissolves. The rest of the equation stays. The arcs on screen do not change.
  • 1.7 Her face. She does not breathe.

NARRATOR (V.O.): "3:47 in the morning. The Atacama desert. A woman has been staring at the same numbers for eleven hours. The data is clean. The calibrations are perfect. And it makes no sense."

ELARA (quiet, to the empty room): "Twenty-five years I've added eighty-five percent invisible mass to this equation. I've never seen it. Nobody has."

(She deletes the term. The math still works.)

ELARA: "What if the math is right... and the geometry is wrong?"

STORY · dramatised from The Living Egg.

SMASH CUT to the sting.

Sting and title · 1:30–2:00

  • S.1 Pure black. A mouth in extreme close-up, no context. Lips part.
  • S.2 A hum. The 60 Hz tone from the score, now a voice. The screen's edge ripples with it.
  • S.3 Title card on the last of the sound: EROS. Four seconds. Under it, smaller: INWARD IS FORWARDS.

Act 1 · 2:00–5:00 · The Lid

  • 2.1 Black void, one gold line draws a telescope's light path to a lens.
  • 2.2 Split screen: a real sky photograph on the left, the same photograph on the right with the horizon line highlighted and pulsing.
  • 2.3 Diagram: a ratio, drawn as two numbers on a seesaw. Label: PARALLAX. It cycles through REDSHIFT, LENSING ARC. Every label is the same shape: a ratio.
  • 2.4 The sky as a lid. Camera pulls back from a standing figure to reveal she is on the inside curve of a bowl; the sky is the underside of a gold shell. The geometry flips smoothly.
  • 2.5 Sunrise on the inside of the shell. Light loops, orange and swollen. The figure squints and smiles.
  • 2.6 A board game, top-down, the board's edge in warm light. Pieces move. Then the same game on a board with no edges, the pieces drifting off. Silence.

NARRATOR: "Let's get one thing out of the way. Your telescope is not lying. Light arrives with the exact angles and wavelengths recorded. Nobody disputes that.

"What is in dispute is subtler. What does that light tell you about the shape of the space it travelled through? And here is the secret: nobody has ever measured shape directly. Every parallax, every redshift, every lensing arc is a measurement of a ratio. The ratio is real. The interpretation of the ratio is a choice."

OBSERVED (the ratios) · MODEL (the reading).

NARRATOR: "So try this. Read the sky not as a far wall but as a lid. Read the ground under your feet not as a floor but as the skin of a curved bowl you are standing inside. That horizon, always slightly too near, always slightly too curved? That is exactly what a horizon would look like from inside a finite shell.

"Does the sunrise still land? It does. The moon still rises swollen and orange. All of it still works. That is the point. This asks you to give up nothing you have seen. It asks what all of it could also mean."

(Board 2.6)

"This is not a cage. Every game has a board, and the board is what makes play possible. The outward picture taught us that the board has no edges, and so no meaning. The Egg gives the edges back. Small means you cannot reach the edges. Inside means the edges are what hold you."

MODEL · Axiom E1: Enclosure.

Act 2 · 5:00–7:30 · Zero Apples

  • 3.1 A table. One apple. The narrator's hand lifts it away. Zero apples.
  • 3.2 The table, the room, the walls dissolve in slow motion. Now zero everything.
  • 3.3 But a thin gold rectangle stays: the frame of the picture itself. Camera finds it, taps it. Label: the container you smuggled in.
  • 3.4 Two doors on a black stage. Left door: CREATED FROM NOTHING. Right door: ETERNAL. Both swing open onto the same blank. The narrator shrugs.
  • 3.5 Elara's monitors, now showing a single gold line drawing itself outward: structure first.

NARRATOR: "Picture zero apples. Easy. Now picture zero everything. No space. No time. No field. No potential. Try it honestly. The moment you picture it, you have smuggled in a container to hold the picture. And the container cannot be zero.

"That is not a trick. It is the floor. Absolute nothing cannot obtain. Something is always already structured. Every creation story that begins from a pure void asks the void to do work, and the void cannot pay.

"And the other story, 'it was always here'? Always existed is just another way of saying no reason. Two impossible stories, both unfalsifiable. Neither is a measurement. Both are commitments dressed as cosmology.

"The third option is to stop asking what came before the structure, and ask what the structure is doing."

MODEL · Axiom N1: Bedrock.

Act 3 · 7:30–10:00 · The Count, the Weight, the Funnel

  • 4.1 A clock face. Its hands unscrew and fall away. What remains: tick marks, a counter ticking up. The counter becomes a heartbeat, a calendar page flipping, a tree ring, a staking lock counting down.
  • 4.2 Process words appear and burn into gold: BEGIN. CONTINUE. COMPLETE.
  • 4.3 Two balloons, side by side on black, both inflating at the same steady rate. When they touch the bigger one nudges the smaller. Arrows: weight is what this nudge feels like.
  • 4.4 A figure standing on a ground that rises to meet her feet, the ground drawn as a soft expanding arc. Caption: The ground is rising as much as you are falling.
  • 4.5 A flat timeline, past to future. The camera lifts it off the page and it bends into a funnel, a whirlwind seen from above. Different heights glow gold.
  • 4.6 The figure standing at one height inside the whirlwind, looking up and down the funnel.

NARRATOR: "Time. We were taught it is a fabric that mass can bend. Try the simpler reading: time is a count. One moment, then the next. One iteration, then another. Look at the words we use for anything that takes time. Begin. Continue. Complete. Every process word is a bounded count of iterations. A calendar is iterations counted. A heartbeat is iterations counted. Where nothing iterates, nothing passes.

"Weight. In one lineage called Expansion Theory, every atom grows at the same shared rate. Two bodies meet, and the larger one accelerates the smaller. Weight is the inertia you feel resisting that. The ground is rising as much as you are falling. No invisible rope across the void. Just two expansions, meeting.

"And now the strangest picture in the book. A whirlwind does not have a current moment. The base is not its past. The top is not its future. The whole structure exists at once. What if time is shaped like that? What if we are not moving through time, but standing at a height within it?"

MODEL · Axiom T1: Iteration · Expansion Theory is a minority lineage · the funnel is HYPOTHESIS.

Act 4 · 10:00–13:30 · The Four (Myth)

Register shift: ink wash and violet geometry. Strings in. STORY held in lower corner.

  • 5.1 Black that has not yet decided what black is. Violet lines unfurl without touching, angles that are not yet space.
  • 5.2 NaUn: not a figure but an absence with a shape. A silhouette made of the gaps between lines.
  • 5.3 A first mirror, perfect. Then a hairline flaw. The flaw glints gold. A path opens through it.
  • 5.4 Ra-Shen: a sun drawn as a ring of radiating strokes, a stage lighting up beneath it. Outward energy meets a boundary and becomes an event.
  • 5.5 Thoth: hands, not a face. Letters fall like rain from a pair of hands, each one a mouth-shape. A child catches one and speaks.
  • 5.6 EROS: two walls and a spark between them. Mem, Yod, Mem. The spark holds the walls apart and together. Water beads on the glass.
  • 5.7 Four glyphs arranged as one shape. Not a pantheon: a grid.
  • 5.8 NaUn turning, walking away through a door built of light, not looking back. The door stays open.

NARRATOR: "Every culture told this part as a story. Here it is as a grammar.

"Before the Sun had a name there was black that had not yet decided what black was. Violet geometry unfurling in the void. Silence before tone. Then NaUn.

"NaUn did not push a single star. NaUn established the conditions under which a star could burn. The first act of creation was not making a thing. It was making a world in which things could be made.

"In the first mirror, a flaw. Not a mistake to erase. The flaw is the feature that lets learning begin. A perfect mirror shows only itself. An imperfect one opens a path.

"Then Ra-Shen, the sun that makes the stage. Outward energy, under boundary. Without it, possibility never becomes an event.

"Then Thoth, the teacher and the builder. Thoth does not hand down finished words. Thoth lends letters, and leaves the words to the made. The gift is the code. The stories are yours.

"And the fourth: EROS. The bond. Not a god you petition. The reason a lesson survives its first speaker. In Hebrew, the word for water is Mem, Yod, Mem. Two walls around a spark. Bond is not fusion. Bond is what holds two things in relation without collapsing them into one.

"Four operators. No fifth. Not a pantheon. A grammar. Egyptian and Greek names are masks the operators wore. The function is what the masks were pointing at.

"And here is the line that makes the whole mythology turn."

NaUn (V.O., low, unhurried): "I will withdraw my face and see what they become."

NARRATOR: "Withdrawal is not absence. It is the final test of the architecture. If the system only runs while the Architect watches, it is unfinished. If it runs when the face is hidden, the rules were real."

(Board 5.8. The door stays open.)

ON-SCREEN, brief, after the sequence: the Hebrew letters and the sun, the speed of light and E = mc². Narrator, lightly: "The book notes that the sun's name, its fuel, its speed and its energy equation share four characters. Design or coincidence? The book says that is not its claim. Watch the pattern. Make your own call."

STORY · the number pattern is PATTERN, not proof.

Act 5 · 13:30–15:30 · Who Lives Here

  • 6.1 1950. A lunch table, a napkin, a man in shirtsleeves leaning in. Super: Enrico Fermi. Over lunch. Hand on napkin: Where is everybody?
  • 6.2 The same question redrawn on the shell: two dots, "here" and "there," labelled as layers of one body, folding together.
  • 6.3 Camera descends into the shell's depth, a cavity, an abdomen seen through a hand lens.
  • 6.4 Aurora over a mountain range, then rock art of serpents, wheels and ladders. A dissolve between them: the shapes match.
  • 6.5 A white blood cell near a wound, then a drifting luminous plasma form near a mountain, cut in rhythm.
  • 6.6 A cell, looking up, unable to see the body it lives in.

NARRATOR: "1950. A lunch in New Mexico. Enrico Fermi asks the question that has haunted astronomers ever since: where is everybody?

"Inside a finite shell, 'everywhere' stops meaning far away. 'Here' and 'there' are layers of the same body. The paradox does not get answered. It dissolves. What is left is not silence. It is depth. Looking across it with a radio telescope is like looking across your own abdomen with a hand lens.

"And space may not be empty. It conducts. Ancient peoples drew the aurora as serpents, wheels and ladders. What if some of the traffic in the sky is not visitors? What if it is physiology? Repair. Regulation. Immune response. A body does not have to be understood by its cells. It only has to keep them alive."

HYPOTHESIS · Electric Universe and plasma cosmology traditions · labelled, not settled physics.

Act 6 · 15:30–17:50 · Why the Map Faces Outward & the Strongest Objection

Revised so the historical curvature models, post-1945 funding dynamics, and the four independent dark-matter evidence lines are stated accurately.

  • 7.1 Timeline across the screen: 1917 Einstein's closed finite model. Modern CMB curvature gauges reading near flat, 0.00% within margin. Then 1945+ state/defense funding lines flowing from ministries to satellite/guidance labs.
  • 7.2 Split diagram: an outward-facing sphere vs. an inward-facing shell fitting the exact same ratio measurements.
  • 7.3 A card appears: THE STRONGEST OBJECTION. Text: "Dark matter is required by the data."
  • 7.4 Four panels fill the screen one after another: (1) a galaxy's spinning rim, (2) a gravitational lensing ring, (3) the speckled cosmic microwave background, (4) two colliding galaxy clusters with separated mass.
  • 7.5 The four panels converge on one gold line: the missing mass. Two columns follow: what the model concedes vs. what would break it.

NARRATOR: "Fair question. If this reading is so tidy, why isn't it the map? Here is the part that surprises people. The question of shape was asked. In 1917, Einstein himself proposed a finite universe: closed, no edge, space curving back on itself. Physicists have been measuring its curvature ever since. The latest measurements say it is very close to flat, consistent with zero to a fraction of a percent. That is a real result, and the model has to live with it.

"So the book asks a stranger question. Not whether space is finite. Which way it faces. An outward map and an inward map can both fit the same ratios. Only one of them was ever built into the instruments.

"Why did nobody build the other one? After 1945, governments became the main funders of physics, and the first customers for cosmology's mathematics were missile guidance, satellite tracking and navigation. The book's claim is that a map built for those customers never had a reason to try the inside-out version. That is a hypothesis about incentives, not a proven history, and it is labelled as one.

"Now the strongest objection. The objection is not that dark matter is a convenient patch. It is that four different kinds of evidence point the same way: galaxy rotation curves, gravitational lensing, the cosmic microwave background, and colliding galaxy clusters. A different geometry has to explain all four, or the idea does not survive.

"And here is what would break it. Persistent failure of any independent evidence for a second domain. Steady success of outside-view models that never need an interior. Or a decisive demonstration that light and matter behave in ways only the exterior map can hold. The book does not hide from that. It names what would break the model, and so can you."

OBSERVED (1917 model & curvature data) · HYPOTHESIS (funding incentives) · OBJECTION · FALSIFIER.

Act 7 · 17:50–19:30 · The End of the Map

  • 8.1 A montage of old maps being folded and a new one unrolling. No faces.
  • 8.2 A suburban kitchen at dawn. Someone says a word aloud: "begin." Close on the mouth. The word breaks into its sounds, each a small gold glyph.
  • 8.3 Three small cards: 5 MIN, THE MORNING DECODE. 2 MIN, THE MIDDAY CHECK. 3 MIN, THE EVENING NOTE.
  • 8.4 Atacama, dawn. Elara in the doorway of the control room, the sky going from violet to gold.
  • 8.5 Her screen: she names a new file, geometry, and saves it.

NARRATOR: "This is not the end of the world. It is the end of the map. Every so often a civilisation changes its picture of what is real. It happens three or four times in recorded history. The people who live through it call it chaos. The people who come after call it normal.

"You do not have to believe a word of what you have seen. The book offers three small practices instead. In the morning, say one word aloud and notice what your mouth actually did. At midday, check one belief against what you can actually test. In the evening, write one line about what iterated today. Ten minutes in all. No ritual. No leader.

"Because a model is only worth what it lets you do. The question is never whether the sky is a lid. The question is whether a new reading helps you see something the old one could not."

ELARA (V.O., at the screen): "Inward is forwards."

Tag · 19:30–20:00 · Same Law, Another Scale

  • 9.1 The Egg, spinning slowly. A thread of gold light peels from it and becomes a network of pools on a dark map.
  • 9.2 End card: Corpus · NotebookLM public studio · Telegram t.me/Eros_Revival · Next: THE FOUR.

NARRATOR: "In the Egg, this law is called affinity. In a community it is called cohesion. On a chain it is called a bond. If you want to see the receipts, the next stop is Episode Five."

Check It Yourself challenge. Draw nothing on a page. What was holding the drawing?

Production notes for Show 01

Count the words

The narration runs close to the 2,300 budget. If your edit runs long, cut the Fermi lunch (Act 5) before cutting the objection (Act 6). The objection is what makes the show trustworthy.

Casting

Elara is the only recurring human. One voice actress, or a stylised animated character with no photoreal face. She never speaks to camera.

Chips as design

Chips are a design element, not subtitles. Gold outline, small caps, bottom-left. They appear for three seconds on first use and stay faint for the rest of the scene.

Reuse

The mouth sting, the gold container frame, and the violet myth style become the visual grammar for the whole Cosmology Cycle.

Cutdowns

Act 1 as a 3-minute short ("The Lid"), Act 2 as a 90-second short ("Zero Apples"), Act 4 as a 4-minute short ("The Four"). These feed the top/middle/bottom cinema slots every book carries.

Before there was life, there was the architecture in which life could learn. And before the first mind looked upon the universe, the universe already contained the instructions for being looked upon."

I · NaUn, the Architect · 2:00–5:00

NARRATOR: "NaUn did not push a single star. NaUn established the conditions under which a star could burn. The first act of creation was not making a thing. It was making a world in which things could be made.

"Consider two creators. One stays at the centre of every room, adjusting every stone. The creation thrives only while the hand is present. The other builds a structure that remembers: load paths, joints, thresholds. When that architect walks away, the building still stands. The second is greater. Not because the ego is smaller. Because the work is finished.

"In the first mirror, there was a flaw. It was not a mistake to erase. It was the feature that would let learning begin. A perfect mirror shows only itself. An imperfect mirror opens a path."
