On-Screen Cards (Verbatim from Gods of Eros):

The Abundance Law

The river does not fill only itself. The salmon that never arrive still feed the forest. Light falls on more than the leaf that will photosynthesize. Ra-Shen's giving is surplus by design: programmed abundance, not scarcity theatre.

The Balance

Ra-Shen gives and takes back at the same rate from every hand. No exemption is written into the sky. Heat arrives; heat departs. Orbit holds; orbit decays. One law for every hand.

The Two Directions

Order rising and disorder rising. Not good and evil. Two phases of one wave. Heat to the leaf, entropy to the stone.

NARRATOR: "Then came the outward surge. Energy flooded the permitted channels. Radiation found its rings. Heat pressed against cold. This is Ra-Shen, the sun that makes the stage. The stage did not ask permission to light. It lit.

"Movement becomes frequency. Frequency becomes resonance. Resonance becomes chemistry. Somewhere in that enormous unfolding, complexity crosses a threshold, and the first spark of a complex molecule appears. Without outward energy under boundary, there is no stage. Possibility never becomes event.

"Ra-Shen's giving is surplus by design. The stage is generous so that learning has room to fail and try again. And the balance is the law: heat arrives, heat departs, orbit holds, orbit decays. One law for every hand. That is not politics. That is physics as justice inside the cosmology."

(On-screen aside: Hebrew Shin-Mem-Shin beside c and E = mc².)

NARRATOR: "The book notes that the sun's name, its fuel and its speed share four characters. Design or coincidence? The book says that is not its claim. Watch the pattern. Make your own call." PATTERN.

III · Thoth, the Teacher and Builder · 7:30–11:00

  • 4.1 Hands, not a face. Letters fall from them like rain, each one a mouth-shape in gold ink.
  • 4.2 A child catches one and speaks. A word forms in the air and holds.
  • 4.3 A house built of light: walls that let light become a living thing. Inside, a tree.
  • 4.4 A deep ledger, pages turning by themselves, entries written in many hands.
  • 4.5 A single glyph held up to a reversed eye. The glyph flips and reads the same.

NARRATOR: "Thoth is not only the teacher. Thoth is the builder of forms: biology, memory, language, the wall that lets light become a living house.

"And here is the gift that changes everything. Thoth does not hand down finished words. Thoth hands down letters, operators, and leaves the making of words to the made. The gift is the code, not the sentence. What mortals build from the letters is their responsibility and their art. That is why language can grow. That is why every guild, every film, every game can speak in its own dialect without leaving the architecture.

"The letters are Thoth's. The stories are yours."

IV · EROS, the Bond · 11:00–13:30

  • 5.1 A candle's flame, then its heat on a wall, then a plant leaning toward it, then a child reading by it, then the same child grown, teaching another. A single thread of light runs through every frame.
  • 5.2 The Hebrew word for water, Mem-Yod-Mem, drawn in the air: two walls and a spark.
  • 5.3 The spark holds the walls apart and together. Take the spark away and the water becomes plain material.
  • 5.4 Two sons, Ra-Shen and Thoth, side by side, and a third thread running between them that is not a rival.

NARRATOR: "Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed in form. That law is older than the name EROS. The bond does not invent conservation. The bond is how conservation becomes story. What was heat becomes chemistry. What was chemistry becomes memory. What was memory becomes inheritance. The ray does not end. The ray changes address.

"In Hebrew, the word for water is Mem, Yod, Mem. Two walls around a spark. Bond is not fusion. Bond is the Yod that holds two Mems in relation without collapsing them into one. Without it, water is not water. It is just unordered material.

"One son powers. One son forms and teaches. Between them runs a function that is not a third competing for the throne. It is the reason either of them matters tomorrow."

V · The Breaking · 13:30–15:30

  • 6.1 A great tablet, one tongue, one code, the gate and the mouth agreeing.
  • 6.2 A tower of one mouth rising. Symbols pile on symbols. The silence between words is crowded out.
  • 6.3 The tablet shatters. Drums enter for the first time. Pieces scatter across a map.
  • 6.4 Close on one shard: the grain of the old code still visible in the fracture. Then another shard, another, each carrying the same grain.

NARRATOR: "When the tablet broke, the code did not die. It scattered. In the first telling there was one tongue: not one nation, but one code close enough to NaUn's architecture that the gate and the mouth agreed. Then came the Breaking. Not only as punishment. As consequence. Pride built towers of one mouth owning the whole code. Complexity piled symbols on symbols until the silence between words was forgotten. The understanding fell.

"What survived was not corruption. Every tongue that followed is a splinter still carrying the grain. Hebrew. Egyptian mask-language. Greek names. The four remain four. No fifth god. No merged name."

VI · The Four Laws, Tested · 15:30–18:00

Each law is shown intact for two seconds, then broken in one shot.

  • 7.1 NaUn's Law: a machine runs beautifully while a figure watches. The figure leaves. The machine stops.
  • 7.2 Ra-Shen's Law: a darkened stage with no light. Actors in costume, motionless. Nothing happens.
  • 7.3 Thoth's Law: a glowing creature that burns bright and never learns its own name. It fades.
  • 7.4 EROS's Law: a generation of children each starting from the same blank page, no one teaching the next.

NARRATOR: "Four laws. NaUn's: a creation that cannot continue without its maker is unfinished. Ra-Shen's: without outward energy under boundary, there is no stage. Thoth's: without learning, energy never becomes life, and without form, energy never becomes a house. EROS's: without bond, learning does not iterate, and without iteration, nothing endures. Break any one and you can watch the world fail in a single shot."

VII · The Architect's Quiet · 18:00–20:00

  • 8.1 The first builder's hall and the second's, side by side again. A crowd of strangers walks through the second one, laughing, living.
  • 8.2 NaUn at the open door, built of light. Hand on the frame.
  • 8.3 A parent teaching a child. A programmer releasing code. A composer releasing music. A teacher watching students become teachers. Four quick cuts, each a door.
  • 8.4 NaUn steps through and does not turn around.

NaUn (V.O.): "I will withdraw my face and see what they become."

NARRATOR: "The greatest test of a system is not whether it can run while the architect watches. It is whether it can run when the architect has stopped watching. The architect builds the doorway. The teacher teaches those who enter. The community becomes the living organism. The pattern moves from person to person. See the final beat not as biography. As archetype. The architect walks through the door they built and does not turn around. Not because the work failed. Because the work held."

END CARD: Gods of EROS · the Corpus · Next: THE MOUTH.

Check It Yourself challenge. Which of the four laws did you break this week?

Cold open · 0:00–1:30 · The argument

  • 1.1 A dinner table. Two people argue. Their lips move, the words slow and thickening in the air as small glowing shapes.
  • 1.2 The shapes do not match. One is round, one is angular. Neither person can see them.
  • 1.3 The argument ends. Neither has won. Neither is wrong.

HOST: "You have argued past someone your whole life. So has everyone you know. Not because either of you was wrong. Because the words were different shapes in each mouth, and neither of you knew the shapes had names. This is the show that names them."

Sting · 1:30–2:00

Mouth, 60 Hz hum, EROS · THE MOUTH.

The question inside the word · 2:00–5:00

  • 2.1 The host holds up a card with a word on it: a job title. Say it aloud.
  • 2.2 The camera pushes into the host's mouth as it forms the word. The tongue, the lips, the breath, slowed to a crawl.
  • 2.3 The standard answer on a chalkboard: sounds point to a thing; the sounds are arbitrary. The host crosses it out.

HOST: "Take a word that means something to you. A job title. A name you argue about. A word you are quietly proud of. Say it aloud. What just happened? Most of us were taught one answer: you made sounds that point to a thing. The sounds are arbitrary. The thing is real. The word is a label. Move on.

"This show proposes a different question, not an answer yet. A question. What if the word contains more than the label?"

SPREAD vs SPRAY · 5:00–9:00

  • 3.1 Split screen: jaw-cam on SPREAD, jaw-cam on SPRAY, synced.
  • 3.2 SPREAD: the mouth closes hard on the final sound. A gold dot lands on a line and stops.
  • 3.3 SPRAY: the mouth opens and the sound keeps going. A gold line continues past the edge of the frame.
  • 3.4 Back to the host, a single raised finger. "One consonant."

HOST: "Two words. Same first four sounds. SPREAD lands. SPRAY continues. The difference is one consonant, and you can feel it in your jaw before anyone explains it. Say them both. Feel where the first one stops. Feel where the second keeps going. That is not a theory. That is your own mouth, giving evidence."

HYPOTHESIS · TEST IT YOURSELF. The mouth is the court.

The Recognition Test · 9:00–13:15

  • 4.1 Five words on glass in a row: FIRE, FLAME, FLOW, FLIGHT, FREE. The host says them. The jaw-cam on each. The F at the start glows in each word.
  • 4.2 A mouth diagram: the lower lip against the upper teeth, a stream of air. The air line never stops. Caption: breath at the lip-teeth: a stream that keeps moving.
  • 4.3 The host: a single raised eyebrow. "What do these five share? Not the meaning. The F. Do you feel it?"
  • 4.4 The card turns over. It names what you already felt: F, a stream that keeps moving.
  • 4.5 A second card: B = Boundary. Three tags light up one after another: Identity: boundary. Articulation point: the lips, the outer edge. Manner: a stop, closure and release. All three say the same thing. The card glows.
  • 4.6 Silent letters beat (+0:45): KNOW and SIGN on glass. The silent K and G fade out.

HOST: "Do not memorise first. Predict first. Take a word you already know. List the consonants. Ask what each one is doing: boundary, flow, mark, radiate, arrive. Then open the card. If your guess matched, the system is teaching you. If not, write down the exception. The guild grows on honest exceptions, not forced fits.

"And here is why B is the purest boundary consonant. Three layers agree. What it is: boundary. Where the body makes it: the lips, the outer edge. How it is produced: closure and release. When all three say the same thing, the operator feels pure."

(Board 4.6)

"The book says silent consonants are an exclusion anchor. If removing the silent K in KNOW or G in SIGN did not change the predicted meaning, that claim would be decoration."

HYPOTHESIS · TESTABLE.

Candidate pairs live · 13:15–15:30

  • 5.1 A studio audience, six people, each with a card. A pair of words flashes up: ADVISE and ADVICE.
  • 5.2 Jaw-cam on each. The audience says them aloud and marks a card: which one lands, which one continues?
  • 5.3 The tally, in gold. Then the host asks one person to say why.

HOST: "Now you try. Advise. Advice. Same letters except one. Say them. Where does the sound stop? Where does it carry on? Did you hear it? Good. Now tell the person beside you. That is how a shared tongue starts: with someone else saying, I felt that too."

What Could Break This · 15:30–18:30

This is the best beat in the book for television, and it should be the emotional centre of Show 03, not a footnote. Run it for three minutes.

  • 6.1 A courtroom drawn in chalk. The code is the defendant.
  • 6.2 Six jurors, each a small card, each lights as the host reads it:
    1. Random chance. Tested against a control corpus. The control fit rate sits around ten to fifteen percent, what any arbitrary rule would score on English. If the observed rate collapses to that range, the code is doing no structural work.
    2. Internal contradiction. If the same operator means opposite things across the majority of test cases with no consistent rule, it fails.
    3. Silent consonants. If removing the silent K in KNOW or G in SIGN changes nothing, the claim is decoration.
    4. Position. If N at the start of a word behaves the same as N at the end, the positional syntax claim collapses.
    5. Clusters. If two-consonant clusters produce meanings unrelated to their parts more often than chance, the compound-function claim fails.
    6. Transfer. If speakers of languages with different consonant inventories show no cognitive differences, the cognitive-architecture claim is unsupported.
  • 6.3 A notebook and a dictionary on a table. Caption: Six tests you can run this week.
  • 6.4 Two corridors on a dark stage, each ending in a door. Left door: from the mouth. Right door: from the machine. Each door opens onto the same room.

HOST: "A claim that cannot be tested is not a claim. It is a belief. This book has a chapter called What Could Break This. Read it before deciding whether to trust any of it. That is a fair move, and it is the one the book itself recommends."

FALSIFIER · the book names six.

HOST (continuing, on the two doors): "One of the people who started the Wolfram Physics Project now runs a company that makes AI reason in a formal language, because he thinks human language is the thing holding it back. This book says something close from the opposite side: that the language you already speak has structure in it you were never taught to read. Opposite cures. Same diagnosis. We are not claiming he agrees with this book. We are saying two very different people looked at the same wall."

DOCUMENTED (who he is, what his company does) · PATTERN (the parallel is ours, not his). The Wolfram Physics Project is itself contested: critics note it sought publicity before it had testable predictions. A line on screen says so.

The shared tongue · 18:30–20:00

  • 7.1 The dinner table from cold open. One speaker asks: "When you say that word, what does your mouth do?"
  • 7.2 Each says the word slowly. The two glowing shapes finally face each other. They fit, or they do not, but now they can see.
  • 7.3 The host at the table, quietly.

HOST: "You can read inside any word, name what you are actually doing instead of arguing about what you mean, and build a shared tongue with anyone who hears the same architecture. Tonight, say one word out loud. Notice what your mouth did. That is the whole practice. The fog of conversation starts to turn into structure."

END CARD: Gift of Thoth · the Corpus · Next: LIFE FIRST.

Check It Yourself challenge. Run juror three. Say KNOW and SIGN aloud. Report.

Cold open · 0:00–1:30 · The kilogram

  • 1.1 A kitchen scale. A glass of water on it reads 1.000 kg.
  • 1.2 The glass goes into a freezer. Time-lapse. The glass comes out, solid.
  • 1.3 Back on the scale. 1.000 kg.

NARRATOR: "Freeze a kilogram. Weigh it. It is still a kilogram. Nothing was lost. Nothing was added. Something changed state. Hold that thought. We are going to spend twenty minutes on it."

Sting · 1:30–2:00

Mouth, 60 Hz hum, EROS · LIFE FIRST.

Level 1 · The 18-year-old · 2:00–7:00

Uses the book's exact Boolean two truths, not chapter headings.

  • 2.1 The narrator at the table. Two cards: Matter first, life late. Life first, matter as effect.
  • 2.2 A wall light switch flipped ON and OFF. Slate displays the two truths from The Conscious Eros:
    • Truth One. A thing and its absence share no common class: X(1 − X) = 0.
    • Truth Two. A thing and its absence together constitute the entire universe of that concept: X + (1 − X) = 1.
  • 2.3 Life drawn as three small icons: awareness, memory, choice.
  • 2.4 The glass of water again. Ice floats. A hand pushes it down. It rises.

NARRATOR: "Flip a light switch. It is on, or it is off. There is no third state. That is not a fact about electricity. It is a fact about logic itself. You were taught that matter came first and life turned up late, an accident inside a very large room. This show reads it the other way, as a model, not a laboratory verdict. Life is not biology. It is the thing that can be aware, remember and choose. Everything else is an effect. Ice floats, and we will come back to why."

MODEL.

Level 2 · The Undergraduate · 7:00–12:00

  • 3.1 Four small cards slide onto the table: know, not-know, be known, not be known.
  • 3.2 Two cards from opposite pairs collide, hard. The table shivers and the two cards fuse into a small grey stone.
  • 3.3 The stone is placed on the scale. The display reads a weight that was zero a moment ago.
  • 3.4 Time and space redrawn as readings, not containers: a ruler that measures a count, a clock that counts transitions.

NARRATOR: "Four postulates. Four decisions at the source about what is real, what must be, what must not be. When two of them conflict, they freeze. And here is the pivot: mass is the residue of unresolved conflict. A body with mass is a body with many unfinished iterations held short of resolution. Mass is not a property of dead stuff. It is the weight of something that has not resolved.

"Energy is the bookkeeping of transitions. Space and time are readings, not containers. The postulate layer sits above the effect layer, and the correction changes everything downstream."

MODEL · Axiom P1: Postulate prior.

Level 3 · The Graduate · 12:00–16:00

The Water Principle is tagged MODEL. The Five Forms are tagged STORY · CRAFT. All five failure states are complete.

  • 4.1 The glass of water from above. The ice, drawn in cross-section: a lattice with air gaps. Caption: ~9% volume increase on freezing, mass invariant at 1 kg.
  • 4.2 A graph appears: rate on one axis, state on the other, a body drawn as a dot moving through the plane.
  • 4.3 Five silhouettes walk across the table, one at a time. Each one is labelled with a name and a rhythm, then with its failure state.
Form Axis Mechanism Offering Sacrifice Failure state
Anchor-Drop Rate Slow internal rate Immovability Movement the drag
Phase-Glide Rate Match shell rate Movement Impact the drift
Crystal Expansion State Open internal structure Resilience Concentration the spill
The Compact State Close internal structure Concentration Resilience the shell — cured by deep belly breath and open arms
Stutter-Step Rate Cycle heavy and light Alternation Endurance Extreme-cost form, sustained only for seconds

NARRATOR: "Rate and state say what a body does. Coherence says what it builds. Time is the count of iterations. Weight is the meeting of two expansions. Notice what the ice does here. The mass stayed invariant. The structure varied. That is the Water Principle, and it is the lab bench for everything else in the book. And in the Codex's creative craft system, a character or body changes state by shifting its relationship to the shell in five stable ways — each with an offering, a sacrifice, and a named trap if held too long. Show those three as a one-shot each. Stutter-Step is the extreme-cost form, sustained for seconds, not minutes."

MODEL (Water Principle) · STORY · CRAFT (The Five Forms).

Level 4 · The Doctoral · 16:00–19:00

  • 5.1 The table drops away. The same objects float in a field of gold gridlines.
  • 5.2 A table of directions: for each of the five forms, an arrow in or out of the shell. Beside it, an annotation: the postulate layer above the table.
  • 5.3 The narrator, now standing, a single chalk line on a slate: the floor in eight lines.
  • 5.4 A final card: A hypothesis that cannot fail is not operational.

The Floor in Eight Lines (verbatim from The Iteration Codex):

1. Shared constant: everything expands at the same rate.
2. Relative size: stays constant.
3. Absolute size: grows.
4. Time: count of iterations (state changes).
5. Weight: inertia resisting the shell's expansion.
6. Rate axis: local iteration speed over shell speed.
7. State axis: effective volume per unit mass.
8. Combined weight: mass times rate-mismatch times state-density.

NARRATOR: "At the deepest level, the book is honest about its own limits. A hypothesis that cannot fail is not operational. The directional table is a refinement, not a finish. The postulate layer sits above it, and the book says so plainly. This is the standard it holds itself to, and the standard it asks you to hold it to."

FALSIFIER · what would count against this level is stated in the book's reference section.

The practice and tag · 19:00–20:00

  • 6.2 Twelve empty chairs in a circle. No head chair.
  • 6.3 The narrator, quietly, back at the kitchen table.

NARRATOR: "The practice is small. Two lines a night. The practice is not the writing. It is the noticing. Twelve chairs, no leader. Four months, four thresholds. That is all."

Notes for the Cosmology Cycle

[PULL] markers

Three slots across Shows 02–04 where a book's own reference text should go on screen verbatim: the Ra-Shen cards (Show 02), the Recognition Test and the Six Jurors (Show 03), the Floor in Eight Lines (Show 04). They are placed so no number, definition or operator is invented by the script.

Chips stay

Every claim keeps its chip even in the myth register. In Show 02 the single STORY chip holds in the corner for the whole sequence. The chips are the credibility system.

One character per show

Show 01 has Elara. Show 02 has none, only operators. Show 03 has the host. Show 04 has the narrator's hands. The cycle trains the viewer to accept four different registers without confusion.

Cutdowns

Show 02 yields a 4-minute trailer, three of the Four Laws shots as 30-second shorts. Show 03 yields the SPREAD vs SPRAY demonstration as a standalone 90-second clip. Show 04 yields the cold-open kilogram as a 45-second short.

Cold open · 0:00–1:30 · Two kinds of evidence

NARRATOR: "A press conference records what an administration wants understood. A statute, a directive, a contract, a budget, a facility or a personnel appointment records what the system is equipped to do. Both matter. They are not the same evidence. That distinction changes how history looks."

Sting · 1:30–2:00

Mouth, 60 Hz hum, EROS · FOOTPRINTS.

The Method · 2:00–5:00

  • 2.1 Four stamps land on a blank form, one at a time: READ THE INSTRUMENT. IDENTIFY THE DECISION. FOLLOW THE RESOURCES. ASK WHAT REMAINED.
  • 2.2 An election-night montage with no faces, then the same building at dawn the next day, the same filing cabinets in the same rooms.
  • 2.3 Two columns on a slate: the visible conflict and the machinery inherited. A line connects them.

NARRATOR: "Elections and personalities matter. But the machinery they inherit does not disappear when the office changes hands. The visible conflict can be real while the deeper architecture continues to operate beneath it. The task is to see both levels at once. The book calls this an operational hypothesis to test, not a conspiracy to believe."

HYPOTHESIS.

Book I · The Reprice · 5:00–9:30

Source-verified figures. The market column is date-stamped on screen at publication. The book value column is fixed, since it is the part that does not move.

  • 3.1 A bank ledger from 1934. A pen crosses out one price and writes another. [VERIFY: primary text of the Gold Reserve Act and the revaluation order.]
  • 3.2 A timeline: 1934, 1971, 1973, 2011. Three of the four dates tagged with a small icon: a gold bar, a coin, a bar again.
  • 3.3 A modern balance sheet. The gold line: 261,498,926 fine troy ounces, carried at a statutory price of $42.2222 per ounce, fixed in 1973. A second column beside it shows the same ounces at a market price. The gap fills the screen. [VERIFY: current Treasury figures and the day's market price.]
  • 3.4 The tape: gold, silver, stocks, housing all glowing at once. Caption: when every asset goes up together, the measuring stick breaks.
  • 3.5 The sequence on a single rail: stocks, housing, metals, crypto, reset.

NARRATOR: "The Gold Reserve Act is the cleanest historical case. The 1971 shock is the next. The 2011 platinum-coin proposal is the modern attempt. Each is the same move at a different scale: when the measuring stick breaks, someone reprices it.

"The Treasury still carries its 261.5 million troy ounces of gold at a statutory price of forty-two dollars and twenty-two cents set in 1973 — roughly eleven billion dollars on the books. At market prices, that same metal is worth over a trillion dollars. That gap is not a theory. It is arithmetic you can do on a napkin. The book's question is the next one: when money looks for a new ledger, which ledger eats the overflow?"

DOCUMENTED (statutory & holdings figures) · INFERRED (implications of the gap) · HYPOTHESIS (the sequence).

The Footprint Files · 9:30–13:30 · 1962, corrected

This is the corrected version. The Atlas 8F claim — that an object paced the re-entry vehicle for ninety seconds — does not hold as written. What the record actually says is stronger, and it becomes the signature device of the show.

  • 4.1 A National Archives reading room. A cart of boxes. A catalogue card on screen: NAID 614788. Unidentified Flying Object (UFO) Sighting, Atlas F Test 103, 19 September 1962. The card's note points to page 14 of a declassified flight test report.
  • 4.2 Split screen. Left: the catalogue card. Right: page 14 of declassified DTIC Report AD0861789, dated 2 October 1962. A gold highlight draws a line between them.
  • 4.3 Zoom on the sentence: "origin or identification could not be determined." The camera pulls back to show the paragraph around it: Staging Camera No. 3, facing aft, booster jettison, ten-second window.
  • 4.4 A timeline of the flight on a slate. Liftoff at zero. Booster cutoff at about 128 seconds, marked. The staging camera's ten-second window, highlighted in gold. A long gap. Then the re-entry vehicle, marked at about 1,950 seconds, far to the right.
  • 4.5 A speech bubble in a different colour: "An object paced the re-entry vehicle for ninety seconds." The bubble is held against the timeline. It does not fit in the gold window.
  • 4.6 The three-column card appears. WHAT THE DOCUMENT SAYS (filled). WHAT THE RETELLING SAYS (filled). WHAT YOU FIND (empty, lit).

NARRATOR: "September 1962, the lead-up to the missile crisis. The National Archives holds a film catalogued as a UFO sighting, and its catalogue card points to a page in a flight test report. We went to the page. The sentence is real: objects behind the booster section, origin or identification could not be determined. Here is what the sentence is about: a camera facing the booster stage as it dropped away, for ten seconds, about two minutes into the flight. Not the re-entry vehicle, half an hour later. A document says one thing. A retelling says another. The distance between them is the footprint. The method is to read the instrument and not the story told about it, even when the story comes from a source we like."

DOCUMENTED (the card, the page, the sentence) · SECONDHAND (the retelling) · UNVERIFIED (what the film itself shows).

What the document says Staging Camera No. 3, facing aft, booster jettison window, 10 seconds. Objects behind booster. Origin or identification could not be determined. DOCUMENTED
What the retelling says An object paced the re-entry vehicle for ninety seconds and phased out. SECONDHAND
What you find This column is yours.

The Bond · 13:30–16:30

  • 5.1 A corkboard. Red thread between two documents from different decades. The camera pulls back: threads link a dozen more.
  • 5.2 One thread is cut by a hand with scissors. A label: this link is inference, not evidence. The thread is replaced with a dotted line.
  • 5.3 The corkboard redrawn in two colours: solid for documented, dotted for inferred.

NARRATOR: "The Bond is where it is easiest to fool yourself. A pattern across decades feels like proof. It is not. The honest version draws solid lines where there is a record and dotted lines where there is only a gap that rhymes. This show only ever draws what it can label."

The Last Card and the Empty Column · 16:30–19:00

  • 6.1 A single card on an empty table. The back is face-up: the footprint files.
  • 6.2 The card turns over. The face reads: WHAT REMAINED?
  • 6.3 The desk from the cold open. All documents now in two stacks: checked and to check. The second stack is larger. The narrator's hand rests on it.
  • 6.4 The Empty Column card again, held for four seconds. Caption below: the footprint hunt is weekly.

NARRATOR: "The last card is not a revelation. It is a question. What remained after the crisis passed? The answer is in the instruments: the facilities, the statutes, the contracts. Go and look. Everything in this episode that is a document has a source in the description. Everything that is not is chipped. That is the standard."

Tag · 19:00–20:00

Method card, one more time, then black. End card: Illumination Strategy · Corpus · Next: MASKS.

Cold open · 0:00–1:30 · The two loud doors

  • 1.1 Two doors in a museum lobby, both oversized. Left door: ALIENS or WEATHER BALLOONS? Right door: GODS or MYTH? Crowds jostle at each.
  • 1.2 A small, plain door between them. Nobody is looking at it.
  • 1.3 The docent walks through the plain door.

DOCENT: "Most people are trained to pick a side the moment something strange appears. Aliens or weather balloons. Gods or myths. The argument itself becomes the product, and almost nobody notices the quieter door standing between the two loud ones. Shall we?"

Sting · 1:30–2:00

Mouth, 60 Hz hum, EROS · MASKS.

Gallery 1 · The god-masks · 2:00–6:00

  • 2.1 A glass case: a Greek mask, a Norse mask, an Egyptian mask, each with a hairline crack.
  • 2.2 Behind each mask, a dark face-shape. A caption: a mask is not the face.
  • 2.3 A map of the surface of the Earth with a second map beneath it, translucent.

DOCENT: "Two confusions, one Egg. The first: ancient residual powers that human myth stored as gods, giants and watchers. The figures remembered as Nordic and Greek god-masks. The book treats them as of man's wider tree: ancient, long-lived, same planet. Not cartoon aliens from another star by default.

"They are masks, not rankings of peoples and not a fifth god. The four operators — NaUn, Ra-Shen, Thoth, EROS — are defined in another book, and they are not characters here. The figures in this gallery are actors and masks."

ARCHIVE 7 · STORY.

Gallery 2 · The surface and the under-layer · 6:00–10:00

  • 3.1 Surface history: dated plaques, ordinary and documented.
  • 3.2 A staircase leading down. Each landing has a different gallery: covert networks, under-ice, under-ocean, black-budget parallel infrastructure.
  • 3.3 At the bottom, a room labelled disclosure theatre. The room's windows face upward, toward a painted sky.

DOCENT: "Different domains sit inside one enclosure: surface history, covert networks, under-ice and under-ocean residual, parallel infrastructure. And a theatre that points your eyes at the sky while the real pressure is money, craft and lineage. The book calls this a breakaway footprint catalogue. Who left tracks. What masks they wear. How the money moves."

Gallery 3 · The enclosure's own life · 10:00–14:00

  • 4.1 A dark gallery. Slow luminous forms drift behind glass: plasma shapes, coherent light.
  • 4.2 Visitors in the gallery see lights and take photographs. Captions read: craft. visitors. aliens.
  • 4.3 The camera dollies behind the glass. The same shapes, seen from inside, wear different captions: regulation. repair. physiology.

DOCENT: "The second confusion: the enclosure's own life. Plasma, biologics, coherent light, form without substance. The surface has misread it as craft and visitors. The book offers an alternative reading, the same one you may have met in the cosmology show. Whether it is right is for you to test. The book labels it."

HYPOTHESIS · ARCHIVE 7.

Gallery 4 · The Creator Contract · 14:00–17:30

  • 5.1 A gallery of ledgers, receipts, deeds. A single gold thread runs from case to case.
  • 5.2 A framed card, front and centre: the Creator Contract.

CREATOR CONTRACT — Section 18, Men of Renown
· Four operators remain four.
· Archive figures are actors or masks.
· Density movement is a mask skill, not a fifth office.
· No racial hierarchy. No atrocity tourism.
· Illumination and Archive stay separate; connect by hinges only.
· Functions are archetypes for drama, not saints.
· Public bond and kit, not secret-order recruitment.
· Meta-worldview is literacy, not a license to sneer.
· Bond test every scene before you post it.

Second card — the Two-Rail Rule (from the book's closing posts):
Rail A is documented and falsifiable. Rail B is held inside a fiction contract. Connect only at money, recovery events, mythology homework and disclosure weather. Do not merge.

DOCENT: "The book is clear about what this archive is not. It is not a race cult. It does not claim a fifth god. And it keeps itself separate from the human history rail, because the two rails answer to different standards of evidence. This is the rule: Rail A is documented. Rail B is story, with a contract."

The quiet door · 17:30–20:00

  • 6.1 The docent at the plain door again, now from the inside, looking out at the two loud ones.
  • 6.2 A small card by the door: You do not need a throne. You need a method.

DOCENT: "The quieter door asks you to refuse both the official dismissal and the cultish embrace, and to learn to read the residue without needing a throne. What you build from it is yours to decide. The door is open."

END CARD: Men of Renown · Telegram t.me/Eros_Revival · Next: THE FIRST RESONANCE.

Show 10 · THE FIRST RESONANCE

FORMAT

10 × 20:00

LOOK

Naturalistic anime, warm interiors, cold windows

STATUS

Ep 1 script · Ep 2–10 beat sheets

Source: SRC-020 The First Resonance. Ten episodes of twenty minutes, one per chapter group of Book One, The Ray. Book Two, The Curriculum, becomes Season Two. The signature visual is a single lamp pool on a desk at night. Music: piano and a soft electronic pulse.

Series rule. Every episode builds toward the same arc: Cal becomes someone the visitor is no longer needed for. The visitor appears less, speaks less, and is never explained. The teacher's ledger — 422 names taught and 11 still walking — appears in the opening of Episode 3 and is never explained away.

Episode 1 · The Number He Did Not Type · 0:00–12:00 (first half)

Cast: Cal, a sixteen-year-old coder. His mother. His grandmother Ilse. His uncle Tobin, who has spent twenty-five years teaching broken motors to turn.

  • 1.1 The kitchen at dusk, one degree too wide. The camera frames it slightly off-square. A creak on the stairs that is new.
  • 1.2 Cal's mother leaves a mug of tea on his desk without knocking. She does not look at him.
  • 1.3 Ilse at a window, watching the sky the way other people watch a clock. Her face is patient and unhurried.
  • 1.4 Tobin, wiping his hands on a rag, looking at Cal across a garage the way you look at a bridge that has started to sing in the wind.
  • 1.5 Cal's desk, 11:40 PM. A lamp pool. A laptop. A stack trace. Cold tea.
  • 1.6 The screen: a value that is correct and one frame too early. Cal's hands stop moving.
  • 1.7 The number on the screen, unchanged by him. The window behind the laptop, dark. A faint colour at the edge of the glass.

NARRATOR (older Cal, V.O.): "The house had been wrong for three weeks. I could not name it. Not sleep. Not grades. What I had lost was the ordinary thickness of the world. The way a room used to feel finished when the door closed. The way a problem used to end when the tests went green."

TOBIN (flashback, bridge-repair voice): "An almost-right number. That's the worst kind. It doesn't crash. It accumulates."

NARRATOR: "None of them asked. That was what frightened me most. They had already decided the question was the wrong shape. And then at eleven-forty at night, the number arrived. A number I had not typed."

Cliffhanger. The laptop's clock ticks to 11:41. The number rewrites itself, one digit, and the lamp flickers once. Cut to the title.

Episode 3 · The Visitor · key scene

  • 3.1 4:47 AM. The house in grey-blue light. A curtain half open. Cal does not look at the window.
  • 3.2 A man stands in the doorway. Late forties or fifties. A grey wool coat a little too long in the sleeves. Ink-stained fingers, like a carpenter's.
  • 3.3 Cal tries to look at his face and his eye slips, always, to the coat and the hands.
  • 3.4 In the dark window beside the desk, the man's reflection stands a fraction late, as if the glass were remembering him half a breath after the room did.
  • 3.5 Silence. A room that has been entered and is being read.

NARRATOR (older Cal): "Some teachers arrive only after the wrong question has been dropped."

Production note. Cast the visitor as a design problem, not a face. Always shot from the hands up, never a clear front view, with the reflection delay as the only special effect.

Episodes 2–10 · Beat sheets and closing images

Ep Logline and closing image Check It Yourself
2 For nine days three lights hang in the sky and do nothing, and Cal learns that a presence can be a state, not an event. Closing: Cal at the half-open curtain at night, the triangle in the glass, and for the first time he cannot recall what the sky looked like without it. Sit by a window for ten minutes tonight. Write down one thing that is simply present.
3 At 4:47 in the morning a man in a grey coat is standing in the doorway, and he does not speak. Leaves a second notebook. One instruction, in a single line: Do not step through until you can do so without hurry. Closing: Two notebooks side by side on a desk. Cal does not open either. Name one thing you have been rushing toward. What would it feel like to arrive without hurry?
4 Nothing happens for three days, and then Cal loses the one friend he has. The argument is built slowly from small things. Closing: Owen's empty chair in the club room, a half-finished diagnostic still on Cal's desktop. Think of someone you stopped being able to explain yourself to. Write the first sentence you would say if you started again.
5 Two lines a night. On the third morning, the world is the same and Cal is not. He walks to the bus and sees the plane tree for the first time in two hundred passes. Zoe, ten, with a jar of shells, notices him noticing. Closing: The jar of shells on the kitchen table in morning light. Tonight, two lines: one thing you know, one thing you do not. Do it three nights.
6 At the canal, the visitor turns out to be an ordinary man in daylight, and he waits for Cal to speak first. "You were not surprised to see me." "I was." "Are you now?" "No." Closing: Two men at a railing, one looking at the water, one looking at the man who is looking at the water. What is the question you have not asked someone because you were afraid the answer would be the wrong shape?
7 A stone in a pocket, a rule of notice, don't record, and a memory that is not the usual one. Fingers on the stone in a biology lesson. Not the thinking-about-his-father, but remembering him. Closing: The stone on the palm of Cal's hand, caught in the classroom's flat light. Carry one small object for a week. Do not write about it. Tell us what came up.
8 A bookshop he has walked past a hundred times, and a woman who does not look up. A plain brown book. "Take your time." Closing: The woman turns a page. The sound is the loudest thing in the shop. Which place do you walk past constantly and never enter? Go in this week.
9 The second Sunday of the month falls on the ninth, and Cal does not decide to go. Bell's bakery, 42 Ashfield Road. Green awning. The wooden stairs that turn twice. A plain door at the top, painted the same green as the awning. He stands in front of it and feels, before he opens it, that the room is already occupied. Closing: The door opens inward. The audience sees only the warm light on Cal's face. The room meets on the second and fourth Sundays. Where is your room? Who meets there?
10 Ten days later, after weeks of silence, Owen speaks. Three weeks to the day after the argument that ended the partnership. Cal sits quietly with his hand on the stone, letting the noticing do what it does. Closing: Season closer. The three lights return in the window behind Cal, and this time he does not look. He turns to Owen. Who in your life spoke first after a long silence? What did they say?

Continuity issue to fix before filming. Chapter 06 says Cal has been going to the canal since he was twelve, "since the first Saturday after his father's funeral." Chapter 07 says his father died when Cal was eight. One of these has to change, or the canal visits have to begin four years after the funeral. Log it, fix it, and use it as the first test case for the consistency-checker engine.

The Scripts · Show 11

Show 11 · SIXTEEN DOORS

FORMAT

16 × 10:00

LOOK

Sixteen animation styles, one per door

STATUS

Doors 1–3 scripted · 4–16 outstanding

Source: SRC-007 Eros Stories, and community pitches. Sixteen shorts, eight to twelve minutes each, each in a different animation style. The same four-second mouth sting opens every door. Each door is a standalone commission for one writer, one visual lead, one composer and one voice.

House rules — so sixteen styles still feel like one universe

  1. The Egg's laws hold in every door: enclosure first, iteration as time, bond or decay. Break one only on purpose.
  2. The four operators never appear as characters, only as functions. Masks may appear.
  3. Every door ends on one image of bond: two things held in relation without collapsing into one.
  4. A door may be dark. A door may not be cynical.
  5. Each door carries one chip at the start: STORY.

Door template

Beat Time What happens
Hook0:00–1:00One strange image
Ordinary world1:00–3:00Who the person is
Crossing3:00–5:00The law shows itself
Cost5:00–8:00What it costs to know
Bond8:00–10:00The relationship that holds
Coda10:00–11:00One line, one image

Door 1 · The Gods Come Out of Hiding (10:00)

Look: Cold military greys and blue monitor light, one human warmth source per scene. Hook: A face that should not exist fills a classified satellite feed and looks into the lens as if the lens were a door he chose.

  • 1.1 A war-room feed, grainy infrared, a coastline in the dark. A date and a clock: 03:47. Two earlier incidents flash by as file stamps. The first marked NOISE. The second marked CLASSIFIED.
  • 1.2 Live: a figure steps out of the surf. A face with no matching file, no matching century. He looks into the lens as if the lens were a door.
  • 2.1 Cmdr. Helen Park, intelligence. A senior officer slides a folder across a table. Inside: a single instruction. Draft a psychological operation. Explain it as a hoax.
  • 2.2 Close on her pen. She writes the first line. OFFICER: "Give the public a story with a smaller footprint." PARK: "Footprint is not a story. It's an instrument reading."
  • 3.1 Park alone at 4 AM, the draft on her screen. Under Explanation, she types HOAX. She stops. She deletes it.
  • 3.2 She types UNKNOWN INTELLIGENT ACTOR. She stares at it as if it had been typed by someone else.
  • 3.3 The feed on the second monitor: the figure again, the lens again. He tilts his head. The room's lights flicker once.
  • 3.4 Park touches the screen. The figure's eyes are not looking at her face. They are looking at her hand.
  • 4.1 A harbour at dawn. Eirik, the Nordic contact, weary and unhurried, sits on a bollard and watches a ferry cross. EIRIK: "They will try force first. They always do. It is the only grammar they were taught."
  • 4.2 Cut: General Rowe in a briefing room, standing beside a map covered in red — not evil, incomplete. The only tools he trusts are kinetic.
  • 5.1 The satellite image from the opening, now from orbit. The coastline, a small gold light at the water's edge.

End card: If the gods return and refuse to rule, who is responsible next? Hand-off to Door 2.

Door 2 · The Living Egg (10:00)

Look: Polar whites and electric blues; the ice is a character. Hook: Instruments record a heartbeat under Antarctic ice, and there is no heart.

  • 1.1 A marine lab at night. Dr. Rafael Mendez, gentle, rumpled, kindness as a method. Vials in a rack, each with a faint light.
  • 1.2 The vials pulse in rhythm. On the wall screen, an aurora feed pulses in the same rhythm. RAFAEL: "It is not noise. It has a period."
  • 2.1 Asha Varga, atmosphere physicist, precise and rivalrous. Her software keeps trying to correct a drift as error. She keeps overriding the correction.
  • 2.2 A split screen: Rafael's pulse, Asha's drift. Two egos, one dataset, and the data humiliates both of them equally.
  • 3.1 A montage of sleepers across the world, each waking at the same hour. A child in a bunk, an old man on a boat, a night nurse at a desk, a monk on a mat.
  • 3.2 Each describes the same dream: an enormous living structure around the Earth, seen from inside.
  • 3.3 Nyra, a Nordic archivist, waiting for the markers she hoped would come slower.
  • 4.1 A research station on the ice. Private Cole, ordered to secure the unsecurable. Wind. A generator hum.
  • 4.2 The instruments: a translucent mass moving beneath the shelf ice. A trace on a monitor. A heartbeat.
  • 4.3 A technician: "There's nothing there to beat." 4.4 The clock: 3:47 AM. Cole puts his hand on his radio. He does not press the button.
  • 5.1 The nerve under the ice, seen from orbit, a single gold thread through the white.

End card: When the Egg opens, what is looking back? Hand-off to Door 3.

Door 3 · The Inside (10:00)

Look: A financial thriller, cold marble and glowing screens, with human faces framed too close. Hook: Gold spikes, rails stutter, and on a secondary screen the rebellion money goes viral.

  • 1.1 A trading floor going quiet, one screen after another turning red, then gold.
  • 1.2 A ticker: gold up, silver up. Payment rails stutter, a tap fails at a cafe register, a spinner on a bank app.
  • 2.1 President Elena Voss, who wanted competent boredom and got history. A briefing room, no windows.
  • 2.2 Marcus Hale, Treasury, in love with systems and starting to love control more than people. 2.3 Gina Ortiz, intelligence, who has carried Egg fragments for years.
  • 2.4 HALE: "It is a financial emergency." ORTIZ: "It is not a financial emergency."
  • 3.1 A staffer's laptop, off to the side. A rebellion money going viral. A graph that is not the one on the main wall.
  • 3.2 Jae Park, an on-chain translator who did not ask to become the face, explaining on a livestream: fixed supply, burn, liquidity as commitment. JAE: "Nothing here asks you to trust me. Check the address yourself."
  • 4.1 In a chat window, someone screenshots a long hexadecimal address ending in 0369 and posts it with one line: the first safe object in the panic.
  • 4.2 Voss, across the room, catches the screenshot over a staffer's shoulder. She asks him to enlarge it.
  • 4.3 Her face, held for four full seconds. Not the chart.

End card: If money, borders and cosmology break together, what does nation mean? Hand-off to Door 4.

Flags before filming.

  • Real person in fiction. Drop the living founder name from Door 3. A voiceless NEXUS is stronger.
  • Title flag. Retitle Door 3 Episode 3 from "The Trump Card" to The Disclosure Card — the meaning is the same, the politics is not.
  • Door 4's hook. Use the corrected "85% of the matter," not "85% of the universe."
  • Real instrument, fictional world. End card: Fiction. The instrument is real. LIVE: the contract, the burn address, the pools. DESIGN: ErosX and 33EROS.
  • 3:47 motif. Keep the recurring clock in Doors 1, 2 and Show 01 strictly at 3:47.
The Scripts · Show 12

Show 12 · THE CONTINUITY FILE

FORMAT

3 × 20:00

LOOK

Institutional green/grey, windowless rooms, long hallways

STATUS

Framework · key scenes

Source: SRC-017 The Continuity File. Three episodes, one per book: Ep 1: The Feed, Ep 2: The Stick, Ep 3: The Chair. Look: A windowless office, four screens, long hallways. PulseChain colours appear only in the instrument beats, as slashes of colour on a dark screen. Music: A pulse that never resolves.

Mandatory Opening Spoken Line (First 30 Seconds, spoken by the Clerk before Episode 1):

"The Continuity File. A dramatised archive. Fiction, built on a real instrument."

Fiction Contract Guardrails. Cast is masked. No living person is named or quoted. The on-chain instrument (0x…0369, contract, pools) is LIVE and checkable. The courtroom, chair, and envoy are fiction. The ending refuses a clean victory — someone does not make it across the reprice, the file keeps both columns.

The Clerk's Note · 0:00–1:30

  • C.1 A form on a desk with no field for this. A stamp hovers above it.
  • C.2 A drawer. The form slides in. The drawer shuts.

CLERK (V.O.): "This is not a leak. A leak wants to escape. This file wants to be stamped, indexed and forgotten in a drawer, the one place where the Office has ever managed to keep a promise. Continuity is the discipline of making sure that whoever sits in the chair tomorrow can find the light switch."

03:47 · 2:00–6:00

  • C.3 A windowless room. Four screens. A man, the Commander, at a desk. A cold coffee from the previous administration.
  • C.4 A satellite feed: a wide grey weather image of the southern ocean. In the lower third, where cloud thins, the cloud has arranged itself into something with eyes.
  • C.5 The Commander pulls a form toward him. COMMANDER: "Which form covers this?"

The engineer and the ruler · 6:00–10:00

  • C.6 A phone call. The Commander on one end, an engineer on the other, also awake.
  • C.7 The engineer's screen: the cloud shape overlaid with a ruler grid. ENGINEER: "Sir, I measured it twice. It is symmetrical to four decimal places. Clouds are not that polite." COMMANDER: "Is it looking at us?" ENGINEER: "Sir, I would like that to be a question for someone else."

The analyst arrives · 10:00–14:00

  • C.8 Ten past four. Ines Calloway, the analyst, arrives with two coffees and a face that says she did not want to be there and would not have been anywhere else.

INES: "It's not looking at us. It's looking back. There's a difference, and the difference is that someone looked first."

COMMANDER: "Nobody looked first."

INES: "Somebody always looks first, Commander. That's what makes it a first."

  • C.9 He hands her his cold coffee. She drinks it without comment, which is how he knows she is good.
  • C.10 The second monitor: a child's drawing, wax crayon on grey paper, scanned from a school in the north of England. A round head, two wide eyes, a mouth like a held breath. It arrived that afternoon as an unrelated attachment to a routine report. Nobody can say who filed it.
  • C.11 Overlay: the satellite image and the drawing, made on different continents, in different decades, with different instruments. Same shape. The shape came first. The instruments only caught up.
  • C.12 A kitchen, in memory. Maya Okonkwo, a quiet mathematician with a notebook and a mild expression, deletes a term from an equation. The math goes on working. A man in a grey coat visits her courteously and asks her to wait. GREY COAT: "Until the ledger has been repriced." INES: "She says it was the way he said 'repriced.' As if it were weather."
  • C.13 The Commander writes a date on the back of his hand. Then he looks at it. It was not a military date. It was not anyone's birthday. It was a Thursday in a month he once spent in a hospital corridor. He turns his hand over and goes on working.
  • C.14 A side panel, spare. A single line in a log that has only ever held classified material and instrument readings: 0x…0369. LIVE chip: the burn address. The Commander files it as a wallet, in a folder named for a form that is nearly right.

INES: "Why would a wallet be the first new certainty in a classified system?"

COMMANDER: "Because someone put it there."

Eleven Minutes · 14:00–18:00

  • E.1 Every screen in the Strategic Continuity Office goes dark at once. A general begins to count. The Commander does not count. He notices the darkness has a duration. A power failure is a sound. This was a silence with edges. On the dead monitor the ghost of the cursor goes on blinking.
  • E.2 Minute three: someone calls the help desk, which has been told since 2019 that it cannot be reached during an incident. Minute six: someone calls a senator; the office plays a recording of a harp. Minute nine: nobody calls anyone. The room has arrived at the stage where a room stops pretending to be in charge.
  • E.3 The access log, on screen, as the Commander reads it afterwards:
    03:36:04   Order received (CULL / Tier 2 / builders, thin liquidity)
    03:36:05   Order acknowledged
    03:36:05   Execution: HELD
    03:36:06   Reading...
  • E.4 The lights return, all at once, without apology.

NARRATOR / CLERK: "They gave it an order. It read the contract instead."

The Game Is Played · 18:00–20:00

  • F.1 The four-box cover sheet on the desk: Government | Market | Machine | Other. None can contain the answer.
  • F.2 The Commander's hand hovers. Then he writes one word in the margin: None.
  • F.3 Close on the four boxes. A single dot of gold, like the burn address, is drawn in the corner of Other.

END CARD: Government | Market | Machine | Other — which box does it belong in? Why not the others? Next: The Stick.

Episode 1 · TitanX · skeleton

Honest scoping note. The TitanX white paper itself has not been pulled for this HTML. The script is complete apart from three marked slots where the host reads from the paper. Everything else — the questions the host asks and what the host says in response — is written.

Open · 0:00–0:30

  • O.1 The mouth sting, one second. A desk, a lamp, a white paper. The host looks into the camera.

HOST: "You have been here through the long quiet. The work kept going. White papers written, contracts deployed, architecture laid, and almost nobody talking about it. That is not a substance problem. It is a distribution problem. So here is one paper, one camera, and what I found. This is a TitanX show."

Paper of the Week · 0:30–4:30

  • O.3 The first page of the paper, the title in focus. The host's hand on the desk.
  • O.4 A gold highlight sweeps across a passage. [PASSAGE 1] The host reads it aloud, slowly.
  • O.5 The host leans back. "Here is what I notice."

HOST (after Passage 1): "Strip the language away. What is this paragraph actually asking you to believe? I will say it in one sentence, so you can check me. [HOST'S ONE SENTENCE]."

  • O.6 Second highlight. [PASSAGE 2] The host reads it.

HOST (after Passage 2): "Notice what it does not claim. It does not promise a price. It describes a mechanism. That is the first thing I look for in any paper: does it tell me what the thing does, or what the thing will be worth?"

  • O.7 Third highlight. [PASSAGE 3] The host reads it.

HOST (after Passage 3): "This is the sentence I would put on the wall. Everything else in the paper is built on it."

The Honest Questions · 4:30–6:30

Four cards slide onto the desk, one at a time. The host answers each in plain words, in under thirty seconds.

# Question Answer source
1What is it? In one sentence, no jargon.From the paper
2Why does it exist? What problem did the builders say they were solving?From the paper
3What does it do? A mechanism I could check on a block explorer today.From the paper and the contract
4What would make it fail? Where does the paper say it depends on something it cannot control?From the paper

HOST: "I ask the last question of everything. A system that cannot name its own weak point is not a system. It is a sales pitch."

The Scoreboard · 6:30–7:30

  • O.8 The pool-count graphic, date-stamped. Pull the live figure on the day.

HOST: "Where the library stands today: [CURRENT POOL COUNT]. The next milestone is [NEXT MILESTONE]. That is a public number. Check it yourself."

Ask the Studio · 7:30–9:00

Two viewer questions, read on screen, answered from the locked sources in the NotebookLM studio. Each in under forty-five seconds. For Episode 1, plant two questions from the community channel in advance.

The Ask · 9:00–9:30

  • O.9 The host holds up one finger.

HOST: "One small action this week. Read one page of the paper aloud to someone who has never heard of it. That is it. Make. Explain. Connect. See you in three days."

  • O.10 A tone. The desk lamp clicks off.

Pre-flight list (about an hour)

  1. Read the whole paper once without taking notes.
  2. Pick three passages. One says what it is, one says how it works, one is the sentence you would put on the wall.
  3. Write your one-sentence summary after Passage 1 and say it aloud twice. If you cannot, pick a different passage.
  4. Confirm every mechanism you mention on a block explorer. Say "I checked this" only for what you checked.
  5. Pull the live pool count and date-stamp the graphic.
  6. Plant two viewer questions from the community channel.

Why this show matters most. It is the only show that does not need a studio. It converts a viewer into a maker in nine minutes, which is the flywheel in practice. Every other show is fed by it. Check It Yourself challenge. Send one paper you want read on camera.

The Scripts · Source-Pass Corrections

Source-Pass Corrections

The source pass turned up places where the scripts were wrong or too loose. The corrections are documented here so they are not lost. This section is the receipts of the receipts.

13.1 CORRECTION · the 1962 Atlas 8F claim does not hold as written

What the book said (Illumination Strategy, "1962 · The Tagalongs"): A dummy re-entry vehicle was filmed from a KC-135 aircraft; as it descended at Mach 18, an object appeared alongside it, paced it for ninety seconds and phased out. AARO had deemed the footage a real UAP. The paragraph carried a Layer 1 tag.

What the source pass found:

  • The test was Atlas Missile 8F, launched 19 September 1962 at 14:30 EST from Complex 11, Atlantic Missile Range, range test number 103.
  • The flight test report is public on DTIC as AD0861789 ("Flight Test Report, Atlas Missile 8F", dated 2 October 1962, declassified from Secret).
  • The National Archives holds a film of the flight, catalogued as NAID 614788, titled "Unidentified Flying Object (UFO) Sighting" and described as aerial coverage of a flight of Atlas F (Test 103).
  • The sentence the book quotes is real and is on page 14. But it sits inside the section on the staging cameras, which filmed the booster section being jettisoned at booster cutoff, roughly two minutes into the flight. Camera No. 3 was mounted outside the missile facing aft and ran from about booster cutoff plus 0.5 seconds to plus 10 seconds.

What this means: The "paced the re-entry vehicle for ninety seconds" description is not what the report says. It is about debris around a separating booster stage, in a ten-second window, about half an hour before the re-entry vehicle came down. The fix is a stronger scene, not a weaker one: it dramatises the method the show is about.

The fix, for the book and for the show.

  1. In the Illumination Strategy paragraph, drop the Layer 1 tag from the Atlas 8F paragraph until the film has been watched and the claim rewritten to match what the documents say. The report page and the NARA entry are Layer 1. The "paced the re-entry vehicle" description is not.
  2. In Show 08, replace the original 1962 beat with the version scripted above: the catalogue card, the split screen, page 14, the timeline, the speech bubble, the Empty Column.

What still needs verification. That AARO "deemed the footage a real UAP" — no primary AARO document about the Atlas F film was found in the source pass. Being in NARA's UAP Records Collection means the Archives grouped it there. It does not mean anyone concluded it was anomalous. Do not use the AARO claim until a primary document turns up. Bluegill Triple Prime remains unverified — the date is disagreed (25 vs 26 October local/UTC), and every account of an object tumbling out of the fireball found in the source pass was a forum post or a blog.

13.2 CONFIRMED · the gold ledger

The gold figures in Show 08 hold, with dates attached.

  • The Treasury holds 261,498,926 fine troy ounces of gold, per its Status Report of U.S. Government Gold Reserve as of 30 September 2026.
  • The statutory price is $42.2222 per fine troy ounce, set under 31 U.S.C. § 5117(b) following the 1973 Par Value Modification Act, unchanged since.
  • The book value is therefore about $11.04 billion. The Federal Reserve's gold certificate account matched it at $11.037 billion in the 21 October 2026 weekly report.
  • At the LBMA gold price of $4,026.70 on 23 October 2026, the same ounces are worth about $1.05 trillion, roughly ninety-five times the book figure. Gold reached about $5,502 on 29 January 2026, which would have put the reserve near $1.44 trillion.
  • In 1971 the dollar's gold convertibility at $35 an ounce ended, and in 1973 Congress reset the statutory price to $42.22.

Production rules. The market column is a number that changes daily. Date the graphic on screen ("as of"), recompute it on the day of publication, and keep the book-value column fixed, since it is the part that does not move. [PULL] the Status Report PDF itself and the 1934 Gold Reserve Act text for the 1934 beat.

13.3 THE LAST TWO PULL SLOTS

The Compact's named failure state (Show 04, Level 3)

The Codex's warning for this form: held too long, The Compact becomes a fixed pattern, called the shell. The cure is openness: a deep breath into the belly, arms extended. Its scene is the precision strike, where the martial artist's cost is that the body locks into the compact arrangement and needs half a second to open again. The failure states are now complete: the drag (Anchor-Drop), the drift (Phase-Glide), the spill (Crystal Expansion), the shell (The Compact), and Stutter-Step, which the book frames as an extreme-cost form sustained only for seconds.

Men of Renown Creator Contract (Show 09, Gallery 4 card)

Section 18 of the book. On-screen text, in the book's own wording:

· Four operators remain four.
· Archive figures are actors or masks.
· Density movement is a mask skill, not a fifth office.
· No racial hierarchy. No atrocity tourism.
· Illumination and Archive stay separate; connect by hinges only.
· Functions are archetypes for drama, not saints.
· Public bond and kit, not secret-order recruitment.
· Meta-worldview is literacy, not a license to sneer.
· Bond test every scene before you post it.

The Archive's own rail rule, from the book's closing posts, goes in the second card: Rail A is documented and falsifiable. Rail B is held inside a fiction contract. Connect only at money, recovery events, mythology homework and disclosure weather. Do not merge.

One conflict to know about. Men of Renown also carries real-world, Layer-1-style claims (the OAP contract, the Tso patent and similar items) alongside its fiction. Under the rail rule those belong in Illumination and in Show 08, not in Show 09. As scripted, Show 09 avoids them. Keep it that way, and do the same source pass on them before they appear anywhere.

14.1 SHOW 01 · fixes that made it stronger

Fix 1 · the hook

The library's headline said a scientist erased "85 percent of the universe." The figure that holds up is that dark matter is about 85 percent of the matter and roughly a quarter of the universe's total energy budget, with dark energy making up most of the rest. A knowledgeable viewer will spot the overreach in the first ten seconds. The corrected line loses nothing.

Fix 2 · Act 6, rebuilt

Two statements in the Living Egg's history did not hold up. Einstein did propose a finite, closed universe in 1917 — the shape question was asked, and seriously. And the dominant state and military funding of physics belongs to the period after 1945, not the interwar decades. What survives, narrower and more interesting, is the book's own idea: not whether space is finite, but which way it faces.

Fix 3 · the objection becomes the climax

An earlier script called dark matter "a placeholder." That undersells it, and a sceptical viewer will notice. The honest version is more dramatic: there are several independent lines of evidence — galaxy rotation curves, gravitational lensing, the pattern in the cosmic microwave background, and colliding galaxy clusters where the mass and the visible matter separate. A model that wants to drop the term has to explain all of them, not one. The corrected Act 6 does this, with the four panels filling the screen one after another and converging on one gold line: the missing mass.

14.2 SHOW 03 · the Wolfram parallel, restated so it is true and sharper

The book names the mathematician: Jonathan Gorard, co-founder of the Wolfram Physics Project and now CEO of Lanyon AI. Both facts check out. The convergence the book claims is narrower than "he agrees with the consonant code," and the accurate version is a better story, because the two sides come at language from opposite instincts.

  • Gorard's company builds AI that reads, writes and reasons in a formal language instead of ordinary human language. His public question is why agents are still reasoning in imperfect human languages.
  • The book argues the opposite about English: that ordinary words already carry hidden structure that nobody was taught to read.
  • Same diagnosis, opposite cures: language is the bottleneck.

No source was found for the specific Sapir-Whorf attribution the book gives him, so the show does not attribute it. It reports only what is documented.

The Show 03 replacement (as scripted in Chunk 10):

Two corridors again. Left door: a mathematician who builds AI in formal language. Right door: a mouth, saying a word. Each door opens onto the same room. Written on the far wall: LANGUAGE IS THE BOTTLENECK.

14.3 SHOW 08 · the Empty Column as the signature device

The Atlas 8F finding is the best thing that happened to Show 08. It hands the production an original device that the rest of the slate can use: the three-column card. The third column is always blank and always lit. The narrator ends the beat on it: "This column is yours."

The device turns every verification gap into an invitation, which is what a participation loop needs, and it means no episode ever claims more than the record supports. The Footprint Hunt is the standing weekly community event built on top of it.

Creator's Toolkit

The Creator’s Toolkit

Everything a contributor needs to choose a format, respect the limits of the tools, plan engagement and make a first short. All of it is reusable.

Presentation formats: which style for which show

Picking a format is picking a trade-off between consistency, cost, emotional reach and how many people can contribute. Here is every option on the table, followed by the recommended approach.

Format Best for Strength Trade-off
Narration over images (essay film) Footprints, Masks Cheapest, most flexible, authoritative tone Needs a strong narrator and strong stills
Motion-graphic explainer Tokenomics, Life First Clean, consistent, scales across many episodes Can feel cold without a character
Painterly animated docudrama Inward Is Forwards Emotional reach plus explanation Needs a locked character and style bible
Anime or cel-shaded serial The First Resonance, Sixteen Doors Lowest barrier for young audiences; fans can contribute fan art Long runtime; style drift is the main risk
Comic or webtoon Every show Storyboards become the comic with almost no extra work Static; needs motion for the flagship
AI actors and virtual host Continuity File, Open Call The masked cast makes it a natural fit Uncanny valley; keep them stylised and disclosed as synthetic
Podcast and NotebookLM overviews All, as the audio layer Already part of the EROS pipeline Not a replacement for picture
Interactive 3D Shows 00 and 01 Three 3D Universe pages already exist Needs hotspots tied to each episode
Community-made anthology Sixteen Doors The one format a guild can build in parallel Needs a house style so it feels like one universe

Recommendation: layer by purpose.

  • Cosmology gets the painterly animated docudrama with Elara as the human thread, because it needs both wonder and explanation.
  • Myth gets ink and violet animation. Different art style per operator.
  • Tokenomics gets motion graphics with analogy sets (hotels and housing, the rock and the river). It is the most reusable template and the cheapest to produce at scale.
  • Archive shows get narration over images. The documents are the star.
  • Fiction gets anime-style animation for the serial and the anthology, and AI actors for the Continuity File.
  • Community show gets a stylised virtual host plus viewer-made clips.
  • Every show ships with a comic cut, a three-minute short, and an audio overview. One storyboard feeds all of them.

Library integration. Each book already has top, middle and bottom cinema slots. Fill them the same way for every book: a 60 to 90 second trailer at the top, a three to four minute cutdown in the middle, the full twenty-minute episode at the bottom. The cutdowns marked in Show 01's production notes are the template.

Production notes and limits

These are the genuine technical limits, not caveats.

  • Shot length. Current AI video tools produce short clips, a few seconds each. A twenty-minute episode is a few hundred shots. Every board in this document is written as a single prompt unit, so the storyboard is the shot list.
  • Character drift. Faces and costumes drift between clips. Lock Elara and the narrator's avatar with a character sheet before generating anything. The myth sequences are safer because the figures are abstract.
  • Text in video. Generated text is unreliable. Every chip, contract address, equation and caption is composited in the editor, never generated.
  • Voice. Record the narrator once, as a scratch track, and cut an animatic from stills first. Cutting the script against a voice is where the 2,300-word budget actually gets tested.
  • NotebookLM. Feeding a script into NotebookLM as a source gives you a style-consistent rough cut and a mind map for free. It will not hold the three-register look, so treat it as a rough cut, not a master.

Six ready-to-shoot shorts for the Instrument cycle (Shows 06 and 07)

Six shorts, forty-five to sixty seconds each, designed to travel on their own. Every short opens on the first line shown, carries the mouth sting only as a one-second tail, and ends on an open loop. Badges (LIVE, DESIGN, PROPOSED) appear wherever a mechanism is named.

SHORT 06-A · "HOTEL NIGHTS" (from The Web, cold open)

  • A.1 A hotel lobby, guests checking in and out. Caption: spot trades are hotel nights.
  • A.2 Pan to a neighbourhood of lit houses. Caption: deep, multi-pair liquidity is housing stock.
  • A.3 An exit sign. One hotel empties in a minute. The neighbourhood does not.

VO "Spot trades are hotel nights. Guests arrive, guests leave, and the building is empty by morning. Deep liquidity across many pairs is housing stock. Harder to empty in one exit. That one picture is most of what you need to understand about why a network of pairs beats a single big pool."

Open loop. "So how many pairs does it take? The number is on the next one."

SHORT 06-B · "A POOL IS A WINDOW" (from The Web)

  • B.1 A window onto a city. Only some of the buildings are visible.
  • B.2 Seesaw diagram, a coin dropped into a shallow pool: the seesaw swings wide. Same coin, deep pool: barely a tilt.
  • B.3 Two viewers at one window. One owns the asset. One provides the pool.

VO "A pool is a window, not the whole city. In a shallow pool a small trade moves the price a lot. In a deep one it barely moves. Your view depends on what you own. If you own the asset, depth is your exit. If you provide the pool, depth is your infrastructure. And pool count alone does not tell you how deep the market is. The book says so. We say so."

Open loop. "Why would anyone build a pool on purpose?"

SHORT 06-C · "BRIDGE, BOND, BRANCH" (from The Web, The Tree)

  • C.1 A seedling. Three words rise as three icons: a bridge span, a handshake, a branch.
  • C.2 Ten coin icons pair with EROS and sprout pools. The pools pair with each other, level by level, up to one root.
  • C.3 Counter: Ten coins. Nineteen pools. One root. Badge: DESIGN.

VO "Bridge. Bond. Branch. Three moves, and that is the whole thing. Bring each token across the official bridge. Pair it with EROS and keep the receipt. Pair the receipts with each other, level by level, up to one root. Ten coins make nineteen pools. It adds no contract. It is an arrangement of pieces that already run."

Open loop. "Which ten? Tell us which you would add."

SHORT 07-A · "THE MINE AND THE ROCK" (from Rock, River, Gates, cold open)

  • A.1 A gold mine at dusk. The price board rises. The machines roar. More gold comes out of the ground.
  • A.2 The market floods. The price board falls.
  • A.3 A single rock in a stream. The water goes around it. Badge: LIVE.

VO "If the price of gold rises, people mine more gold. The supply expands. EROS has a fixed original supply, and a burn address that only grows. That is the difference between a metal and a standard."

Open loop. "A rock is only half of a river."

SHORT 07-B · "EARNED, NOT SCHEDULED" (from Rock, River, Gates, The Gates)

  • B.1 Three gates across a river. Each gate is a panel of real instruments: MARKET DEPTH, POOL COUNT, VERIFIED CODE.
  • B.2 A calendar page tries to push a gate open. The gate does not move.
  • B.3 A gauge reaches its mark and the gate swings open by itself. Badge: PROPOSED.

VO "The next layer is not on a date. It waits for three things: market depth, pool count and verified code. A calendar cannot open these gates. Only the conditions can. To be clear, this part is a design discussion, not a deployed product."

Open loop. "Where does your favourite project stand on the three gates?"

  • C.1 Ten cards flip onto a table, each a claim: fixed supply, the four-way transfer split, burn address, ErosX, the Tree, 33EROS, the official bridge, staking, the final root pool, a locked liquidity position. (Replace this sample with ten accurate claims from the Bridge and Platinum Standard when you cut.)
  • C.2 A viewer drags each card into one of three bins. A buzzer for a wrong bin.
  • C.3 A score card: how many did you get?

VO "Ten claims. Three bins. LIVE means you can check it on a block explorer today. DESIGN means every piece already exists and we are just arranging them. PROPOSED means nothing has been deployed. Sort them. Post your score."

Open loop. "The answer key is in the description. Show us where you disagreed."

Show 11 door rules, template and a worked example

Format sixteen shorts, eight to twelve minutes each, one door at a time, each in a different animation style. The same four-second mouth sting opens every door. Each door is a standalone commission for one writer, one visual lead, one composer and one voice.

House rules so sixteen styles still feel like one universe.

  1. The Egg's laws hold in every door: enclosure first, iteration as time, bond or decay. Break one only on purpose.
  2. The four operators never appear as characters, only as functions. Masks may appear.
  3. Every door ends on one image of bond: two things held in relation without collapsing into one.
  4. A door may be dark. A door may not be cynical.
  5. Each door carries one chip at the start: STORY.

Door template.

Beat Time What happens
Hook 0:00–1:00 One strange image
Ordinary world 1:00–3:00 Who the person is
Crossing 3:00–5:00 The law shows itself
Cost 5:00–8:00 What it costs to know
Bond 8:00–10:00 The relationship that holds
Coda 10:00–11:00 One line, one image
