PART FIVE: THE 14-SHOW SLATE

PART FIVE: THE 14-SHOW SLATE

5.1 The decision

The working production architecture is the 14-show slate, numbered 00–13. It is the most developed and coherent structure in the uploaded production documents.

The earlier four-strand concept remains the public navigation system. The earlier 22-episode proposal remains a historical development plan and a source of ideas. It is not a competing production slate.

The 14 shows are organised into six cycles and one central hub.

5.2 The six cycles

Cycle 1 — Cosmology and Mythology (Shows 01–04). The world model, the four operators, language, and the concept of life and iteration.

Cycle 2 — Tokenomics and Participation (Shows 05–07). The instrument, liquidity architecture, the standard, and the economic participation thesis.

Cycle 3 — Historical Investigation (Show 08). The documented historical and institutional record, investigated through primary sources.

Cycle 4 — Mythic and Speculative Archive (Show 09). The imaginative and interpretive material, explicitly separated from documented history.

Cycle 5 — Narrative Fiction (Shows 10–12). The First Resonance, Sixteen Doors, and The Continuity File.

Cycle 6 — Community and Production (Show 13). The Open Call and the ongoing creative work of the Guild.

The Hub — Show 00: The Map. The entry point. It explains how the cycles connect and lets a viewer choose a direction.

5.3 Show 00 — THE MAP

Cycle: Hub / Spine.

Core purpose: Introduce the complete EROS library and its four doors.

Status: Full script and storyboard.

What the show is: The Map is the cold-viewer entry point. It does not assume the viewer knows what EROS is. It explains the four doors, the 14 shows, the cycles, and the production invitation. It ends with a choice: which door does the viewer want to walk through next.

What the show must accomplish: It must make the whole system legible in 20 minutes without overwhelming the viewer. It must establish the EROS visual identity — the Egg, the Torus, the Tree, the Bridge, the four operators — in their first complete appearance. It must make the viewer feel that there is a world here, and that the world is navigable.

Deliverables for this show: Full episode, three-to-five-minute overview, short clips, illustrated map, website page, transcript and audio.

Failure mode to avoid: The Map becomes a corporate explainer. The Map should feel like the opening of a great documentary — awe, curiosity, invitation — not like a pitch deck.

5.4 Show 01 — INWARD IS FORWARDS

Cycle: Cosmology.

Core purpose: Explore the Living Egg and the enclosure model.

Status: Full script and storyboard.

What the show is: The central cosmology episode. It introduces the Cosmic Egg, the enclosure, the shell, the inner rind, the two-lobed toroidal geometry, the crossover, and the Isotope. It is the first time the EROS world model is presented at length.

What the show must accomplish: It must make the model feel physically real, visually spectacular, and intellectually serious. It must present the model as a model — labelled as EROS MODEL, not as established science — while still being genuinely awe-inspiring. It must leave the viewer with a shape in their mind: the Egg, the Torus, the observer inside the enclosure.

Source material: Living Egg (SRC-012), The Eros Enclosure (SRC-019).

Failure mode to avoid: The episode becomes a lecture on a scientific theory with no emotional or visual hook. The model must be experienced, not explained.

5.5 Show 02 — THE FOUR

Cycle: Mythology.

Core purpose: Present NaUn, Ra-Shen, Thoth, and EROS.

Status: Full script and storyboard.

What the show is: The mythology episode. It presents the four operators as functions of existence, not as four personalities. It shows what each one does to the world rather than what each one looks like as a character.

What the show must accomplish: It must give each operator a distinct visual grammar that is recognisable across every medium — animation, comics, documentary, interactive — without turning them into a pantheon of rival gods. It must reveal them through function. The dramatic line from the source is: "The gods did not leave. They became the rules."

Source material: Gods of EROS (SRC-010).

Failure mode to avoid: The operators become a conventional pantheon — humanoid figures in costumes holding weapons, with rivalries and personalities. That contradicts the canon. The operators are functions.

5.6 Show 03 — THE MOUTH

Cycle: Language.

Core purpose: Explore the Gift of Thoth and the physical articulation of language.

Status: Full script and storyboard.

What the show is: The language episode. It investigates the physical anatomy of speech — the mouth, the tongue, the teeth, the breath — and the proposed consonant operators. It is structured almost like a mystery: why do words have the structures they have? Can the proposed patterns be tested?

What the show must accomplish: It must make the audience curious about language in the way that the best linguistic documentaries do. It must present the EROS framework as a proposed interpretation, not as an established linguistic rule. It must invite the audience to investigate rather than accept.

Source material: Gift of Thoth (SRC-009).

Failure mode to avoid: The episode becomes a series of assertions that the EROS framework has "discovered" a linguistic truth. That overclaims. The Gift of Thoth is a proposal, and the episode should treat it as one.

5.7 Show 04 — LIFE FIRST

Cycle: Cosmology.

Core purpose: Explore Conscious EROS, iteration, and the Garden.

Status: Full script and storyboard.

What the show is: The philosophical episode. It asks what it would mean if life, awareness, memory, and choice were more fundamental than matter. It introduces the Conscious Eros, the Iteration Codex, and the Garden of Eros.

What the show must accomplish: It must be intellectually ambitious and emotionally resonant. It must not be a lecture on panpsychism. It must be a story about what it feels like to consider that the universe might be alive, and what follows from that.

Source material: The Conscious Eros (SRC-016), The Iteration Codex (SRC-025), The Garden of Eros (SRC-023).

Failure mode to avoid: The episode becomes a philosophy seminar. The emotional register must be as strong as the intellectual one.

5.8 Show 05 — RECEIPTS

Cycle: Tokenomics.

Core purpose: Explain the instrument, its architecture, and how to inspect it.

Status: Full script and storyboard.

What the show is: The first instrument episode. It teaches the viewer how to inspect what they actually own. It distinguishes deployed, designed, and proposed mechanisms. It demonstrates how to read the contract, how to check the chain, how to verify a claim.

What the show must accomplish: It must be the trust-building episode. It must show that the project is not asking for blind faith. It must teach the viewer how to check. It must demonstrate that EROS means it when it says "sensationise the question, not the evidence."

Source material: The Eros Plan (SRC-028), EROS Newcomer Dossier (SRC-006), Eros Narrative (SRC-005).

Failure mode to avoid: The episode becomes a crypto tutorial. It must be intelligent, practical, and calm — the opposite of hype.

5.9 Show 06 — THE WEB

Cycle: Tokenomics.

Core purpose: Explain liquidity, the bridge, bonding, and the Liquidity Tree.

Status: Full script and storyboard.

What the show is: The liquidity episode. It introduces the Liquidity Tree, the bridge, bonding, branching, and the constant-product AMM model (x × y = k). It shows how a token travels through the system: Bridge → Bond → Branch. It explains LP tokens, liquidity versus wallet supply, slippage, impermanent loss, and the risks.

What the show must accomplish: It must make the liquidity architecture feel like a living system — a tree, a web, a network — while being mechanically accurate. It must show both sides of the mechanism: the elegant design and the real risks.

Source material: EROS Liquidity Tree (SRC-004), The Bridge (SRC-015), The Flywheel (SRC-021), Architecture of Participation (SRC-001).

Failure mode to avoid: The episode presents the liquidity architecture as a guaranteed success. The source is explicit that number of pools is not proof of depth. The episode must show both.

5.10 Show 07 — ROCK, RIVER, GATES

Cycle: Tokenomics.

Core purpose: Explore the Platinum Standard, future mechanisms, and the two vaults.

Status: Full script and storyboard.

What the show is: The standard episode. It introduces the three instruments — EROS (the standard), ErosX (the river), 33EROS (the engine) — and the proposed transformation paths between them. It explores the two vaults — the on-chain instrument and the cultural archive — and the relationship between them.

What the show must accomplish: It must make the Platinum Standard legible without overclaiming what is deployed. It must distinguish clearly between what exists, what is designed, and what is proposed.

Source material: The Platinum Standard (SRC-027), The Hopeful Future (SRC-024).

Failure mode to avoid: The episode presents proposed mechanisms as existing products. The distinction between deployed and proposed must be visible on screen.

5.11 Show 08 — FOOTPRINTS

Cycle: Archive — Rail A (Documented History).

Core purpose: Investigate documented human history and public records.

Status: Full script and storyboard; research verification remains.

What the show is: The historical investigation. It examines the documented institutional record — financial systems, government instruments, monetary history, public statements, statutes, primary sources. It is investigative documentary, not mythology.

What the show must accomplish: It must maintain the distinction between:

  1. What a primary document actually says.
  2. What a source or commentator claims it means.
  3. What the EROS analysis infers.
  4. What remains unverified or speculative.

It must be compelling without overclaiming. It must show its sources. It must be honest about the limits of what the record can support.

Source material: Illumination Strategy (SRC-011).

Failure mode to avoid: The episode presents a contested interpretation as an established fact. The source is explicit: sensationalise the question, not the evidence.

5.12 Show 09 — MASKS

Cycle: Archive — Rail B (Mythic and Speculative Archive).

Core purpose: Explore the mythic and speculative archive.

Status: Full script and storyboard.

What the show is: The speculative archive. It explores ancient civilisations, the Electric Sky, the Gnostic framework, lost histories, and the Men of Renown. It is explicitly separated from documented history.

What the show must accomplish: It must be as dramatic and imaginative as it wants to be, while carrying an explicit fiction or speculation contract. The source material already separates its two rails; the show must preserve the separation.

Source material: Men of Renown (SRC-014), Eros Stories (SRC-007).

Failure mode to avoid: The show blends its speculative material into the documented history of Show 08. The two shows are separate rails. They can be compared at clearly identified structural points, but fictional events must never be presented as documented history.

5.13 Show 10 — THE FIRST RESONANCE

Cycle: Narrative fiction.

Core purpose: Adapt the novel as a ten-episode anime-influenced serial.

Status: Episode 1 script; Episodes 2–10 treatments.

What the show is: The human story. It adapts the First Resonance novel — Cal, Hana, Owen, the Visitor, Ilse, the practice, the stone, the ledger, the room above the bakery. It is the emotional centre of the series.

What the show must accomplish: It must make the audience care about the people before it asks them to care about the ideas. It must show the practice as a practice, not as a power. It must earn the final handover — the moment when Cal is no longer the centre, and the network continues through others.

Source material: The First Resonance (SRC-020), The Continuity File (SRC-017).

Failure mode to avoid: The show becomes a generic chosen-one origin story. The novel is not that. The novel's arc is the opposite: Cal discovers that he is not the centre. The adaptation must preserve that.

Specific characters and continuity:

  • Cal — 16-year-old coder. Starts capable but unsettled. Arc: from private uncertainty to independent practice, then to understanding that he is not the centre. Visual language: intimate close-ups, screens, handwritten notes, restrained light. Avoid superhero framing.
  • The Visitor — a role, not a specific person. The shape the network takes when it needs to make contact. Defining object: the ledger. Visual language: grey wool coat, stillness, slow movement, very little music.
  • Hana — the room keeper. Natural daylight, books, tea, practical warmth. She does not become Cal's new master. She confirms what he has learned and opens the door to the community.
  • Owen — the estranged coding partner. Returns to finish the abandoned project. He has not been recruited or taught the practice. The second signal. Their repaired collaboration is more important than a dramatic conversion.
  • Ilse — Cal's grandmother. Sensed the change before Cal could explain it. Anchors the extraordinary events in an ordinary family. Window light, kettle, stillness.

5.14 Show 11 — SIXTEEN DOORS

Cycle: Fiction anthology.

Core purpose: Sixteen independent stories and creative interpretations.

Status: House rules and pilots for Doors 1–3.

What the show is: The anthology. Sixteen standalone stories that each enter the EROS universe through a different door. The form is closer to Black Mirror or The Twilight Zone than to a serial. Each episode is self-contained.

What the show must accomplish: It must demonstrate that the EROS universe can hold many kinds of story. It must let contributors propose their own doors. It must be the most community-driven of the 14 shows — a place where a new writer, a new artist, or a new animator can make something that stands alone.

Source material: Eros Stories (SRC-007), and community pitches.

Failure mode to avoid: The anthology becomes a bin of rejected ideas. Every door must be a real door into the universe, not a random short that happens to use the EROS vocabulary.

5.15 Show 12 — THE CONTINUITY FILE

Cycle: Narrative thriller.

Core purpose: Adapt the novel as a three-episode limited series.

Status: Three-episode framework; some scenes and episodes developed.

What the show is: The institutional thriller. It adapts the Continuity File — a story about records, institutions, and the people who maintain them. It is set in the same universe as the First Resonance but in a different register: colder, more procedural, more suspicious.

What the show must accomplish: It must be a genuine thriller, not a lore delivery vehicle. It must respect the source novel's tone. It must give the audience a different reason to care about continuity than the First Resonance gives them.

Source material: The Continuity File (SRC-017).

Failure mode to avoid: The show treats its fictional institutions as real historical institutions. The fiction contract applies. Dr. Elara Vance and the Atacama scene, the Visitor, the First Resonance ledger, and the Continuity File's institutional events are all explicitly fictional.

5.16 Show 13 — THE OPEN CALL

Cycle: Community.

Core purpose: Establish the recurring community production and review format.

Status: Weekly format and Episode 1 script.

What the show is: The community show. It is not a narrative episode. It is a recurring format: contributor profiles, open calls, production updates, community reviews, work-in-progress showcases, behind-the-scenes documentation.

What the show must accomplish: It must demonstrate the Guild in action. It must show that a contributor can start from zero and end up in a published piece. It must be the show that makes the rest of the project feel like a real community rather than a broadcast.

Source material: The Open Call (SRC-026), We Are With You EROS (SRC-029), Architecture of Participation (SRC-001).

Failure mode to avoid: The show becomes a low-effort vlog. It must be produced with the same care as the flagship episodes. It is the show that proves the Guild works.

5.17 The master slate summary

The full proposed master slate, organised by series:

Series 1 — The Instrument

  • Episode 1: The EROS Flywheel ★ Pilot (The Flywheel, TheErosPlan, Architecture of Participation)
  • Episode 2: The Rock, the River and the Engine (The Platinum Standard, The Eros Plan)
  • Episode 3: The Liquidity Tree (EROS Liquidity Tree, The Bridge)
  • Episode 4: Bridge. Bond. Branch. (The Bridge, The Hopeful Future)
  • Episode 5: From Holding to Building (Architecture of Participation, WeAreWithYouEros)
  • Episode 6: The Platinum Standard (The Platinum Standard, EROS Newcomer Dossier)

Series 2 — The World Model

  • Episode 7: The Crack in the Sky ★ Pilot (Living Egg, The Eros Enclosure)
  • Episode 8: The Living Egg (Living Egg, The Eros Enclosure)
  • Episode 9: Time Is the Count of Iterations (The Iteration Codex, The Conscious Eros)
  • Episode 10: The Geometry of Weight and Expansion (The Conscious Eros, The Garden of Eros)
  • Episode 11: The Living Enclosure (The Eros Enclosure, Living Egg)

Series 3 — Mythology and Human Continuity

  • Episode 12: The Gods Were Operators ★ Pilot (Gods of EROS, Gift of Thoth)
  • Episode 13: The Gift of Thoth (Gift of Thoth)
  • Episode 14: The First Resonance ★ Pilot / crossover (The First Resonance, The Continuity File)
  • Episode 15: The Garden of EROS (The Garden of Eros, Eros Stories)

Series 4 — Illumination

Important editorial distinction: Series 4 is not a fictional extension of the EROS mythology. It is a documentary and investigative strand. Its source claims need independent verification, primary documents, dates, counterarguments, and explicit falsification tests.

The four pilots — The Crack in the Sky, The Gods Were Operators, The EROS Flywheel, The First Resonance — are distributed across the series and serve as the first audience entry points. They test four different production pipelines before the project commits to a full season.

PART SIX: THE OPERATORS AND VISUAL CANON

PART SIX: THE OPERATORS AND VISUAL CANON

6.1 The correction

The earlier plan suggested creating four character models for the four operators. The source material corrects this. The operators are not four ordinary characters. They are functions of existence, not four personalities walking around a universe. That distinction should shape the entire visual language.

The source says: NaUn does not answer, forgive, or intervene. NaUn holds. Ra-Shen is the light itself, not the person holding the lamp. Thoth is a role that can appear through different people — anyone who learns, records, and passes knowledge forward can embody that function. EROS is what happens between things that remain connected without becoming one.

The production form for each operator is therefore not a character model but a visual grammar: a set of colours, shapes, motions, sounds, and portrayal restrictions that can be applied across animation, documentary, comics, CGI, and live-action without breaking continuity.

6.2 NaUn — The Architecture

Function: Permission, structure, boundaries, and enduring law.

Visual language: Negative space, geometry, structural lines, doors, load-bearing forms. Violet treatment. The effect of NaUn in a scene should be the feeling that the space has rules, and the rules are visible.

Sound: Deep resonance, almost silence. The sound of a NaUn scene is the sound of a large room where something is being decided.

Portrayal restrictions: Avoid a humanoid architect, a speaking god, or a conventional character portrait. NaUn does not appear. NaUn is the condition under which appearance is possible.

The line to protect: "NaUn does not answer, forgive, or intervene. NaUn holds."

6.3 Ra-Shen — The Stage and Force

Function: Energy under containment; radiation, movement, and physical expression.

Visual language: Gold and white light, aurora, solar fire, expanding rings, contained currents. The stage on which events happen.

Sound: Rising harmonic energy and controlled percussion. The sound of a Ra-Shen scene is the sound of something being generated and held.

Portrayal restrictions: Avoid a conventional sun god holding a weapon or standing in a costume. The source describes Ra-Shen as the light itself, not the person holding the lamp.

The line to protect: "Ra-Shen is the light itself, not the person holding the lamp."

6.4 Thoth — The Teacher and Builder

Function: Learning, language, medicine, memory, form, and transmission.

Visual language: Hands, mouths, eyes, glyphs, writing, correction, archives. Thoth is a role, not a single face. Anyone who learns, records, and passes knowledge forward can embody Thoth.

Sound: Human voice, whispered language, ink and page textures. The sound of a Thoth scene is the sound of something being written down.

Portrayal restrictions: Avoid treating Thoth as one fixed person in every era. The operator can appear through different human embodiments across the series. A recurring visual motif — the hand, the eye, the writing implement — should carry the continuity, not a single character design.

The line to protect: "Thoth is a role that can appear through different people. Anyone who learns, records, and passes knowledge forward can embody that function."

6.5 EROS — The Bond

Function: Cohesion, continuation, and the preservation of relationships across time.

Visual language: Threads, connected structures, two walls holding a central spark, joined-but-distinct forms. EROS is what happens between things that remain connected without becoming one.

Sound: Separate musical notes resolving into harmony. The sound of an EROS scene is the sound of two things that were already there becoming audible as a relationship.

Portrayal restrictions: Avoid a humanoid EROS, a mascot, or a conventional god figure. EROS is not a character. EROS is a relationship.

The line to protect: "EROS is what happens between things that remain connected without becoming one."

6.6 The Cosmic Egg

Function: The bounded vessel or enclosure. The first major reusable CGI asset. The master 3D environment.

Visual elements to establish:

  • The enclosure (the outer shell)
  • The shell and inner boundary (the rind)
  • The two-lobed toroidal geometry (the shape of the interior)
  • The crossover (the point where the two lobes meet)
  • The Isotope (the infinitely approached centre)
  • The relationship between the interior and the observer

What these are not: They are not four separate universes. The Egg is the vessel; the Torus is its geometric reading. The interior is the inhabited space; the observer is the position from which the space can be seen. The Isotope is the centre that cannot be reached.

On-screen classification: EROS MODEL — not established scientific fact. The visual can be spectacular without suggesting that the cosmology has been experimentally demonstrated.

6.7 The five visual pillars

The Eros Plan defines five visual pillars. They are the common design language across the television universe.

  1. Cosmic Egg — the seed within; the gateway to the world model.
  2. Gravity — connection, attraction, bonding, unification.
  3. Umbrella — one ecosystem, many communities and identities.
  4. Illumination — civilisation, systems, power, and the investigation of evidence.
  5. Gamification — stages, milestones, creative participation, visible progress.

These are not five unrelated art styles. They are five recurring visual ideas. Each programme can use a different medium while retaining a recognisable EROS identity.

6.8 The colour language

  • Gold: Evidence markers, receipts, links, geometric proof.
  • Violet: NaUn, geometry, mythic architecture.
  • Teal and orange: Community, participation, instrument-related visuals.
  • Black: Space, silence, transition, the signature opening.

The colour language is consistent across every show, every medium, every asset. A viewer who has seen one EROS production should be able to recognise the next one by the palette before any other element confirms it.

6.9 The four-second sting

The recurring four-second EROS sting is retained as a proposed series identity. The sequence: black, extreme close-up of a mouth, a sustained hum, the EROS title. It is the signature of every programme. It is the visual equivalent of the house motto.

PART SEVEN: THE EVIDENCE SYSTEM

PART SEVEN: THE EVIDENCE SYSTEM

7.1 The four-tier canon

The production system must protect the integrity of the source library while allowing creative expansion.

Tier 1 — Core Source Canon. The 29 foundational source files and verified technical records. These establish what the original corpus says.

Tier 2 — Verified Expansion. Scripts, diagrams, adaptations, and production material checked against Tier 1.

Tier 3 — Community Variations. Independent creative work that honours the core framework but may have its own artistic interpretation.

Tier 4 — Experimental Branches. Alternative, divergent, or deliberately speculative work. It may be explored, but it must not be silently merged into the source canon.

The tiers are not a hierarchy of quality. They are a hierarchy of authority. A Tier 4 work can be better than a Tier 2 work and still not be part of the canon.

7.2 The epistemic labels

Every important factual or conceptual claim must be classified. The labels are:

  • OBSERVED — a measurement, record, or event that can be independently checked.
  • MODEL — a conceptual or structural model stated by the books.
  • STORY — fiction, mythology, or dramatised narrative.
  • HYPOTHESIS — a proposed explanation that remains unproven.
  • PATTERN — a comparative interpretation.
  • OBJECTION — a substantive challenge.
  • FALSIFIER — a condition or observation that would weaken or disprove a claim.

The labels should be visible in the production where they matter. In documentary-style shows, they can be displayed as small on-screen icons. In fiction, they are handled by the fiction contract.

7.3 The mechanism labels

Technical and token-related material must use a separate system:

  • LIVE — deployed and verifiable at the stated date.
  • DESIGN — a design or arrangement of existing components.
  • PROPOSED — a future or undeployed mechanism.

A mechanism's status must be checked before publication. The PDFs are explicit: the older Flywheel source states a 2% burn and renounced ownership, but those must be verified against current contract and chain data before being presented as current facts.

7.4 The two-rail separation

Rail A — Documented History. The Illumination Strategy and Show 08. Primary sources, statutes, public records, dates, citations, and falsifiable claims.

Rail B — Mythic and Speculative Archive. Men of Renown, Masks, and the fictional material. It must carry an explicit fiction or speculation contract.

The two rails may be compared at clearly identified structural points, but fictional events must never be presented as documented history.

7.5 The fiction contract

Fictional characters, organisations, events, and dramatic devices must remain identifiable as fictional. This includes:

  • The Dr. Elara Vance Atacama scene
  • The Visitor
  • The First Resonance ledger
  • The Continuity File's fictional institutional events
  • Cal, Hana, Owen, Ilse
  • The Ray, the Stone, the Room
  • The 422/11 ledger

The story can ask powerful questions without pretending that its invented events happened. The fiction contract is what allows the project to be both dramatic and credible.

7.6 The Illumination special rule

The Illumination Strategy covers financial history, government instruments, national security, monetary policy, public statements, and other contentious subjects. Its programmes must show the difference between:

  1. What a primary document actually says.
  2. What a source or commentator claims it means.
  3. What the EROS analysis infers.
  4. What remains unverified or speculative.

Sensational questions are welcome. Unsupported conclusions presented as facts are not.

7.7 The on-screen display

In the documentary and investigative shows, the evidence classification should be displayed subtly but visibly. A small icon in the corner of the frame can indicate whether the claim currently being presented is OBSERVED, MODEL, STORY, HYPOTHESIS, PATTERN, OBJECTION, or FALSIFIER. In the fiction shows, the contract is handled by the framing — the audience knows they are watching fiction, and the fiction does not pretend otherwise.

The evidence system is not bureaucracy. It is the thing that lets the project be bold without being dishonest. It is the reason a viewer can trust the cosmology episode even when it is presenting a model, because the model is clearly labelled as a model. It is the reason a viewer can trust the tokenomics episode even when it is describing a proposed mechanism, because the mechanism is clearly labelled as proposed.

PART EIGHT: THE GUILD AND PRODUCTION ENGINE

PART EIGHT: THE GUILD AND PRODUCTION ENGINE

8.1 The seven studios

The Guild is the community's production structure. It should allow people with different skills, experience, and available time to contribute without needing to understand every book.

Writers' Studio. Scripts, dialogue, narration, and articles. Typical contribution: one scene or explanation.

Visual Studio. Illustrations, comics, and design. Typical contribution: one image or character sheet.

Animation Studio. CGI, motion graphics, anime, and video. Typical contribution: one short sequence.

Sound Studio. Narration, music, and audio. Typical contribution: one recorded passage.

Research Studio. Source checking and evidence. Typical contribution: one verified reference.

Web Studio. HTML, interactive diagrams, and 3D. Typical contribution: one web component.

Publishing Studio. Editing, subtitles, and distribution. Typical contribution: one finished cutdown or upload.

These studios are functional groups, not status levels. A contributor should be able to join one studio, complete one task, and see the result become part of the larger project.

8.2 The contribution brief

Every Guild task must contain eight fields:

Task title. What needs to be made.

Source. The book, episode, or production brief it belongs to.

Purpose. Why the contribution is needed.

Deliverable. The exact item required.

Format. File type, aspect ratio, length, or other technical requirement.

Reference. The visual, script, or example to follow.

Acceptance criteria. What makes the work suitable for publication.

Credit. How the contributor will be acknowledged.

This is the smallest practical production unit. A contributor should be able to open a brief and know exactly what to make, in what format, and to what standard, without needing to read the rest of the project documentation.

8.3 The Book-to-Media Engine

Every source book should be processed through the same production sequence. This is the core operating system of the project.

Stage 1 — Source extraction. For each book, record: canonical title and filename, purpose and subject, main thesis, major sections, key terminology, verbatim passages, characters and narrative material, diagrams and visual concepts, technical mechanisms, evidence and citations, questions and objections, links to other books. The extraction must preserve the author's actual meaning and wording where needed.

Stage 2 — Pattern matching and synthesis. Identify recurring ideas across books. Compare repeated concepts, shared terminology, common mechanisms, contradictions, complementary explanations, repeated characters and symbols, similar visual structures, and ideas that build on one another. Record each relationship as one of: same idea repeated, same idea expanded, complementary idea, dependent idea, contradiction, alternative interpretation, new proposal. This is where the natural episode structure emerges.

Stage 3 — Editorial adaptation. Each production receives: one central theme, one intended audience, one learning objective, one opening question, one narrative or explanatory structure, one conclusion, one next step for the viewer. A book does not automatically become one episode. Several books may combine into one episode, and one book may support an entire serial.

Stage 4 — Master production package. Every episode should have: episode brief, source map, claim and evidence ledger, script, storyboard, shot list, character and location references, visual asset requirements, sound and narration requirements, production instructions, short-form cutdown plan, transcript and website copy, community contribution tasks, and editorial approval record.

Stage 5 — Derivative content. Each flagship episode should produce several related outputs. A standard package: flagship episode (8–20 min), trailer (30–90s), short clips (3–6), explainer (3–5 min), vertical videos (3–5), illustrated article, audio (narrated episode or chapter), interactive element, community task.

Stage 6 — Publication and learning. Publish the complete package. Review viewer retention, repeat viewers, website visits, book engagement, audience questions, contributor responses, production effort, and reusable assets created. Use the results to improve the next production.

8.4 The standard episode package

Every flagship episode should have fourteen deliverables:

  1. Episode brief
  2. Source map
  3. Claim and evidence ledger
  4. Script
  5. Storyboard
  6. Shot list
  7. Character and location references
  8. Visual asset requirements
  9. Sound and narration requirements
  10. Production instructions
  11. Short-form cutdown plan
  12. Transcript and website copy
  13. Community contribution tasks
  14. Editorial approval record

This is the checklist that separates a finished production from a draft. If a deliverable is missing, the episode is not finished.

8.5 Examples of first Guild tasks

These are the kind of tasks that can be picked up by a contributor on day one:

  • Design one Cosmic Egg reference illustration.
  • Produce a four-operator symbol sheet.
  • Animate a 10-second toroidal sequence.
  • Create one vertical video from Show 03.
  • Record one passage from the First Resonance.
  • Build an interactive diagram for the Liquidity Tree.
  • Verify one primary historical source for Footprints.
  • Create subtitles for Show 00.
  • Design the Open Call submission page.

No contributor should need to build an entire show to make a meaningful contribution. The smallest contribution should be small enough to be completed, and meaningful enough to matter.

8.6 The contribution process

  1. A contributor proposes an idea, character, scene, or asset.
  2. The submission is checked against the World Bible and the relevant source.
  3. It is classified as canon, compatible expansion, alternate interpretation, or experimental.
  4. Approved material receives a version and an attribution.
  5. Production teams can reuse it without rebuilding it from scratch.

This is particularly important if the EROS universe is eventually built by many independent contributors. The process is not designed to slow people down. It is designed to keep the world coherent as it grows.

8.7 AI production rules

AI can help with: drafting scripts and dialogue, storyboard concepts, visual and video generation, animation assistance, voice and narration drafts, research organisation.

Human approval remains necessary for: canonical story decisions, final character designs, continuity and quality control, technical accuracy, approved voices and performance, evidence and source verification, world-building suggestions, and acceptance into canon.

AI should accelerate production, not become the authority on what EROS means. The project's voice, canon, and editorial standards come from the people, not from the tools.

PART NINE: THE FOUR PILOTS

PART NINE: THE FOUR PILOTS

9.1 Pilot 01 — The Crack in the Sky

Working title: The Crack in the Sky.

Series: The World Model.

Source material: Living Egg (SRC-012), The Eros Enclosure (SRC-019).

Status: Timed outline and source extraction in v0.2 of the database.

The central proposition: The episode opens the mystery. A scientist is looking at the universe. Something does not add up. The question is not whether the data is wrong — the question is whether the model through which the data is interpreted is wrong. The episode introduces the Living Egg and the idea of an enclosed universe, without claiming that the model is established science.

The timed structure (nine segments):

  • 00:00–01:30 — The hook. A fictional opening in Atacama. Dr. Elara Vance is looking at the sky. The data does not match the model. The question is planted: what if the problem is the model?
  • 01:30–04:00 — Observation vs. interpretation. The episode distinguishes between what is observed and what is inferred. It introduces the idea that a model can be wrong in ways that produce correct predictions, and correct in ways that produce wrong predictions.
  • 04:00–09:00 — The Egg and the living membrane. The Cosmic Egg is introduced. The enclosure, the shell, the inner rind. The idea that the universe has a boundary, and the boundary is part of the explanation.
  • 09:00–14:00 — Light and lensing. The episode demonstrates how light would behave in an enclosed universe. The observational signatures that would distinguish the model from the standard picture. The visual is spectacular.
  • 14:00–17:30 — The two-lobed geometry. The torus is introduced. The two lobes, the crossover, the Isotope. The model becomes geometric.
  • 17:30–19:00 — Iteration, affinity, and plasma. The dynamic elements of the model. Time as the count of iterations. Affinity as the mechanism of connection. Plasma as the substrate.
  • 19:00–20:00 — The observer and falsifiability. The episode ends with the observer's position in the model, and the question of what would have to be true for the model to be wrong. The cliffhanger: the four operators.

What the episode must not do: It must not present the EROS cosmology as established scientific fact. It can be dramatic, cinematic, and awe-inspiring. It must be honest about what is model, what is hypothesis, and what is evidence.

The production format: Cinematic CGI, narrated investigation, scientific comparisons, clearly labelled speculative models.

9.2 Pilot 02 — The Gods Were Operators

Working title: The Gods Were Operators.

Series: Mythology and Human Continuity.

Source material: Gods of EROS (SRC-010).

Status: Timed outline, character bible, and scene map in v0.3 of the database.

The central proposition: The four operators — NaUn, Ra-Shen, Thoth, EROS — are not four competing gods or superheroes. They are functions of existence. The episode reveals them through what they do, not through what they look like. The dramatic line from the source: "The gods did not leave. They became the rules."

The sequence structure (twelve sequences):

  1. The First Silence. Before the operators. The state of the world before function.
  2. NaUn emerges. The architecture. Permission. The rules that allow a world to exist.
  3. Ra-Shen emerges. The stage. Energy under containment. The light itself.
  4. The world becomes possible. The two functions in relationship. The stage and the architecture.
  5. Thoth emerges. The teacher. Learning, language, memory, correction. The function that turns energy into meaning.
  6. The world becomes legible. The three functions in relationship. Architecture, stage, meaning.
  7. EROS emerges. The bond. Cohesion, continuation, the preservation of relationship across time.
  8. The four laws are established. The four functions in relationship. What the world is, once all four are present.
  9. The test begins. The world is set in motion. The functions are tested by what happens in the world.
  10. The first failure. A function is missing, or misapplied, or refused. The world breaks.
  11. The restoration. The function is restored. The world continues. The pattern is established.
  12. The four laws are tested. The episode closes with the four operators as ongoing functions, not as past events. The laws are tested every time the world runs.

Character bible requirements:

For each operator, the character bible must specify:

  • Function (what the operator does to the world)
  • Visual identity (colour, form, motion, recurring motifs)
  • Voice (if any — the operators are not all voiced)
  • Dramatic function (the role the operator plays in a scene)
  • Portrayal guardrails (what the operator must never become)

The critical guardrail: the episode must never turn the four operators into a conventional pantheon of rival personalities. That would contradict the source canon.

The visual direction: The operators should have recognisable visual identities, but they should not be conventional character designs. NaUn is geometry and negative space. Ra-Shen is light and motion. Thoth is hands, mouths, eyes, and glyphs. EROS is threads and connected forms.

9.3 Pilot 03 — The EROS Flywheel

Working title: The EROS Flywheel.

Series: The Instrument.

Source material: The Flywheel (SRC-021), The Eros Plan (SRC-028), Architecture of Participation (SRC-001).

Status: Source reviewed; treatment written. Workbook update not yet saved.

The central proposition: The source's thesis is more than a token attracting attention. It proposes a connection between two different forms of accumulated value:

  • Vault One — the on-chain vault: contract, rules, transactions, supply mechanics, liquidity arrangements, integrations.
  • Vault Two — the cultural vault: books, mythology, art, education, videos, characters, websites, archives, creative assets.

The flywheel is the connection between them. The token may create an initial reason to look; the cultural world gives people somewhere to go; participation can create new work; and that work may generate further discovery.

The source explicitly describes this as a proposal to build and test, not a promise of market outcomes.

The timed structure (eleven sequences):

  • 00:00–01:30 — The two vaults. Two enormous vaults appear in darkness. One contains code and transactions; the other contains books, art, characters, and worlds.
  • 01:30–03:00 — A token is not a world. A token chart occupies the screen. Beside it, a vast creative archive remains unseen. The question: how do they connect?
  • 03:00–05:00 — Vault One: the instrument. Contract architecture, supply rules, permissions, transactions, liquidity. Actual chain evidence must support every technical claim.
  • 05:00–06:30 — Vault Two: the cultural archive. Books transform into comics, films, characters, educational material, games, and interactive environments.
  • 06:30–08:30 — The attention engine. Market movement attracts attention. Newcomers begin investigating the project. The film shows both the opportunity and the volatility.
  • 08:30–10:30 — Discovery becomes meaning. A newcomer follows the front door into the books, mythology, tokenomics, and the wider EROS universe.
  • 10:30–12:30 — The demand equation. The holder becomes a participant: reading, asking, testing, translating, drawing, writing, and building.
  • 12:30–14:30 — Participation becomes creation. Community contributions become new stories, artwork, assets, tools, and experiences.
  • 14:30–16:00 — The world expands. The EROS universe progresses from books and images to 3D exploration, interactive stories, games, and immersive environments.
  • 16:00–18:00 — The economic layer. Liquidity pools, AMM mechanics, hybrid NFTs. Explain the actual mechanisms separately from the fictional world and its proposed economy.
  • 18:00–20:00 — The flywheel tested. The cycle returns to attention. But what happens if people look and do not participate? The episode ends on that unresolved challenge.

The six-stage flywheel:

  1. ATTENTION — a reason to look.
  2. DISCOVERY — a clear front door.
  3. UNDERSTANDING — the pieces connect.
  4. PARTICIPATION — a first useful action.
  5. CREATION — new work and assets.
  6. RENEWED ATTENTION — useful work travels outward.

The cycle is a strategic hypothesis. Each transition needs to be built and demonstrated.

The AMM section: The source discusses more than 133 liquidity pools and a target of 333, and explains the constant-product AMM model: x × y = k. A purchase changes the quantities of assets in a pool and therefore the ratio and quoted price. But the same mechanism can amplify selling, slippage, and volatility. The number of pools alone does not establish the depth or resilience of liquidity. The episode should visually demonstrate both sides of the mechanism.

The hybrid NFT sequence: The source takes the idea further. An asset in the EROS world could carry an economic component, such as locked EROS, EROS X, Titan X, or X28. A cinematic example could show an artefact with: a creative identity and history, an embedded economic component, interactive behaviour in a game, and economic consequences when it is upgraded, traded, damaged, or repaired.

This is a proposed model, not evidence that these implementations already exist. Locked tokens do not automatically guarantee the NFT's market value or liquidity.

The media evolution sequence: The source gives four clear stages: representation, exploration, participation, immersion. The episode should show the progression from books and illustrations, through 3D models and navigable spaces, through games and interactive cinema, to VR and spatial projection.

The strongest dramatic moment: The transition from holder to builder. A newcomer arrives because of a chart. They find a book. They discover an idea. They ask a question. Someone answers. They create something. Another person uses it. The camera pulls back and reveals that the archive has grown.

The narration: "A token can attract a visitor. A story can hold their attention. But the real transformation begins when the visitor becomes a creator."

Production guardrails:

  • Do not present a price increase as guaranteed attention or demand.
  • Do not present the number of liquidity pools as proof of liquidity depth.
  • Do not treat a revoked administrative key as proof that liquidity or market value is protected.
  • Do not describe proposed hybrid NFTs, internal economies, or holographic environments as completed products.
  • Keep fictional economic systems distinct from actual financial rights and deployed mechanisms.

The recommended format: Financial thriller that gradually reveals it is actually about world-building and human participation. Start with the chart, open the vaults, then reveal the larger ambition.

9.4 Pilot 04 — The First Resonance

Working title: The First Resonance.

Series: Mythology and Human Continuity.

Source material: The First Resonance (SRC-020).

Status: Source reviewed; treatment written. Workbook update not yet saved.

The central proposition: A young coder thinks he has been singled out by something extraordinary. Gradually, he discovers that the real story is not the Ray, the visitor, or even the stone. It is the practice — and the people who quietly carry it.

The source itself describes Cal's arc as becoming unnecessary. The practice is meant to continue without him. That is the episode's emotional destination.

The timed structure (ten sequences):

  • 00:00–01:30 — The Ray. A 16-year-old coder, a failing line of code, a number he did not type, and three lights holding an impossible triangle.
  • 01:30–03:00 — The House That Feels Wrong. Cal's mother, grandmother Ilse, and uncle Tobin notice changes in him. The ordinary world begins to feel unfamiliar.
  • 03:00–05:00 — The Visitor. A quiet stranger arrives. No grand explanation: questions, observation, a notebook, and the beginning of a practice.
  • 05:00–07:00 — The Stone. Cal is given a physical reminder. The practice becomes simple enough to carry: touch the stone, notice that he is touching it.
  • 07:00–09:00 — The Room Above the Bakery. Hana introduces Cal to a room of people. Twelve chairs, tea, biscuits, no leader. The room is a support structure, not a hierarchy.
  • 09:00–11:00 — The Second Signal. Owen, an estranged coding partner, approaches Cal and asks to finish their abandoned project together. He has not been recruited or taught the practice.
  • 11:00–13:00 — The Ledger. The visitor reveals 422 names. Only 11 are still practising. The episode's emotional centre: the cost of beginning and stopping.
  • 13:00–15:00 — The Curriculum. The story opens into functions, instruments, verification, the five-layer EROS stack, and the network.
  • 15:00–17:00 — The Demand Equation. Attention, community, liquidity, and creation are shown as a proposed reinforcing system — not a guaranteed market outcome.
  • 17:00–18:30 — The Room Cannot Hold Everything. Cal discovers that the practice cannot be reduced to one room, one teacher, or one form. The network must live in different people and places.
  • 18:30–20:00 — The Next Node. Cal's role changes. The practice continues through others. The final image points beyond him to the next person.

Character and visual direction:

Cal — the first node. Starts as a capable but unsettled 16-year-old. His arc is from private uncertainty to independent practice, then to understanding that he is not the centre. Visual language: intimate close-ups, screens, handwritten notes, restrained light. Avoid making him a superhero.

The Visitor — the doorway. The source says the visitor is a role, not a specific person: the shape the network takes when it needs to make contact. His defining object is the ledger. Visual language: grey wool coat, stillness, slow movement, very little music.

Hana — the room keeper. She does not become Cal's new master. She confirms what he has learned and opens the door to the community. Visual language: natural daylight, books, tea, practical warmth.

Owen — the second signal. Owen is essential because he shows the practice's effect beyond formal instruction. Their repaired collaboration is more important than a dramatic conversion. Visual language: ordinary school coding room, awkward silence, then a small human reconnection.

Ilse — the quiet recognition. She senses that something has begun before Cal can explain it. She anchors the extraordinary events in an ordinary family. Visual language: window light, kettle, stillness, no supernatural effects needed.

The episode's strongest dramatic moments:

  • The Ray: the number appears in Cal's code. The audience sees the event through his uncertainty, not through an explanatory voice claiming it is real.
  • The stone: a simple object becomes a recurring visual motif. It gives the audience a physical anchor for an internal practice.
  • The room: twelve chairs, a kettle, and biscuits. A deliberate contrast with grand temples, secret societies, or command centres.
  • The ledger: 422 names; 11 still walking. The episode's major reversal. The visitor's work is not presented as effortless success.
  • Owen's return: the second signal is a human relationship changing, not a supernatural transmission.
  • The final handover: Cal is no longer the centre. The network can continue without him.

How to make it television rather than a narrated book:

  • Cinematic live-action / AI actors: Cal, his family, the visitor, Hana, and Owen.
  • Stylised animation: the Ray, the number, the stone's recurring visual motif, and the transition from individual to network.
  • Documentary-style inserts: notebook pages, code, dates, ledger entries, and the five-layer stack.
  • Graphic animation: the network expanding from a room into a web of independent nodes.
  • Sound: restrained. Let silence, room tone, typing, kettle sounds, and footsteps do much of the work.

Evidence and presentation guardrails:

  • The Ray, three lights, Shadow, and visitor: fictional narrative events.
  • Cal, Hana, Owen, Ilse, and the ledger: characters and story devices.
  • The practice and resonance: EROS philosophical / narrative framework.
  • The five-layer stack: EROS architecture as described in the book; mark proposed elements accurately.
  • Token contract, ownership, burn, and liquidity claims: verify against current on-chain evidence before presenting as fact.
  • The demand equation: strategic hypothesis, not a proven economic outcome.

The 422/11 ledger: It is a powerful dramatic device, but it must not be presented as real-world research or a verified historical statistic. The book uses it to make the cost of the practice visible.

The source's own distinction: The practice is not a secret, and the network is not a hierarchy. The story is not about recruiting followers or creating a new authority structure. It is about a practice that can continue without its first teacher.

PART TEN: PARALLEL CREATION AND FRACTAL BRANCHING

PART TEN: PARALLEL CREATION AND FRACTAL BRANCHING

10.1 What it is

The community does not have to wait for the central team to finish a show. They can take a source, concept, character, visual, or task and begin developing something in parallel, while keeping the relationship to the larger EROS project clear.

This is the central community invitation of the project. It is what makes the Guild a production network rather than a fan club. It is what makes the EROS universe expand beyond what any central team could produce.

10.2 How it works

A contributor identifies a piece of the EROS world that interests them. They check the source material. They check the canon tiers. They decide what tier their work will be in. They propose a contribution. The proposal is reviewed against the World Bible and the relevant source. If accepted, the work enters the production pipeline. If experimental, the work is published as a branch and clearly labelled as such.

The contributor can work alone, or form an independent studio cell with other contributors. A studio cell is a small group — two to five people — who take on a larger contribution together. The cell operates under the same contribution brief format as an individual contributor, but the brief can be larger.

10.3 The independent studio cell

A studio cell can be formed around any part of the EROS universe. A cell might focus on the Gift of Thoth, or on the operators, or on the First Resonance characters, or on the liquidity architecture, or on the 3D Universe, or on a community-created corner of the world that does not yet exist.

The cell does not need central permission to form. It needs to register with the Guild, adopt the contribution brief format, and agree to the canon tiers and the evidence rules. Once registered, the cell can produce work and submit it for review.

The cell's work is published under the EROS banner with the cell credited. The cell can grow, split, or dissolve as its members choose. The point is not to create a permanent organisation. The point is to let people make things together.

10.4 The relationship to canon

Parallel work does not automatically become canon. It is classified by tier. Tier 1 work is the source library. Tier 2 work is verified expansion. Tier 3 work is community variation. Tier 4 work is experimental.

A parallel studio cell's work can be Tier 2 if it is checked against the source and approved. It can be Tier 3 if it is a creative interpretation that honours the framework. It can be Tier 4 if it is deliberately divergent. All three are legitimate. The tier determines how the work relates to the rest of the universe, not whether it is good.

10.5 The contribution pathways

There are several pathways a parallel contributor can take:

  • The single task. Pick up a Guild brief, complete it, submit it, see it published. The smallest unit of contribution.
  • The personal project. Take on a larger piece of work — a comic, an audio episode, a visual novel chapter — and produce it under the Guild structure.
  • The studio cell. Form a small group to produce a larger work together.
  • The experimental branch. Produce work that deliberately diverges from the canon, and publish it as a Tier 4 branch.
  • The research contribution. Verify sources, build evidence registers, check claims. Research is a contribution pathway equal to production.

The pathways are not mutually exclusive. A contributor can start with a single task, move to a personal project, form a studio cell, and eventually produce a branch. The system is designed to let contribution grow.

PART ELEVEN: DISTRIBUTION

PART ELEVEN: DISTRIBUTION

11.1 One permanent home, many discovery channels

The EROS website should be the permanent home of the work. YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, audio, and Telegram should distribute and connect people to it.

The principle: Publish everywhere appropriate. Keep the library organised in one place.

11.2 The EROS website

The website should become the central EROS Media experience. Each show receives a dedicated page with:

  • Title and short description
  • Trailer
  • Full episode
  • Short clips
  • Original source books
  • Transcript
  • Relevant diagrams and illustrations
  • Interactive material where useful
  • Evidence and source references
  • A simple viewer challenge
  • A contribution pathway

The existing EROS Corpus and Media pages provide the starting point. The website should be mobile-first, fast, searchable, and easy to navigate. The 3D Universe should be an optional deeper experience, not a requirement for understanding the material.

11.3 YouTube

YouTube should be the main public video channel. Use it for flagship episodes, series playlists, three-to-five-minute explainers, Shorts, production diaries, community discussions, and occasional live Open Calls.

The 20-minute programme remains the flagship format, but not every subject needs 20 minutes. The length should serve the subject. Use audience-retention data and recurring format performance to decide what to produce more of.

11.4 TikTok, Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts

These channels are the front doors. Produce original vertical versions of the strongest moments in the books and episodes.

A short should normally have:

  1. A strong opening question, statement, or visual.
  2. One idea.
  3. A clear demonstration or explanation.
  4. A memorable closing thought.
  5. A route to the full episode or source.

Use captions, readable text, and mobile-safe framing. Do not simply crop a landscape episode and expect it to work as a vertical video.

The short-form examples in the source material include:

  • The Mouth — 30 seconds: "Say SPREAD. Now say SPRAY." A visual demonstration, then an invitation to see the full episode.
  • Inward Is Forwards — 45 seconds: "What if the boundary is part of the explanation?" A question, an animated diagram, and a link to the cosmology.
  • The Web — 45 seconds: "Why might a network of smaller liquidity pools behave differently from one giant pool?" An analogy that leads into the technical explanation.

11.5 Audio and podcast

The books should also become an audio library. Possible formats: narrated book chapters, full audio episodes, short audio explainers, interviews and discussions, production diaries, weekly community reviews.

This is a relatively accessible contribution pathway for people who do not have animation or video skills. A single recorded passage is a complete contribution.

11.6 Telegram and X

Telegram remains the community coordination and distribution environment. Use it for: new releases, production briefs, contributor recruitment, feedback, work-in-progress previews, Open Call submissions, community discussion.

X can be used for public announcements, short extracts, discussion, and directing new audiences to the library.

Platform policies and content restrictions should be checked before publishing token-specific material. The website should always retain the complete, properly contextualised source package.

11.7 The release sequence

The first public release package should be:

Release 1 — The EROS Trailer. A short, visually strong introduction to the world and the library. Deliverables: 90-second trailer, 30-second cut, 15-second cut, vertical versions, website introduction.

Release 2 — The Map. The first complete flagship episode. It explains the four volumes, the four doors, the shows, and the production invitation. Deliverables: full episode, three-to-five-minute overview, short clips, illustrated map, website page, transcript and audio.

Release 3 — Receipts. The first instrument-focused episode. It demonstrates how a viewer can inspect the architecture and distinguish verifiable mechanisms from claims or proposals. Technical data must be checked at recording time.

Release 4 — Inward Is Forwards. The first major cosmology episode. It introduces the EROS world model through strong storytelling and visual explanation, while clearly identifying what is model, hypothesis, evidence, and fiction.

Release 5 — The Open Call. The first public demonstration of the Guild. Show people what they can make, how to contribute, and how the work will be reviewed and published.

This release sequence gives the project both a public face and a working community structure.

PART TWELVE: THE 90-DAY PLAN

PART TWELVE: THE 90-DAY PLAN

The schedule is a practical starting plan. It assumes a small coordinating team and volunteer or part-time contributors, with production pace adjusted to actual capacity.

12.1 Days 1–15 — Establish the foundation

  • Adopt this Master Project as the working blueprint.
  • Confirm the Unified Bible as the current show-writing reference.
  • Reconcile the 29-file register.
  • Audit the source extraction database.
  • Establish the master claim and terminology registers.
  • Confirm the four public doors and 14-show slate.
  • Begin the visual asset register.
  • Define the Guild contribution brief.

Milestone: One coherent production system.

12.2 Days 16–30 — Build the first production package

  • Complete the EROS title and identity direction.
  • Create the Cosmic Egg master reference.
  • Create the four-operator visual reference.
  • Prepare the Show 00 production package.
  • Prepare the trailer production package.
  • Build the first version of the website's show structure.
  • Prepare the first ten small Guild tasks.

Milestone: The community has something tangible to make.

12.3 Days 31–60 — Produce and publish

  • Complete the trailer.
  • Produce Show 00.
  • Produce the first short-form clips.
  • Publish the Map and its source materials.
  • Prepare Show 05 for production.
  • Open the first Guild contribution cycle.
  • Publish the first Open Call.

Milestone: EROS has a functioning public media presence and an active production process.

12.4 Days 61–90 — Establish the rhythm

  • Release Show 05 or its first complete production package.
  • Begin Show 01 production.
  • Expand the visual asset library.
  • Publish further short-form content.
  • Review viewer and contributor feedback.
  • Improve the website and production briefs.
  • Establish the next six-month production schedule.

Milestone: The Guild is producing repeatable work rather than waiting for a central production team.

PART THIRTEEN: MEASURES AND PRINCIPLES

PART THIRTEEN: MEASURES AND PRINCIPLES

13.1 Audience measures

  • Video retention
  • Returning viewers
  • Website visits
  • Episode completion
  • Book and source-page engagement
  • Viewer questions
  • Movement between related shows

13.2 Guild measures

  • Contributors participating
  • Tasks accepted
  • Tasks completed
  • Time taken to complete tasks
  • Number of reusable assets created
  • Number of community productions published
  • Contributors returning for another task

13.3 Library measures

  • Source files extracted
  • Claims classified
  • Contradictions identified and resolved
  • Episodes completed
  • Assets catalogued
  • Books connected to published media

The most important measure is whether each production makes the next production easier.

13.4 Operating principles

  1. The books remain the source material.
  2. The master project provides the production direction.
  3. Every episode has a clear purpose.
  4. Every contributor receives a manageable brief.
  5. Creative freedom is encouraged within clearly stated boundaries.
  6. Evidence and fiction are never silently mixed.
  7. Reusable assets are preferred over unnecessary reinvention.
  8. The website remains the permanent home.
  9. Social platforms are distribution channels, not the source of truth.
  10. Contributors receive clear credit and recognition.
  11. The project should be understandable to newcomers.
  12. The Guild should gradually become capable of operating without constant central intervention.

PART FOURTEEN: THE ASSET REGISTER

PART FOURTEEN: THE ASSET REGISTER

14.1 Structure

Each asset should have one record with these fields:

  • Asset ID (permanent reference, e.g. EROS-VID-001)
  • Asset name (original filename or descriptive title)
  • Media type (image, video, audio, animation, 3D, document)
  • Source (book, website, Telegram, or newly created)
  • Source reference (file, chapter, page, or Telegram message ID)
  • Subject (what the asset depicts or explains)
  • Programme (Instrument, World Model, Mythology, Illumination)
  • Episode (intended episode or possible reuse)
  • Production role (opening, explanation, transition, character, background, ending)
  • Status (Available, Needs review, Needs editing, Missing, New creation)
  • Rights (ownership or permission confirmed / pending)
  • Verification (factual review required / passed / not applicable)
  • Notes (continuity, technical requirements, reuse limits)

14.4 Audio and community material

The Telegram archive records:

  • 350 audio files
  • 161 voice messages
  • 1,047 video files
  • 38 animations
  • 17 stickers

These are useful discovery categories. They should not be assumed to be usable narration or publishable footage. Each requires listening or viewing, source attribution, permission review, and an editorial decision.

14.5 Asset-to-pilot matching

Pilot 01 — The Crack in the Sky. Reuse first: Cosmic Egg, enclosure artwork, relevant diagrams. New material likely required: Atacama setting, Dr. Elara Vance, cinematic sky sequence.

Pilot 02 — The Gods Were Operators. Reuse first: Gods imagery, Thoth imagery, light and bond visuals. New material likely required: consistent operator visual grammar, operator animations, world transitions.

Pilot 03 — The EROS Flywheel. Reuse first: burn animation, bridge clips, charts, community footage. New material likely required: two-vault animation, flywheel sequence, AMM demonstration.

Pilot 04 — The First Resonance. Reuse first: First Resonance artwork, doors, story visuals. New material likely required: Cal, Hana, Owen, Visitor, stone, ledger, and room scenes.

The rule: reuse existing work where it is suitable, but do not force an existing image into a scene simply because it is available.

14.6 New assets to create

Priority 1 — EROS logo and title animation. Consistent opening identity.

Priority 2 — Cosmic Egg master model. Recurring world symbol.

Priority 3 — Four operator visual reference. Consistency across mythology episodes.

Priority 4 — EROS flywheel animation. Explains the central participation thesis.

Priority 5 — Two-vault visual. Explains the on-chain and cultural architecture.

Priority 6 — Cal character reference. Anchors the human story.

Priority 7 — EROS world map. Connects the books and locations.

Priority 8 — Evidence classification graphics. Distinguishes fact, interpretation, hypothesis, and fiction.

Priority 9 — Standard episode title cards. Makes the programme feel like one production.

Priority 10 — End-credit and contributor template. Supports community production.

14.7 Production status definitions

  • READY — file exists, reviewed, rights checked, suitable for use.
  • REVIEW — asset located but still needs visual, factual, or editorial review.
  • EDIT — exists but needs editing, updating, compositing, or re-rendering.
  • MISSING — referenced in the library, but actual media file is not available.
  • NEW — needs to be created from scratch.

---

PART FIFTEEN: THE EXTRACTION FRAMEWORK

PART FIFTEEN: THE EXTRACTION FRAMEWORK

15.1 The universal per-book extraction sheet

For every one of the 29 files, extract these twelve fields into a structured record. This is the atom of the whole system.

  1. Core thesis. One sentence. The single claim the book exists to make. Episode spine. If you cannot state it in one line, the book is not ready for screen.
  1. Opening hook. The most startling question, image, or anomaly in the text. Feeds the 0:00–1:30 hook. Often already written — pull verbatim.
  1. Key concepts (3–7). Each with a one-line definition and a proposed visual metaphor. The 04:00–14:00 teaching block. The visual metaphor is non-negotiable — if a concept has no image, it cannot be animated.
  1. Narrative arc. The book's own problem → discovery → implication sequence. Maps directly onto the 20-minute formula.
  1. Agents / characters. Every named entity: gods, people, forces, the observer, institutions. Role plus one-line description. Feeds the character bible and casting/animation.
  1. Existing visuals. Every diagram, structure description, or imagery already in the HTML. Reuse before inventing. The Torus, Egg, Tree, Bridge already have descriptions — extract them.
  1. Claims register. Every factual assertion, tagged Established / Interpretive / Speculative / Fictional. Feeds the evidence ladder and on-screen credibility icons.
  1. Emotional beats. Where the text aims for awe, curiosity, unease, hope, or resolve. Quote the passage. The 14:00–17:30 implications block and the finale.
  1. Quotable lines. Phrases with rhythm, imagery, or rhetorical force. Narration script and trailer material.
  1. Cross-references. Which other books this one assumes, extends, or contradicts. Prevents duplication across episodes; flags continuity risks.
  1. Cliffhanger potential. The open question the book leaves unresolved. The 19:00–20:00 hand-off to the next episode.
  1. Tone / genre fit. Which of the five treatments (cinematic doc, anime, AI drama, educational animation, motion comic) suits this material. Assigns the book to a strand and a production pipeline.

Deliverable: a 29-row master sheet. This alone will let you write the Television Bible's episode map without reopening a single HTML file.

15.2 The cross-cutting registers

Some assets are more valuable gathered in one place than per book. Build these six registers:

  1. Master glossary. Every coined term (Eros Enclosure, Iteration Codex, resonance, affinity, operator, etc.) with definition, first appearance, variant spellings, and the visual metaphor attached. This becomes the writers' style guide and the on-screen lower-third source.
  1. Visual language inventory. Every recurring symbol — the Egg, the Torus, the Tree, the Bridge, the instruments (EROS, ErosX, 33EROS) — with all descriptions from all books collated in one entry. You need a single canonical description per symbol, because AI-generated assets will drift otherwise.
  1. Character bible. Every named entity (NaUn, Ra-Shen, Thoth, EROS, and any human characters from First Resonance / Eros Stories) with role, attributes, relationships, visual reference, and which strand(s) they appear in. This is what stops Thoth looking different in Episode 5 and Episode 6.
  1. Claim / evidence ledger. One row per factual assertion, tagged by evidence grade and by episode. This is the fact-checker's bible and the source of the on-screen credibility icons. It also protects you legally and reputationally on Men of Renown and Illumination Strategy.
  1. Cosmology / timeline map. A single diagram showing how the books relate conceptually and chronologically: which is foundational, which is a perspective, which is supporting material.
  1. Contradiction log. Where two books disagree, or where a term is used differently. You will find these across 29 files. Log them now so continuity does not break mid-season.

15.3 Strand-specific extraction

Each strand needs one extra layer beyond the universal sheet.

Cosmology (S1): extract the sequence of unfoldings — the exact order in which the model reveals itself (point → torus → lobes → crossover → enclosure → observer). This sequence is the season arc. Also extract the observer's position in each book, because that is your recurring human anchor.

Mythology (S1): extract operator functions — what each god does in the system, not just what they symbolise. The Episode 5 insight ("gods as operators") depends on having each role stated functionally. Also extract the most cinematic scenes already written.

Tokenomics (S2): extract mechanisms as processes — every flow, loop, gate, and condition described as a thing that moves. Then extract parameters (numbers, ratios, thresholds) separately, because they will be visualised, not narrated. Crucially, tag every mechanism Live / Designed / Proposed — this is your Episode 4 credibility safeguard.

Human story (S3): extract real voices — community contributions, testimonials, the emotional "why" passages from We Are With You Eros, Front Door, Open Call. Also extract fictional characters and situations from Eros Stories / Continuity File and keep them clearly separated from documentary material.

Financial documentary (S4): extract primary sources and citations from Illumination Strategy — every chart, date, institution, and source. This strand lives or dies on source transparency. Extract the repricing thesis chain as a step-by-step argument so each episode can advance it one link.

15.4 What to extract specifically for the Television Bible

The Bible needs a subset, formatted for production:

  • Episode map inputs: for each of the 22 episodes, the source passage(s), the hook, the three key concepts, and the cliffhanger — all pulled from the per-book sheets.
  • Visual identity inputs: the canonical description of every recurring symbol (from the visual inventory) plus a colour palette per strand.
  • Evidence policy inputs: the claim ledger, summarised into the four-grade system and the on-screen icon rules.
  • Character sheets: the character bible, reduced to the recurring cast.

15.5 Extract the four pilots first

Do not extract all 29 books to full depth before piloting. Do these four completely, because they test four different pipelines:

Pilot 01 — The Crack in the Sky. Files to extract fully: Living Egg, Eros Enclosure. What you are testing: cinematic CGI + narration; the "model vs data" hook; the Egg visual.

Pilot 02 — The Gods Were Operators. Files to extract fully: Gods of EROS. What you are testing: character animation; operator functions as drama.

Pilot 03 — The EROS Flywheel. Files to extract fully: The Flywheel, Architecture of Participation. What you are testing: 3D educational animation; mechanism-as-motion; Live / Designed / Proposed tagging.

Pilot 04 — The First Resonance. Files to extract fully: First Resonance. What you are testing: cinematic animated drama; human emotional payoff.

Extract these four at full field depth, build the pilots, then extract the remaining 25 using the lessons learned.

15.6 What not to extract

Equally important — leave these in the books:

  • Dense argumentation and repeated justifications. The show demonstrates; it does not argue.
  • Internal caveats and hedging that exist to protect the written text. On screen, the evidence ladder replaces them.
  • Full parameter tables. Visualise the mechanism; do not narrate the spreadsheet.
  • Redundant cross-references. Consolidate once in the glossary rather than repeating per episode.
  • Anything that requires reading to understand. If it cannot be shown or spoken, it does not belong in the extraction.

15.7 The single deliverable

Everything above should produce one structured database — one row per concept, claim, character, and visual — tagged by source file, strand, episode, and evidence grade. That database, not the 29 HTML files, becomes what writers, storyboard artists, and fact-checkers work from.

Build the per-book sheets first (29 rows), then the six cross-cutting registers, then the four pilot extractions. By the time you write the Television Bible, you will be assembling it from structured records rather than re-reading source material — which is exactly how a repeatable production system stays repeatable.

PART SIXTEEN: THE FIRST RELEASE

PART SIXTEEN: THE FIRST RELEASE

16.1 The cold-viewer sequence

The existing production bible recommends a cold-viewer sequence:

Trailer → Show 00: The Map → Show 05: Receipts → viewer choice of world.

This sequence establishes the whole project, explains the instrument, and then allows the viewer to choose the subject that interests them. It is the recommended primary release path.

16.2 Release 1 — The EROS Trailer

A short, visually strong introduction to the world and the library.

Deliverables: 90-second trailer, 30-second cut, 15-second cut, vertical versions, website introduction.

16.3 Release 2 — The Map

The first complete flagship episode. It explains the four volumes, the four doors, the shows, and the production invitation.

Deliverables: Full episode, three-to-five-minute overview, short clips, illustrated map, website page, transcript and audio.

16.4 Release 3 — Receipts

The first instrument-focused episode. It demonstrates how a viewer can inspect the architecture and distinguish verifiable mechanisms from claims or proposals. Technical data must be checked at recording time.

16.5 Release 4 — Inward Is Forwards

The first major cosmology episode. It introduces the EROS world model through strong storytelling and visual explanation, while clearly identifying what is model, hypothesis, evidence, and fiction.

16.6 Release 5 — The Open Call

The first public demonstration of the Guild. Show people what they can make, how to contribute, and how the work will be reviewed and published.

This release sequence gives the project both a public face and a working community structure.
