APPENDIX A: CRAFT — HOW TO MAKE THE THING ONCE YOU HAVE BEEN ASSIGNED IT

APPENDIX A: CRAFT — HOW TO MAKE THE THING ONCE YOU HAVE BEEN ASSIGNED IT

This appendix is for a contributor who has picked up a task and needs to know how to make it well. It is not required reading for the whole community. It is the reference shelf.

A.1 The adaptation thesis

Before writing a single page of any adaptation, write one sentence:

"This adaptation of [BOOK] uses the grammar of [MEDIUM] to make an audience feel [TARGET EXPERIENCE], by centering [CHARACTER / RELATIONSHIP / QUESTION] and letting go of [WHAT YOU ARE DELIBERATELY CUTTING]."

The sentence commits. It names the loss up front, which means it cannot ambush the production in month four.

A.2 The compression math

  • 400-page novel → 100–120-page screenplay: you will cut roughly 70% of events, and keep 100% of the emotional arc.
  • 400-page novel → 6-episode audio season (~3.5 hrs): you can keep more plot but must lose all narration and most minor characters.
  • 400-page novel → graphic novel (180–220 pages): highest fidelity option in visual media, also the slowest and most expensive.
  • 400-page novel → visual novel (8–12 hrs): you can keep almost everything, but must add choice architecture, which means writing new material.
  • Short story (20 pages) → feature: you must expand 5×. The hardest adaptation there is.

A.3 The unfilmable test

List everything in the book that appears to resist adaptation. Sort each item into one of four buckets:

  • Cut — it cannot survive. It was load-bearing in prose only. Let it go.
  • Convert — same information, new language.
  • Externalize — make the interior visible through behavior, object, or another character.
  • Preserve Elsewhere — it belongs in a different extension of the universe.

A.4 The scene machine

Every scene, in every medium, is built from three components:

  • Want — someone wants something right now, in this room. Not their life goal. The thing they want in the next ninety seconds.
  • Obstacle — something prevents it. Another person's want, a social rule, their own body, a lie they have already told.
  • Turn — the scene ends in a different place than it started. If nothing turns, the scene is furniture.

A.5 The subtext ladder

Good dialogue operates at three levels simultaneously:

  • Text — the literal words. The surface request.
  • Subtext — what the speaker means and the other character understands.
  • Metatext — what the scene is really about, which the audience feels but nobody says.

Example: "You should take the umbrella." Text: a practical offer. Subtext: I don't want you to leave, and I can't say that. Metatext: this is the last time I will be able to offer you anything.

A.6 Six ways to adapt interiority

  • Behavior substitution. Replace the thought with a small, specific action that only makes sense if you know the thought.
  • Object transference. The character's relationship to an object carries the feeling.
  • Third-party displacement. The character says the feeling about someone or something else.
  • Sensory anchor. A recurring sensory detail that the audience learns to read as the interior state.
  • Structural rhyme. Two scenes in identical staging, with one detail changed, imply the entire journey between them.
  • Silence. The character does not speak when a lesser character would. The absence is the line.

A.7 Audio drama craft

Audio is the most intimate mass medium ever invented. It arrives in someone's ears, in bed, alone, at 1 a.m. That is exactly the condition under which EROS books are read.

The core rule: every scene must contain at least one silence longer than three seconds. The listener needs those seconds to feel. Take them or the scene will not land.

The format: time-coded scene headings, ambience notes, SFX notes, dialogue with parentheticals that are production instructions, and a silence map.

The design document: every audio episode needs a one-page Audio Design Document with ambience beds, signature SFX, music policy, silence map, and mix notes.

A.8 Comic craft

The gutter — the white space between panels — is the most erotically charged space in any medium. What happens between two panels is imagined by the reader, and imagination is the EROSverse's home territory.

The format: page and panel numbers, shot and angle, content description, dialogue, caption, SFX.

The pacing toolkit: panel size (small = slower, more intimate; large = faster, more spectacular), gutter width (wide = pause; narrow = continuous action), bleed (overwhelm, climax), silent panel (the reader hears the room), page-turn reveal (the single most powerful tool), repeated composition (same shot, changed detail).

The rule: write what is visible. If the script says "she looks sad," the artist will hate you. Write the mouth, the hands, the distance between two bodies, the object in frame.

A.9 Visual novel craft

The core design principle: choices should not change what happens. They should change what it means.

The relationship state model: four variables — Trust, Candor, Desire, Fear. Each scene can move any of them by −2 to +2. Fear is a subtractive variable: players who maximize desire and neglect trust get a scene that is physically intense and emotionally hollow.

The failure mode: the illusion-breaking choice. A choice like "Kiss him / Slap him / Say nothing" where all three lead to the same next line is worse than no choice at all.

A.10 TTRPG craft

The theme-mechanics rule: the rules must mechanically produce the theme. If your game is about the danger of wanting, then wanting must be mechanically dangerous.

Examples:

  • Vulnerability is a risk with a reward. You may add a die to any roll by revealing a secret; the GM keeps the secret and can spend it later.
  • Desire distorts judgment. Every character has a "Pull" — a person or thing. When Pull is in the scene, your highest die is replaced by your lowest.
  • Consent is ongoing and revocable. Any player may call a "Withdraw" at any time; the scene must be renegotiated, and doing so grants an insight.
  • Intimacy builds power. Shared scenes between two characters create a pool both may draw from — but only while both agree.

A.11 Zine craft

The theme must be a question, not a topic. "What is owed to someone you left?" not "Betrayal."

The ordering is the editing. Arrange pieces so they build an emotional arc across the book. Write the ordering before you solicit the pieces, then reorder as needed.

The pitch call template: theme, length, deadline, canon tier, rights, pay, what we want, what we do not want, pitch format. Never ambiguous. If it is unpaid, say so. If it is paid, state the rate.

A.12 Short-form craft

Three formats that work:

  • The Exchange. A single line of dialogue, then silence, then a second line that recontextualizes the first. 7–15 seconds.
  • The Object. One prop from the Sensory Palette, slowly revealed, with a single line of voiceover. 10–20 seconds.
  • The Confession. A character says the thing they cannot say in the books, to camera, once, and the video ends before we see the reaction. 20–45 seconds.

The failure mode: summarizing the book. The worst possible short-form content is "here's what happens in Book 3." Show one feeling so precisely that people need to know where it came from.

APPENDIX B: PROMPT PATTERNS FOR AI-ASSISTED PRODUCTION

APPENDIX B: PROMPT PATTERNS FOR AI-ASSISTED PRODUCTION

Most AI tools summarize because summarization is the safest output. You have to explicitly forbid it and give the model a countable structure.

B.1 The volume contract

Open every generation request with an explicit length and structure contract. Vague requests produce vague, short output.

Pattern: "Produce [N] sections. Each section must contain: [exact required element 1], [exact required element 2], [exact required element 3]. Do not summarize. Do not say 'and so on.' Do not use ellipses to skip content. Do not write 'etc.' Every section must be written in full. If you run out of room, stop at a section boundary and say 'CONTINUE' so I can ask for the next batch. Never compress to finish."

The last two sentences convert an unbounded task into a resumable one, which is the single most effective anti-truncation technique.

B.2 Batch then continue

Pattern: "We are writing a long document. Work in batches of 10 items. For this message, produce Batch 1 (items 1–10) at full length. End your message with the exact line: 'END OF BATCH 1. Reply CONTINUE for items 11–20.' Then stop. Do not begin Batch 2."

B.3 The format lock

Pattern: "Lock to this exact format for every item. Do not vary it, do not abbreviate it, do not combine items: ## [Number]. [Title]. What it is: [2–4 full sentences]. Why it suits EROS: [2–4 full sentences]. Page budget: [specific numbers]. Structure: [6–10 bullet points, each a full sentence]. Workflow: [numbered steps, 6–8, each a full sentence]. Failure mode: [2–3 full sentences]. Exercise: [3–4 full sentences with constraints]. If a section would be shorter than the minimum, write more — do not move on."

B.4 The forbidden list

Pattern: "You are forbidden from using any of these words or phrases: 'essentially,' 'in summary,' 'overall,' 'and more,' 'and so on,' 'etc.,' 'various,' 'several,' 'a range of,' 'such as' (as a substitute for listing). If a sentence would require one of these to be shorter, do not shorten it."

B.5 The canon-feed

Pattern: "Here is the canon you must use. Do not invent facts beyond it. Do not generalize from it. Quote it where relevant. [CANON LEDGER EXCERPT]. Now write [TASK] using only these facts plus what I specify below. If you need a new fact, ask me for it. Do not assume one."

B.6 The draft ladder

Pattern: "Rung 1: beat sheet only. 20 beats, one full sentence each. No dialogue. Rung 2: scene cards. One card per beat. Who wants what, obstacle, turn. Rung 3: full prose draft of scene [N] only. Minimum 1200 words. Rung 4: dialogue pass on the same scene. Cut 25% of words. Same events. Do Rung 1 only. Stop. Wait for my notes."

B.7 The length audit

Pattern: "Audit your own output against the contract. For each section, report the sentence count. List every section below the minimum. Then rewrite ONLY those sections, in full, at the required length. Do not rewrite sections that already meet the minimum."

B.8 The voice lock

Pattern: "Study these three paragraphs from the source book. Identify, in writing: average sentence length, ratio of concrete nouns to abstractions, use of fragments, how interiority is punctuated, the three most frequent sentence openings. Then write [TASK] imitating those measurements exactly. Do not imitate the content. Imitate the measurements."

APPENDIX C: GLOSSARY

APPENDIX C: GLOSSARY

Adaptation thesis. A single sentence stating what the adaptation will make the audience feel and what it will cut to achieve that.

Asset register. The catalogue of existing and required media assets, with status, rights, and episode assignment.

Bridge. The mechanism by which value moves between EROS and the wider ecosystem.

Bridge. Bond. Branch. The three-step vocabulary for the liquidity tree.

Canon hierarchy. The four-tier system — Core Source, Verified Expansion, Community Variation, Experimental Branch — that governs how new work relates to the source library.

Claim ledger. The record of every factual assertion in the library, tagged by evidence grade and source.

Compression math. The conversion ratio between source pages and target-medium pages or minutes.

Cosmic Egg. The master 3D environment and the central visual symbol of the EROS world model. The bounded vessel within which the torus is the geometric reading.

Crossover. The point where the two lobes of the torus meet.

EPISTEMIC LABEL. The classification applied to every factual or conceptual claim: OBSERVED, MODEL, STORY, HYPOTHESIS, PATTERN, OBJECTION, FALSIFIER.

EROS. The bond. The function of cohesion, continuation, and the preservation of relationship across time. Not a character. What happens between things that remain connected without becoming one.

Eros Enclosure. The geometric reading of the Cosmic Egg. The shell, the inner rind, the two lobes, the crossover, the Isotope.

ErosX. The river. One of the three instruments of the Platinum Standard.

Externalize. To render interiority as observable behavior, object, or staging.

Fiction contract. The agreement that fictional events, characters, and institutions remain identifiable as fiction.

Flywheel. The six-stage cycle — Attention, Discovery, Understanding, Participation, Creation, Renewed Attention — that connects the on-chain vault and the cultural vault.

Gutter. The space between comic panels, where the reader's imagination completes the action.

Inner rind. The inhabited inner boundary of the Cosmic Egg.

Isotope. The infinitely approached centre of the torus.

Liquidity Tree. The network of pools, bonds, and branches through which value travels.

Mechanism label. The classification applied to every technical or economic mechanism: LIVE, DESIGN, PROPOSED.

NaUn. The architecture. The function of permission, structure, boundaries, and enduring law. Does not answer, forgive, or intervene. Holds.

Open Call. The community invitation format. The recurring show that demonstrates the Guild in action.

Operators. The four functions of existence: NaUn, Ra-Shen, Thoth, EROS. Not four personalities. Four functions.

Parallel creation. The practice of contributors developing work alongside the central team, in independent studio cells or as individuals, under the Guild structure.

Platinum Standard. The three-instrument architecture — EROS, ErosX, 33EROS — and the proposed transformation paths between them.

Ra-Shen. The stage and force. The function of energy under containment, radiation, movement, and physical expression. The light itself, not the person holding the lamp.

Sensory palette. The fixed list of recurring sensory details that identify the world.

Thoth. The teacher and builder. The function of learning, language, memory, and transmission. A role that can appear through different people.

Torus. The two-lobed geometry of the EROS world model. The geometric reading of the Egg.

Two rails. The separation of Documented History (Rail A) from Mythic and Speculative Archive (Rail B).

Two vaults. The on-chain vault (Vault One) and the cultural vault (Vault Two), connected by the flywheel.

Unfilmable test. The exercise of sorting resistant source material into Cut, Convert, Externalize, or Preserve Elsewhere.

33EROS. The engine. One of the three instruments of the Platinum Standard.

APPENDIX D: THE UNRESOLVED QUESTIONS

APPENDIX D: THE UNRESOLVED QUESTIONS

These are the questions the source material leaves open. They are not problems with this document. They are the decisions that must be made before the production system is fully locked.

D.1 The 14-show slate versus the 22-episode map

The Unified Bible treats the 14-show slate as the working master. The Master Series Bible R contains a 22-episode structure. The relationship between the two has not been fully reconciled.

Options:

  • Present 14 as the master, with the 22 as a historical development plan.
  • Present 22 as the episode map, with 14 as the show slate, and treat shows as containers for multiple episodes.
  • Present both side by side and let the community decide.

Recommendation: present 14 as the master, and treat the 22-episode map as an extension — the 14 shows are the containers, the 22 episodes are the contents. This preserves both without creating a false conflict.

D.2 The six-book versus 29-book extraction discrepancy

The Master Series Bible R claims all 29 books have been fully extracted. The Unified Bible says only six have. The PDFs flag this as a reconciliation issue.

Recommendation: treat the six-book extraction as verified, the 29-book extraction as claimed-but-unverified, and complete the audit before any script rewrites that depend on the extraction.

D.3 The evidence ledger visibility

The MD is the source of truth. The HTML is its visual expression. But the "maximum content" instruction pulls toward exposing everything, including the claim ledger and the contradiction log.

Options:

  • Expose everything in the public HTML.
  • Expose the evidence system as a framework, but keep the specific claim ledger behind a Guild-members section.
  • Expose the claim ledger publicly, because transparency is the point.

Recommendation: expose the evidence system and its labels publicly, expose the claim ledger publicly for the documentary strand, and keep the contradiction log behind a Guild-members section — contradictions are working material, not community-facing content.

D.4 The relationship between the books and the expression system

The books are the source of truth. The expression system is downstream. But the expression system will, over time, produce new canon — new characters, new scenes, new facts about the world that were not in the books.

Options:

  • The expression system never produces new canon; it only adapts what exists.
  • The expression system can produce new canon, which is then approved by the Canon Council and added to the World Bible.
  • The expression system produces new canon only in designated open canon spaces.

Recommendation: the second option. The expression system should be able to produce new canon, because otherwise the universe cannot grow. But the production of new canon should be a deliberate, logged, approved act, not an accident.

D.5 The measure of success

The measures in Part Thirteen are a starting point. But the question of what "success" means for the EROS project is not fully answered.

The tentative answer: success is when a person who has never read an EROS book watches a 20-minute episode, understands one idea from the books, and wants to read more. Everything else — views, engagement, token price, community size — is downstream of that.

If the expression system produces that outcome, it is doing its job. If it does not, no amount of production polish will compensate.

---

THE FINAL DIRECTION

The EROS books should not remain a collection of documents that people have to discover and interpret individually. They should become a connected experience.

Someone might first see a 30-second video. They might then watch a programme, explore a diagram, read a chapter, listen to an audio story, or join a discussion. Someone else might arrive as an illustrator, an animator, a researcher, a programmer, or a storyteller. Both should find a place in the same system.

The books provide the material. The series provides the narrative structure. The media platforms provide reach. The website provides continuity. The Guild provides the means to create. And the community gives the project its living expression.

We are not asking the community to invent EROS from scratch. We are giving them an organised world to interpret, explain, illustrate, test, and build upon.

The first task is not to produce everything. It is to make the first complete example of the system — and then make it easy for others to repeat.

One library. Many doors. One Guild.

Inward is forwards.

If you do not own it, you're not in it.

---

Master Project & Guild Blueprint

EROS

One library. A world to enter. A community to build.

Crypto first. Story second. Extraction never. Inward is forwards. If you do not own it, you’re not in it.

Creation has only just begun. The books are written. The next work is expression, meetings, and making — together.

1. The mission

EROS already has a substantial body of written work: cosmology, mythology, language, tokenomics, economic architecture, fiction, community philosophy, and immersive-world concepts.

The books have been written. The next task is to give them a life beyond the page — a connected publishing, entertainment, and creative ecosystem that:

  • Makes the books accessible to people who will never read every volume
  • Communicates difficult ideas through story, visual, demonstration, and explanation
  • Gives each book a place in a larger ErosVerse
  • Creates a permanent, navigable online home
  • Uses modern platforms to reach new audiences
  • Gives the community a practical structure for its own productions
  • Builds a growing archive that can be reused and improved
We are not only making a television series. We are building the EROS expression system — so the written library becomes video, animation, documentary, comics, audio, interactive work, and community-created pieces. Architecture and standards from the centre; life from the Guild.

Central operating idea: one library, many doors, one Creative Guild.

Audience path: Notice → Understand → Explore → Verify → Participate → Create → Share.

2. The path (not the pile)

Do not make newcomers understand the whole universe before they can enter. Give them a small number of clear doors and a repeatable order.

  2. Garden of Eros — the meaning map of the whole

  4. Architecture of Participation — the plan structure
  5. Liquidity Tree — bridge, bond, branch

Lived rooms

Telegram and X Spaces are not side channels. They are rooms of the ErosVerse: Plan · Build · Story.

Weekly cadence. Theme from the books. One concrete ask. Recap with links.

Attention is the spark. Community is the force.

5. First release sequence

Recommended cold-viewer path — subject to real production readiness:

  1. EROS sting / trailer — identity, then Start Here
  2. Show 00 — THE MAP — orientation to doors and slate
  3. Show 05 — RECEIPTS — instrument, LIVE vs DESIGN vs PROPOSED
  4. Show 01 — INWARD IS FORWARDS — cosmology with model/story labels
  5. Show 13 — THE OPEN CALL — Guild invitation with real tasks
Flagship episodes target about twenty minutes and roughly 2,300 spoken words. The rest is picture, music, and silence. Length should serve the subject — not every idea needs twenty minutes.

6. The Creative Guild

The Guild is how the community produces without waiting for one central studio. Parallel work and fractal branches are expected. The centre provides architecture, standards, examples, and coordination.

Seven studios

Writers & Story

Scripts, dialogue, narration, short copy

Visual Design

Identity, diagrams, thumbnails, character sheets

Animation & Motion

2D/3D, explainers, scene assembly

Sound & Voice

Narration, music direction, cleanup

Research & Verification

Claims, citations, on-chain checks

Web & Interactive

Pages, diagrams, archive, accessibility

Publishing & Community

Captions, releases, credits, feedback

Every task brief must include

  • Task title and why it matters
  • Show / episode / source
  • Exact deliverable and format
  • References and constraints (including epistemic labels)
  • Acceptance criteria
  • Credit / attribution
  • Where the finished work is stored

Example first tasks

  • One Cosmic Egg reference illustration
  • Four-operator symbol sheet
  • 10-second toroidal motion test
  • One vertical short from an approved beat
  • One narrated passage from First Resonance
  • Interactive diagram for the Liquidity Tree
  • Verify one primary source for Footprints
  • Subtitles for Show 00
  • Open Call submission page component

No one needs to build an entire show to contribute. One bounded task, reviewed, credited, published into the library.

7. Production grammar (non-negotiable)

Epistemic chips on screen

OBSERVED checkable measurement or record · MODEL axiom the books state · STORY dramatised or mythic · HYPOTHESIS soft, labelled

Mechanism badges

LIVE on-chain today · DESIGN arrangement of existing pieces · PROPOSED not deployed

Token contract, fixed supply, fee split, burn address 0x…0369, and pools are discussed as LIVE only when freshly verified. ErosX, 33EROS, and transform paths stay PROPOSED until deployed.

Two rails

  • Rail A — Documented history (Illumination / Footprints): primary sources, dates, competing explanations
  • Rail B — Mythic / speculative archive (Masks, Continuity fiction): explicit fiction contract; never used as evidence for Rail A

Four-tier canon

  1. Tier 1 — Core source HTML and verified on-chain facts
  2. Tier 2 — Scripts and assets consistency-checked against Tier 1
  3. Tier 3 — Community variations that honour Egg laws and the bond test
  4. Tier 4 — Experimental branches, labelled, not silently merged
House style: warm, intelligent, unhurried, self-correcting. Sensationalise the question — not the evidence. Crypto first. Story second. Extraction never.

8. Distribution

  • Website — permanent home, four doors, show pages, sources, Guild entry
  • YouTube — principal long-form and playlists
  • Shorts / Reels / TikTok — discovery; one idea per vertical; captions; route back to library
  • Audio — narrated chapters and talk formats where vision is not required
  • Telegram & X — coordination, Spaces, briefs, previews — not the only archive

Hub-and-spoke: publish widely; keep the library organised in one place.
